News.title: Andy Burnham admits Britain can’t afford more damaging hikes in Budget and Labour must get ‘balance’ right
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has signalled Britain can’t afford another tax-raising Budget.

He said Labour has to be “conscious” of more damaging hikes and must get the “balance” right.



It came after the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said UK growth will slow next year.

The PM was quizzed on whether the balance between taxing wealth and taxing income is right and whether it will be addressed at the October Budget.



Burnham said: “We have two budgets in 2024 and 2025 and we have to be conscious of the extent to which we have raised revenue. And we have to make sure we get the balance right.”

Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves raised taxes including a national insurance raid on employers and a three-year freeze on income tax thresholds.



Meanwhile, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development report comes just weeks before Chancellor John Healey delivers his Budget where he may need to find £15 billion.

Fresh forecasts show growth of just 1 per cent next year which is a slowdown from the 1.1 per cent predicted in June.

But UK growth for this year has nudged up 0.2 per cent to 1.1 per cent.

They are now expecting inflation to slow down to 2.6 per cent but this is higher than the 2.4 per cent predicted earlier in the summer. The Bank of England target is 2 per cent.



They also say that the Bank of England may be forced to cut interest rates to boost growth.

The OECD latest outlook pointed to “increasingly important risk” to the world economy if debt and deficit levels weren’t brought down.

Separately, IMF boss Kristalina Georgieva said economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven”.

She added that governments had taken “no action to contain that service cost”.

Treasury minister Emma Reynolds said: “Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience.”



Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “The OECD have downgraded the UK’s growth for 2027 to just a third of the average growth rate of the G20.

“We can and should aspire to do much better.”

News.title: Fears of Brexit betrayal after Sir Tony Blair demands Burnham plots a return to EU within a decade
News.content:
Next

SIR Tony Blair has demanded Andy Burnham plots a return to the EU within a decade – declaring “everything” should be on the table.

The intervention has sparked fears of a Brexit betrayal as it comes days after Mr Burnham did not rule out pledging to rejoin the bloc in a future manifesto.



Sir Tony called for a pledge to rejoin a reformed Europe to be put at the heart of the Government’s ten-year plan.

The former PM claimed Brits would vote differently if the 2016 Brexit referendum was held again today and that the promised benefits of leaving the EU had “not materialised”.



The comments are contained in the foreword to a major new report by the Tony Blair Institute setting out a new blueprint for Britain’s relationship with Brussels.

The TBI argued the Prime Minister should work towards rejoining a “significantly reformed” EU over the next decade and drop Labour’s red lines.

Free movement, payments to Brussels, the Single Market and customs union should all be considered again, it said.

Sir Tony wrote: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table, but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.”

The report said ending free movement “deserves to be examined again” and argued it could help Britain secure much deeper access to the Single Market.

Britain should also be willing to follow common EU rules and make financial contributions where ministers decide the benefits are worth it, the report added..



But Sir Tony made clear his proposed EU comeback is conditional on Brussels changing too.

He said he wanted a Europe on a “credible path to reform” on its economy, defence, immigration and the way it operates.

Sir Tony wrote: “We should be clear that we want back into a formal relationship with the EU. But it must be a Europe on a credible path to reform, a Europe of nation states, a Europe capable of being a genuine global power.”

The Tories last night insisted Labour “should stop trying to turn back the clock and instead focus on setting out serious proposals for the future”.

Shadow Cabinet Office Minister Mike Wood blasted: “Andy Burnham has left the door open to rejoining the EU and now Tony Blair is piling the pressure on him to drag us back into the bloc.”



A Reform UK spokesman also said: “Tony Blair needs to accept he lost this battle long ago. And he should know better than anyone that Brussels has never reformed and never will.

“Britain voted to leave the European Union, and we should get on with making Brexit work rather than endlessly discussing how to reverse it.”

News.title: How an island paradise 6,000 miles from UK became vital to Western security after Trump slammed ‘terrible’ Chagos deal
News.content:
Next

PALM-fringed specks in the shimmering Indian Ocean, the Chagos Islands are a tropical paradise that at first glance appear ripe for tourism.

It is easy to imagine their white, sandy beaches becoming crowded with luxury honeymooners’ hotels and scuba-diving schools.



Yet the British archipelago in crystal-blue seas will greet no holidaymakers any time soon.

For as Donald Trump made clear to PM Andy Burnham on Tuesday, the islands are one of the most strategically important pieces of military real estate on Earth.



That is why the US President scuppered UK plans to hand over sovereignty of the islands to Mauritius, telling the Prime Minister the policy was “terrible”.

So why are the Chagos so vital to Western security? And why did Britain strike a deal to give them away to Mauritius in the first place?



Almost 6,000 miles from the UK, the cluster of 60 islands is a relic of Britain’s imperial past.

They form seven ring-shaped coral atolls and have been under British control since 1814.

They were administered from Mauritius, 1,250 miles away from Chagos, when it was a British colony.

In 1942, the RAF opened a base on the largest island, Diego Garcia, to allow war planes to hunt for German and Japanese submarines.



Its mid Indian Ocean location between Africa and Asia led it to be likened to a static and unsinkable aircraft carrier.

In 1965, Britain separated the islands from Mauritius — to which it paid £3million in compensation — and established the British Indian Ocean Territory.

Three years later, Mauritius gained independence from the UK, leaving the Chagos Islands under British administration.



The US had pushed for the deal as it was keen to put a military base on Diego Garcia.

As part of the agreement, the UK promised to cede the islands to Mauritius when they were no longer required for defence purposes.

A joint US-UK military base was built on Diego Garcia in the Seventies, leading to the forced removal by the ­British government of Chagossians who lived there.

The base became a cornerstone of the special relationship between Britain and the US.

During the Cold War, Admiral Sergey Gorshkov, Commander-in-Chief of the Soviet Union’s Navy, said: “Diego Garcia is a dagger pointed at the heart of the Indian Ocean.”



The geographic importance of the Chagos was underlined in 1979 when 66 Americans were taken hostage by Iranian revolutionaries.

Under pressure to keep oil flowing through the Persian Gulf, the US built a 12,000-foot-long runway for its heavy bombers on Diego Garcia.

A deep-water pier — suitable for refuelling and resupplying US and UK aircraft carriers and submarines — was also constructed.



Diego Garcia was a key launch pad for US air operations in the 1991 Gulf War, the 2003 Iraq War and targeting the Taliban and al Qaeda in Afghanistan.

Today, its airfield hosts US long-range bombers the B-2 Spirit and B-52 Stratofortress, as well as C-17 Globemaster transporters and P-8 Poseidon spy planes.

In 2024 and 2025, the US used the Chagos to launch bombing against the Houthis in Yemen. Its deep-water port remains a key resupply hub for vessels deployed in the Indo-Pacific.

The Chagos’s role as a vital intelligence hub is less well known.

Surveillance equipment there gathers intelligence, thwarts terrorist attacks and protects satellites.



Monitoring gear on Diego Garcia is used to detect if countries are testing nuclear weapons.

And it is one of just four locations in the world with a ground antenna that maintains the accuracy of GPS for civilian phone users and the military.

Little wonder, then, that Trump wants its sovereignty to remain with key ally Britain.



Yet in 2019, the UN’s highest court, the International Court of Justice, ruled British sovereignty over the islands was illegal.

It was only an advisory ruling, but the UN General Assembly voted to back a motion that Britain should withdraw within six months.

While the UK failed to comply, it left a cloud of uncertainty over ownership of the remote islands.

In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer’s government agreed to hand the islands to Mauritius — a Chinese ally — and then lease back Diego Garcia for £35billion over 99 years.

The US initially backed the deal, before Trump urged Britain not to “give away Diego Garcia”.



Then came the Iran War. Starmer at first refused to allow the US the use of UK bases for bombing sorties.

It meant US heavy bombers had to use a base in Missouri to launch raids on Iran.

Then, a month into the war, Britain reversed its decision as Iran attacked Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes and stifled the world economy.

Iran responded by launching at least two intercontinental ballistic missiles at Diego Garcia, which failed in flight or were intercepted.

Yet the mullahs had highlighted just how important the Chagos are to Western defences.



On Tuesday, Trump gave Andy Burnham a lesson in superpower might.

Meeting on the fringes of the UN General Assembly, he told the PM the Chagos handover was a “terrible deal”.

The President added: “You know, we had to send our B2 bombers . . . back to Missouri, as opposed to flying for a short period of time. It’s amazing how strategic it is and I think the Prime Minister is going to be looking at it.”

Burnham then replied: “Yep.”

Yesterday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said handover plans were on hold, adding: “We’re not going to go ahead without the Americans.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Now, Burnham, who has signalled he wants to concentrate on domestic affairs, may have to wrangle a new deal the US is happy with.

For the sake of Western security, sun loungers won’t be appearing on the Chagos beaches just yet.

News.title: Trump gives Xi a supersonic bomber flyover & fighter jet guard as he welcomes Chinese dictator for high-stakes visit
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi Jinping as the Chinese leader arrived in the US for high-stakes talks.

The Beijing dictator was welcomed with great fanfare as he landed before exchanging smiles and handshakes with his American counterpart.



A sprawling military procession with soldiers and fighter jets was organised in front of a huge 100ft red carpet during the lavish reception in Maryland.

B-1 bombers roared as they swooped over Joint Base Andrews to celebrate the Chinese president’s arrival.



The US president saluted while Xi remained stone-faced during the deafening flyover.

Trump made the unusual decision to greet Xi at the air base for the dramatic welcome ceremony – despite usually meeting world leaders at the White House.

The two heads of state are set to discuss a range of issues during the crunch summit – including Iran, AI, Ukraine and Taiwan.

A major sticking point was a trade truce agreed in October 2025 which was set to expire in November.



But the two sides have already announced that it has been extended until January.

The three-day trip marks Xi’s first visit to Washington since 2015 when he was received by Barack Obama.

Trump and Xi were previously locked in a bitter on-and-off trade war before Beijing and Washington reached a truce last year following face-to-face discussions in South Korea.



The truce in October 2025 saw Washington suspending tariff increases on Chinese goods as Beijing agreed to pull back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing.

Today’s historic trip comes after Trump travelled to Beijing back in May for a superpower summit.

Both leaders played nice during the visit as Xi even hailed US-China relations as “generally” good.



It comes after reports claimed Xi is rapidly expanding China’s nuclear weapons scheme – with seven secret sites being uncovered.

Satellite images showed the suspected rebuilding of nuke sites scattered across China.

Beijing currently has the third most nuclear warheads behind Russia and the US.

It also comes as Xi remains tight-lipped on his plans for Taiwan – but refuses to rule out using force to take it.

He has repeatedly vowed to take back the island nation by any means necessary – sparking fears of a full-scale invasion.



Speculation has also been mounting about Xi’s health.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Chinese leader is set to claim a fourth term in power next year – with no successor lined up to take the throne.

News.title: Activist who took three lambs from Sandringham wanted King to ‘open his eyes’ to reality of sheep farming
News.content:
Next

AN activist who took three lambs from the King’s Sandringham estate told a court she hoped to “open his eyes” to the reality of sheep farming.

Rosa Sharkey, 26, wore a pink Animal Rising T-shirt as she took the animals.



She was joined by fellow animal rights activists Sarah Foy, also 26, and 37-year-old Rose Patterson for the stunt at Appleton Farm, ­Norfolk, in May 2023.

The trio took the lambs to a sanctuary.



They later reported themselves to police after failing to interest a cop on duty outside Windsor Castle.

In a statement they said King Charles “would have consented to the lambs’ rescue” and they had concerns for their welfare.

Sharkey told Norwich crown court she took the sheep and had “no intention of giving them back”.

She said the King “says he’s an environmentalist and an animal lover”.

She went on: “The reality of sheep farming is quite hidden away. We hoped it would open his eyes to that.”

Sharkey, of Brighton, Foy, of Alfreton, Derbys, and Patterson, from Homerton, East London, deny theft.



The trial continues.

News.title: Far-right activist Danny Tommo arrested a day after ‘slashing migrant boat as it crossed Channel’
News.content:
Next

FAR-right activist Danny Tommo has been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, according to a video he posted this evening.

Tommo is Tommy Robinson’s right-hand man and has rallied hundreds of balaclava-clad supporters to descend on the south coast for anti-migrant protests.



The 37-year-old, whose real name is Daniel Thomas, was reportedly pounced on by cops at a BP petrol station as unmarked police cars surrounded a vehicle he was in.

Dramatic footage uploaded to his YouTube channel appears to show the moment officers swooped in to arrest him.



Tommo can be seen getting out of his car as police approach.

He can then be heard saying: “Yep okay, okay, if I can just speak to my kids, I’m trying to say goodbye to my kids.”



An officer tells him: “At this moment in time we have information to suggest that you have been involved in criminal damage.”

Another officer can then be heard saying “let’s go, let’s go” as Tommo is placed in handcuffs.

The arrest came after cops said they were investigating an incident in the Channel in which a dinghy was allegedly slashed with a blade while a rescue worker was onboard.

The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy.



They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area.

They were then transferred to a UK Border Force vessel and taken to Dover for processing.

Tommo had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.

The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and starting to slash at the side of the migrant boat.

There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille Liberté.



Tommy Robinson today claimed on X that Tommo had been arrested for “criminal damage” and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.

He said the arrest was linked to Tommo “trying to stop the invasion of our country”.

The exact circumstances of the Channel incident and the allegations against Tommo have not been established in court.

Cops have not yet publicly confirmed the arrest or provided further details about the investigation.

News.title: Lonely widow of tech tycoon says ‘male escort scammed her out of £4.5m in ruthless plan’ after she fell in love
News.content:
'MILKED FOR MILLIONS' Lonely widow of tech tycoon says ‘male escort scammed her out of £4.5m in ruthless plan’ after she fell in love







Next

THE widow of a tech tycoon has claimed she was scammed out of £4.5million by a male escort she fell in love with after the death of her husband, court documents show.

Marianne Flippo, 49, has accused Greggory Starr, 38, of “taking advantage of a grieving and ailing widow”, according to a New York lawsuit.



She claims he enacted “a ruthless plan to steal millions of dollars” from her while she was vulnerable following the death of her partner, according to the lawsuit.

The widow claims in court docs she was on potent opioids following surgery and was grieving her husband of 28 years – Roblox programmer Chad Flippo – when Starr allegedly scammed her.



Flippo has alleged Starr convinced her to pay his agency £7million so he could be “freed” and become her exclusive boyfriend, according to the lawsuit.

She alleged she initially coughed up £20,000 to his firm Cowboys 4 Angels for Starr’s translation services during a holiday in Italy in 2024.



As their relationship became increasingly romantic, Starr and his agent Bridget Collins, allegedly told Flippo she needed to pay them £7million in order for Starr to become her one and only love, according to the complaint.

Flippo claims in the lawsuit she was “pressured by Starr and Collins” to sign the exit agreement.



She allegedly handed over £4.5million but claims her decision was affected by her vulnerable emotional state due to the loss of her husband in February.

The widow claimed the pair convinced her to drink alcohol before signing Starr’s “exit agreement”.

In the lawsuit, she claims she was impaired by “multiple prescription medications as well as five alcoholic drinks”.

Flippo’s lawyer, Larry Hutcher, has also said in an affirmation that she was suffering with “Stockholm syndrome” and that Starr had a “Svengali-like control” over her, the Daily Mail reported.

The Sun has approached Starr and Cowboys 4 Angels for comment.



Flippo’s late husband was “an extremely successful computer programmer who made a fortune programming for, as well as creating and patenting inventions related to, the popular online game Roblox”, according to the complaint.

His widow is said to have inherited a “large fortune” following his suicide, the lawsuit says.

But his sudden death “devastated Marianne and shattered her world”, the complaint claims.

She “understandably struggled to cope with the loss”, it adds.

Her difficulties were allegedly “exacerbated” by Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a disease which impacts the body’s connective tissues and shortens life expectancy to around 50 years old.



It also increases sensitivity to alcohol and medications.

Four months after her husband’s tragic death, Flippo went on holiday to Italy but was “nervous about traveling internationally”, according to her complaint.

One of Chad’s former colleagues contacted Cowboys 4 Angels on her behalf, before the agency allegedly paired her with Starr – an Italian speaker who could “assist her on the trip”.

Flippo claims she was not aware that C4A was an escort service at the time.

She says she hired Starr “purely for assistance on her trip”, according to the complaint.



During the trip, Starr, who reportedly had his own room, made several advances on Flippo, the complaint says.

But she turned these down as she was still mourning her husband, it adds.

The lawsuit also says that Flippo had no contact with Starr when she returned home from the trip – until Cowboys 4 Angels started ringing her.

In these calls, they allegedly told the widow that Starr missed her and wanted to talk to her.

He then allegedly “wormed” his way back into her life – in the knowledge she was wealthy and vulnerable, the lawsuit claims.



The lawsuit states Flippo was convinced to keep paying the agency so she could spend more time with him.

She allegedly ended up paying £110,000 to date him exclusively after Starr demanded this sum be paid.

Starr then further integrated himself into her life, the lawsuit says.

He eventually allegedly asked her to pay him the multimillion-dollar fee to free him from his agency.

Flippo’s lawsuit claims that the £7million was never needed to free Starr from his contract, and that it was all part of an elaborate scam.



It requests that the £4.5million sum be paid back by Cowboys 4 Angels.

News.title: Andy Burnham must get a grip on cost of living or football fans won’t be able to enjoy a beer at games
News.content:
Small beer, PM







Next

ANDY Burnham will have football fans cheering over his plan to kick the 41-year-old stadium booze ban into touch.

Many will agree that the game and its facilities have improved dramatically since the law was changed to combat hooliganism.

For some time, fans have been asking why they are allowed to enjoy a drink at other sporting events but not while watching their football team.



The new PM has been hopelessly out of touch on other issues, notably his onslaught against anybody who enjoys a visit to the high street bookies. But this is a long overdue move — presuming it actually happens.



What really matters, though, is the tough stuff.

With families struggling to pay household bills, mounting concerns over illegal migration and serious questions about our defence capability, the problems are piled high.

Burnham’s first nine weeks in power have been defined by feelgood politics — easy, popular wins which avoid hard decisions or confrontations.



Give football fans the right to enjoy a pint, by all means.

But while they raise their glasses, perhaps our PM should raise his sights.

Unless he gets a grip on the cost of living, most won’t be able to afford a beer anyway.

Kemi sense

TRUE leadership is all about backbone and Kemi Badenoch has shown she’s got plenty of it by coming up with a decisive plan to cut the bloated welfare bill.



Her commonsense blueprint to get Britain back to work is exactly the kind of tough love this country needs.

It strikes the right balance between providing a safety net for those who fall on difficult times and giving the workshy a clear incentive to get a job.

The Conservative leader’s proposal will bring much-needed fairness to the system — supporting those who have worked and paid their taxes, and limiting benefits for those who see them as a lifestyle choice.

Her message is clear: reward the workers, support the needy and end the free ride.

This isn’t just common sense — it’s the courage Britain has been waiting for.



Men applause

BOFFINS are finally tackling the two things most men have worried about since puberty.

They are close to developing a pill to avoid making unplanned babies and a jab to stop hair loss.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The future of men’s health is certainly looking bright.

Whatever next? A vaccine against man flu and a cure for the male inability to find anything in the fridge, perhaps?

News.title: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
News.content:
Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.

Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

News.title: What video footage tells us about RAF training jet crash
News.content:
A video of the crash shared on social media appears to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives, crashes and bursts into flames.

The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss residential properties.

Kay - who hosts the BBC's Security Brief - described footage of the pilots ejecting being caught on camera as "quite remarkable" and said the pilots' ejection seat was "one of the big lifesavers in this whole story".

He said there are two options for ejection that can be taken in a T2 jet - which usually involves an experienced pilot trainer and a student.

One option involves both pilots ejecting individually by pulling a black and yellow ring placed between their legs on the jet, the second option is called "command ejection" where one pilot ejects both seats, with whoever sitting at the back going first.

According to Kay, once the pilot decides to eject the seats, it sets off a miniature detonation cord (MDC), a thin explosive line that is used to shatter the canopy of a jet in the event of an emergency.

"The aircraft seat is designed for the pilot to be able to eject at zero speed and zero height, and that will allow enough time for the parachute to inflate, and then the pilots hit the ground," he added.

"As far as I'm aware this is the first known case of this variant, the T2, ejecting pilots out of it," he said, adding that the safety record for these jets is "obviously very good".

News.title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
News.content:
The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.

The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".

It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.

It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".

The squadron will protect British satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the MoD said.

In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy Â£1.4bn a day.

"Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said.

"We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."

Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said the threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".

A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head of the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week".

The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".

Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites.

Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space.

However, Washington has already accused both Russia and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.

News.title: Home secretary says undetected migrant landings 'unacceptable'
News.content:
The Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted.

Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday.

Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe.

Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought.

News.title: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
News.content:
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".

The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.

Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.

The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".

The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.

Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.

Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.

Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.

Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.

"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.

The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.

A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.

News.title: Family tribute to 'devoted' mum and 'precious' children who died in fire
News.content:
The family of a mother and three children who died in a house fire have said they are experiencing an "unimaginable" loss.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, 8, and Prudence, 7, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of Tuesday.

Paying tribute, their relatives said they had been left "heartbroken" and the loss would be "felt forever".

The statement added that "Elisha was a devoted and loving mother" and "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure".

The family said they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence".

"Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, auntie, niece and cousin," they said.

"She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us."

News.title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
News.content:
The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around Â£538m a year.

Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.

Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.

The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".

For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.

Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.

The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair".

"The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said.

"Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."

However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided".

"Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said.

"We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."

Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.

The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.

The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to Â£408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

News.title: Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school
News.content:
New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.

The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.

A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.

Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.

Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.

The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels which colleges are teaching from autumn 2026, and T-levels.

The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications.

News.title: RAF pauses fighter jet training after two pilots eject from plane before crash
News.content:
High-speed Hawk fighter jet training has been "temporarily" paused as a "precautionary measure", the RAF has said, after two of its pilots ejected and parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed, narrowly missing homes.

The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley base on Anglesey when it plummeted to the ground at nearby Pencarnisiog.

North Wales Police said the pilots, who had been flying a training aircraft, were being treated for minor injuries.

The RAF said it had decided to pause Hawk operations whilst investigations are ongoing.

Eye witnesses described how the plane came down near village homes, with debris ending up near a caravan site.

A video of the crash shared on social media appears to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives, crashes and bursts into flames

The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss residential properties.

The Hawk T1, and newer T2 versions are transonic, two-seat training aircrafts used to train fast jet pilots.

The BBC understands the Red Arrows, based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1.

However, they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend in any event. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted.

News.title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
News.content:
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of Â£101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.

In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".

"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."

Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.

He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.

News.title: Police examine video of anti-migrant activist slashing dinghy with knife
News.content:
Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel.

The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area. They were then transferred to a UK Border Force vessel and taken to Dover for processing.

Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.

The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and starting to slash at the side of the migrant boat.

There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille LibertÃ©.

As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Thomas shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."

Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat.

"Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat."

It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat.

"We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Thomas told his followers.

Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting".

News.title: Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios
News.content:
The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios.

Common Bond emailed customers announcing its locations, all of which are currently in London, were closed "until further notice".

The firm describes itself as a wellness collective and charges Â£2,400 for 12 months of unlimited classes. It also runs Reformcore and Triyoga brands and said in August last year it had ten sites.

Its website is no longer publicly accessible. The BBC has contacted Common Bond for comment.

The email sent to customers on Wednesday seen by the BBC said: "We're sorry to let you know that all Common Bond studios are closed until further notice.

"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and disruption this may cause . We understand this is frustrating, and we appreciate your patience while we work through this."

Instructors have told the BBC they were told last week they would not be paid on time and that they only found out about the studios closures from the Wednesday email.

One instructor said she and her colleagues were told their pay would be delayed on the day it was due on 14 August.

She said: "In good faith, I continued to teach my classes without any news on when or if payment would be made. I have heard absolutely nothing since."

News.title: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
News.content:
The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.

The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.

That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC that Britain and the US needed to reduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world.

The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%.

However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%.

Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost".

"[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.

Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside an unexpected surge in government borrowing in August has added to the pressure on Healey.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK's high level of borrowing had left it "over-exposed" to global shocks.

However, he said he stood by his point - made a year ago - that Britain should be less "in hock" to investors in the bond markets. At the time, the comments spooked investors due to fears he was calling for spending restraints to be eased.

Burnham has made easing the cost-of-living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence.

He and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, and stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, the OECD said.

Budget airline Ryanair will put up prices next summer as a result of persistently higher oil prices. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said ticket prices will be "materially higher", adding that carriers are in an "almost unprecedented" situation.

Ryanair's fuel bill could jump by $1.5bn (Â£1.1bn) next year to $7.5bn, he said.

Risks to the global economy include weaker-than-expected returns on AI investment and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.

Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area.

Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added.

In addition, tariffs and export restrictions on trade continue to add to uncertainty, it said. New US tariffs from July as part of the Trump administration's ongoing volatile trade policy have raised its effective tariff rate by 1%.

News.title: Man died of cardiac arrest on flight, inquest told
News.content:
A British man who died on board a Singapore Airlines flight suffered a cardiac arrest after the plane was hit by severe turbulence, an inquest has been told.

Geoff Kitchen, from Thornbury in South Gloucestershire, died on 21 May 2024 after the Boeing 777 plane travelling from London Heathrow to Singapore encountered a sudden drop in altitude near the south western region of Myanmar.

The plane was later diverted to Bangkok, Thailand, where the 73-year-old was pronounced dead.

Dr Peter Harrowing, assistant coroner for Avon, said: "I am satisfied that it was the physiological effect of the aircraft turbulence which precipitated the cardiac arrest and ultimately Geoff's demise."

Harrowing reached the narrative conclusion into Kitchen's death at a hearing at Avon Coroners' Court earlier.

He told the inquest Kitchen, who had a history of coronary artery disease, had also been "thrown from his seat and landed on an adjacent passenger" during the incident.

News.title: Police worker jailed after death of boy in her care
News.content:
A woman who worked at Nottinghamshire Police has been jailed after the death of a nine-year-old boy in her care.

Catherine Walker, 47, was the legal guardian of the boy, who was found unresponsive in his bedroom in Warsop, Nottinghamshire, on 16 December 2024. Despite the efforts of paramedics and people at the scene, the boy died in hospital.

The force said an investigation found "clear mistreatment of the boy over a prolonged period of time".

Walker, of Appleton Street in Warsop, was jailed for six years at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday after pleading guilty to two counts of assault/ill-treat/neglect/abandon a child/young person to cause unnecessary suffering/injury.

The force, which has not revealed what Walker's role was, said her former husband was the boy's primary carer and had been mainly responsible for his treatment.

He died shortly after the boy's death, police added.

News.title: On-the-run killer who absconded after father's funeral arrested
News.content:
A man who was convicted of murder and has been unlawfully at large for over a week has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.

Gary Anderson, 29, was jailed for life in 2023, alongside his brother, for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry.

He was on temporary release from prison to attend his father's funeral when he absconded.

He was arrested on Wednesday by An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na (Irish police) at a property in the town of Buncrana in County Donegal.

Karol Kelly's sister had said the family felt "let down" by the justice system after learning that he was on the run.

The Justice Minister, Naomi Long, welcomed Anderson's arrest.

She said she hopes the arrest "goes some way towards alleviating the anxiety and uncertainty" that Karol Kelly's family have experienced.

Long is due to meet the family later this week.

She added that she recognises that "questions remain about the circumstances surrounding" Anderson's release and abscondment.

"Work is progressing to establish an independent review, and further details will be announced shortly."

The circumstances surrounding Anderson's release sparked a political row in Northern Ireland, with Long denying on Monday that she had misled the assembly over the matter.

MP for Foyle, Colum Eastwood, welcomed Anderson's arrest and said "confidence has been damaged in the institutions involved".

A federal judge overseeing a lawsuit to restore White House access to three major news organizations says Donald Trump’s administration appears to have failed longstanding legal precedent that requires due process before stripping passes from reporters.

Last week, the White House stripped press passes for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after the president announced he was “banning” the publications “effective immediately” for what he called their “FAKE” reporting. Letters explaining how they can get those passes back weren’t sent out until yesterday.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by the president during his first administration, had previously ordered the White House to restore then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass in 2018.

When deciding that case, Kelly relied on previous court decisions that determined journalists are entitled to a “pre-deprivation notice and opportunity to be heard” before those passes are revoked, the judge said during Wednesday’s court hearing in Washington, D.C.

“I think it is fair to say that the process the court laid out [in those cases] wasn’t followed here,” Kelly said before arguments began Wednesday. The judge said he will have a ruling “as soon as I can” but ended the 45-minute hearing without an immediate decision.

open image in gallery CNN, MSNOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration to restore press access to the White House after the president announced he was ‘banning’ the outlets ( Reuters )

Trump and the Department of Justice have accused the outlets of endangering national security by reporting sensitive and classified information that the president has also called “fake news” that is “negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social September 18. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

A federal lawsuit filed by lawyers representing the outlets accuses the Trump administration of “brazenly” violating their First Amendment rights and due process requirements under the Fifth Amendment by discriminating against them based solely on their editorial viewpoint.

Other news organizations agreed to an effective blackout of pool coverage in solidarity with the banned networks. ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — major networks that cover the president as part of the well-connected TV pool that patches transmissions to outlets worldwide — suspended their coverage, and other outlets announced they were temporarily withholding the publication of pool photographs.

Staff from CBS, Fox and NBC joined reporters at Joint Base Andrews air base on Wednesday evening to await Chinese President Xi Jinping after the hearing, but they did not have their cameras rolling as they awaited Judge Kelly’s decision, according to the White House press pool.

Theodore Boutrous Jr., a lawyer for the outlets, told Judge Kelly that there hasn’t been a “semblance of due process here.”

But if the judge were to merely force the Trump administration to provide reporters with some recourse, “the shenanigans will continue,” he told Kelly.

“You can see where we’re headed here,” with “a series of faux due process efforts” to satisfy the courts while continuing to violate the outlets’ First Amendment rights, Boutrous Jr. said.

“I think we all know … none of us are that naive,” he said. “That’s not due process.”

open image in gallery Trump has denied launching an ‘assault on the Free Press’ while claiming ‘FAKE NEWS’ that publishes reporting he doesn’t like amounts to a ‘cancer’ and ‘a threat to our National Security’ ( Getty )

On Monday, Trump denied launching an “assault on the Free Press” and said he is instead “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” he wrote on Truth Social. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

Sensing a potential loss in the federal court battle, he vowed an appeal “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”

He lashed out at “Third Rate Clowns” who “purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish.”

“Virtually every story about me, or anything having to do with me, is negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country!” he wrote. “No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialize and demean.”

He also said he regretted appointing Judge Kelly.

In late-night filings on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security and breaching standards of conduct, including “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” No law explicitly makes it a crime for a journalist to obtain or publish classified information.

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing states.

open image in gallery Trump’s actions have escalated his ongoing war with the press and threats to First Amendment protections as he publicly rages against critical and antagonistic reporting ( AFP/Getty )

The filings included copies of letters from the White House Press Office to the three outlets sent on September 22. The letters point to their reporting on the U.S. military’s munitions shortages due to the ongoing Iran war as well as the administration’s proposed security additions to the White House ballroom — details that the Justice Department itself has discussed at length in court filings stemming from the ongoing lawsuit against the project.

The White House also pointed to a report about low attendance at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that “cites unnamed sources” to paint the event “as a disaster.” (That report from Politico cited a Republican lobbyist close to the White House who said “the vibes are very bad.”)

Only one of the four articles published by CNN and one of the three offending MS NOW articles were written by reporters with White House passes, according to officials at the network.

The White House also pointed to reports of an alleged FBI leak investigation focusing on a journalist and an apparent U.S. military strike on an Iranian girls’ school that killed 156 civilians, including 120 children.

“Publication of sensitive security information, and misinformation about national security information, diverts White House resources and those of the national security team in particular, which must evaluate whether the leaked information is classified, the source of any leak, and the security implications of any such disclosure,” the White House Press Office wrote in letters to the news outlets.

“The spread of misinformation, especially relating to national security, is a threat that undermines the President’s ability to safeguard the national security,” the letters state.

The outlets were given until 5 p.m. September 25 to “contest this initial decision or the factual basis” for their removal.

“It’s so over the top,” Boutrous said Wednesday. “It’s clear retaliation.”

After media outlets sued, “all of a sudden this is a national security case,” he said.

“A light bulb went off: ‘start talking about national security,’” he said. “The idea that reporters can be punished for reporting on national security issues … that the government would rather not be reported on is contrary to First Amendment principles.”

He called the administration’s shifting rationale a post-hoc, pretextual attempt to ban coverage the president doesn’t like.

On Wednesday, a coalition of more than 50 news organizations and press freedom groups filed a brief in support of the outlets, writing that the White House ban over the content of their reporting amounts to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.

“It is designed to have a chilling effect,” they wrote, “with the hope that it discourages other outlets from publishing stories that they fear might provoke similar sanctions.”

Three people who went to California's Six Flags Magic Mountain have filed lawsuits saying they were left with traumatic brain injuries from the park's famed X2 roller coaster that is advertised as the rite of passage for the “ultimate daredevil.”

The filings are the latest against the world-famous amusement park operator and S&S Worldwide, the manufacturer of the X2 roller coaster. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.

According to documents filed Monday, Pamela Guillen and her family visited the park in July for her daughter's 16th birthday and decided to ride the X2 roller coaster. When the ride stopped, her daughter saw her “sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” confused and unable to exit the ride.

Shortly after she got out, the previously healthy 39-year-old collapsed and was taken to a hospital, where she underwent emergency brain surgery, according to the lawsuit.

Just five days later, 25-year-old Naomi Greer-Wilkinson boarded the ride with her siblings. She also collapsed shortly after the ride ended and was taken to a hospital, where she was found to have massive brain bleeding inside the skull that required emergency brain surgery. She remains in a vegetative state in the hospital, unable to speak or move and dependent on a ventilator. Her family filed the lawsuit on her behalf.

Their attorney, Gary Dordick, said the firm has been retained by more than 100 clients that suffered brain injuries after riding the X2 roller coaster within the past two years.

“It’s inexcusable that more isn’t done,” Dordick said. “It was known by Magic Mountain that those injuries and deaths occurred and they kept the ride open.”

A spokesperson for Six Flags said it's their policy not to comment on pending litigation and the ride has been closed since the evening of July 12.

According to the Six Flags Magic Mountain website, the X2 roller coaster reaches a top speed of 76 mph (122 kph) and has a total length of 3,610 feet (1,100 meters). The seats rotate 360 degrees “so your body will be flipping around the entire time,” and the ride features two “raven turns” — half loops that turn into sheer drops midway. It debuted at the park in 2002 as X and reopened in 2008 as X2 with new trains and special effects.

Fans of X2 have discussed on Reddit forums the “unspoken rules” of how to ride the roller coaster without getting injured. Many cite the final raven turn as the most extreme part of the ride and say they have gotten major headaches and what felt like concussions if they didn't brace their heads properly. One even said they wore a soft head helmet the last time they were on the ride.

“The snapping bangs the head against the headrest and it’s causing brain damage, it’s causing hemorrhaging within the skull,” Dordick said.

Another one of his clients, Michael Wilk, visited the park with his daughter and grandchildren in February. Immediately after going on the ride, he felt stabbing pain in his head, dizziness, and had difficulty walking, the lawsuit states.

While he didn't seek medical attention immediately, his cognitive function quickly declined in the following weeks as he tried to return to his job as an insurance defense attorney. An MRI scan a few months later showed massive bleeding and swelling inside his skull, requiring multiple surgeries to relieve the pressure on his brain. He said he continues to suffer debilitating headaches, confusion, dizziness, memory loss, and personality changes, and can no longer practice law.

The lawsuit accused Six Flags of intentionally restricting “public disclosure of evidence concerning X2 injuries and safety issues.”

The new lawsuits follow a settlement for wrongful death in the case of Christopher Hawley, a 22-year-old who died the day after he rode X2 and was rushed to the hospital after the ride with severe brain bleeding. The medical examiner's office said his death was from “blunt head trauma.”

Dordick said the amusement park operator has argued that people are accepting risk by voluntarily going on a thrill ride, and that people who suffer injuries often have preexisting conditions.

“The risk people reasonably assume is they get dizzy, maybe someone might throw up,” Dordick said. “No one goes to a family fun amusement park and assumes the risk of brain damage.”

Donald Trump raised a few eyebrows as a somewhat surreal red-carpet ceremony was put on for Chinese President Xi Jinping at a military base in Maryland on Wednesday for Xi’s arrival.

Video caught Chinese officials looking on as U.S. Marines smoothed out a red carpet for the Chinese president, who descended the stairs and was greeted by his U.S. counterpart, clad in a long winter coat and leather gloves in the 65-degree weather.

The pair, along with their spouses, then stood beside each other awkwardly as the national anthem was played, cannons fired in a salute, and a military jet soared loudly overhead — causing Trump to visibly wince while Xi placidly watched the plane pass overhead.

“[I]t is 64 degrees at Joint Base Andrews right now and yet Trump is wearing gloves are he greets President Xi,” wrote journalist Aaron Rupar.

“Trump -- it’s YOUR airshow. How do you get scared?” asked Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who played video of Xi’s arrival for his viewers.

open image in gallery Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet in an unusual airport greeting for Xi Jinping on Wednesday ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery Trump winced as a U.S. military jet completed a flyover during Xi's arrival ceremony ( AFP/Getty )

The ceremony was a major departure from the typically more reserved setting in which U.S. presidents meet leaders of major U.S. geopolitical rivals, like Russia and China. But Trump has broken protocol on that front before, including when he rolled out a red carpet for Russia’s Vladimir Putin when the latter visited Alaska in 2025.

By comparison, Joe Biden waited to greet Xi until the Chinese president arrived at the site of their summit in San Francisco in 2024. Like Trump, Biden greeted Xi with a military guard and red carpet — though not one carted out to the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews.

Generally speaking, American presidents (other than Trump) typically eschew tarmac greetings for foreign dignitaries. The recent visit to the United States of British monarchs King Charles and Queen Camilla followed standard protocol — Trump greeted them at the White House.

open image in gallery U.S. presidents typically greet foreign dignitaries at the White House or at the meeting sites of high-stakes summits ( AFP/Getty )

Xi’s visit comes as the U.S. and China remain at odds over a number of trade issues including AI and semiconductors, and on both topics the U.S. president has been accused by his domestic critics of being too lax with Beijing. Ahead of Wednesday’s arrival ceremony, Trump faced criticism from a Republican senator typically closely aligned with the White House over putting on a “lavish” welcome for the Chinese president.

“Had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker said in a speech delivered on the Senate floor.

open image in gallery Trump is facing increasing resistance from Republicans on Capitol Hill as his approval ratings slide ( Getty )

He added that Trump, “during every minute of dialogue,” should remember that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”

The senator’s criticism is a rarity on Capitol Hill, but the rebellious nature of GOP members has grown in recent weeks as the president’s approval ratings have remained at record lows and his war in Iran has plummeted to dangerously low popularity levels.

Calls on the Hill and from Republican candidates nationwide for the war to end have grown, while Trump continues to make threats about wiping out the entire country of Iran.

Xi’s visit to Washington comes as his American opposite is facing political turmoil within his Republican Party coalition and facing a potential wipeout for the GOP in the upcoming midterm elections.

The previous week in D.C. was capped off by Trump’s decision to ban MS Now, CNN and Politico from the White House. Journalists were stripped of their White House hard passes and shown to the door as they attempted to enter the premises over the weekend and on Monday, and the three organizations filed a lawsuit to block the ban. On Wednesday, TV networks including Fox News, NBC, ABC and CBS (which make up the remainder of the TV press pool) continued to boycott coverage of White House events in solidarity with their excluded colleagues.

As a result, Trump’s ceremony was largely absent from cable news shows on Wednesday, depriving the president of an audience to look presidential in front of as he battles an image problem and the frustrations of Americans who continue to face a serious cost-of-living crisis.

A 19-year-old college wrestler from California has fallen to his death while hiking near a waterfall in Yosemite National Park, according to reports.

Ryan George’s wrestling team at Santa Rosa Junior College, about an hour’s drive northwest of San Francisco, announced the tragic news in a Facebook post Monday.

“This past weekend we received the tragic news that Ryan passed away at Yosemite National Park, following an accident,” the team wrote.

The Press Democrat, a local newspaper, reported that George was hiking with friends near Illilouette Falls on Sunday when he slipped and fell to his death. The waterfall is roughly 370 feet tall and flows all year long.

“If you knew Ryan, you know he was one of the most genuine, positive people you could ever meet,” his wrestling team said. “He had this way of lighting up a room, making you feel welcome, and bringing out the best in everyone around him. Always smiling, always encouraging, always full of life.”

open image in gallery Ryan George, a 19-year-old college wrestler from California, has fallen to his death while hiking near a waterfall in Yosemite National Park, according to reports ( Maranda Maybee via GoFundMe )

Details surrounding George’s death, such as what led to the fall and the aftermath, are unknown. The Independent has reached out to the National Park Service and the Mariposa County Sheriff’s Office for comment.

George got into wrestling during his freshman year of high school. He was a football player at Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa and was too heavy to join the wrestling team. But that didn’t stop him.

“He worked really, really hard and he got his weight down,” Ian Hesz, who was George’s high school wrestling coach, told The Press Democrat.

George won an individual North Bay League title at Montgomery High, and then earned All-American honors last wrestling season as a freshman at Santa Rosa Junior College, according to the outlet. On Friday, just days before his death, George earned second place at the Dave Pacheco Invitational meet at Sacramento City College.

open image in gallery George was hiking with friends near Illilouette Falls Sunday when he slipped and fell to his death. The waterfall is roughly 370 feet tall and flows all year long ( AFP via Getty Images )

“It was good watching him find what he loved,” George’s older sister, Jaida, told The Press Democrat. “He was always playing and wrestling when he was a kid.”

The siblings’ father died when George was a baby and their mother died just weeks ago, according to the outlet.

In a GoFundMe page created on behalf of Jaida, a loved one wrote, “In July, we lost our Beloved Taji and now, just 2 months later, her daughter Jaida is facing another heartbreaking loss with the passing of her Little Brother Ryan Jr. this past Sunday.”

“She is grieving the loss of two people she loves deeply, while also facing all that comes with losing family members so unexpectedly, on top of it all being a New Mommy to her precious Son who is only 2 months old,” read the fundraising page, which generated more than $9,000 in donations by Wednesday.

HSBC is planning to create 1,000 entry-level roles in the UK over the next year as the bank targets Gen Z workers.

Around a third of all hires the UK bank has made this year have been aged 18 to 24.

The new entry-level positions will comprise of apprenticeships, graduate programmes and internships across 2026 and 2027.

It is also offering 500 one-week in-person work experience placements designed to give secondary school students earlier exposure to the workplace.

The hiring drive is being led by the UK bank and will see the majority of opportunities focused in regions outside of London.

It comes as the wider global bank is undergoing an ovehaul led by chief executive Georges Elhedery, who targeted 1.5 billion US dollars (£1.1 billion) worth of cost reductions.

Earlier this year, Mr Elhedery said a large amount of the savings had come from eliminating duplicate jobs within the group, particularly among the more senior ranks, resulting in a net 15% reduction of managing director positions.

HSBC’s annual report revealed that it had paid out 67.5 million US dollars (£50.9 million) in severance payments to 134 senior bankers in 2025.

This amounted to about a tenth of its so-called material risk takers, who do jobs that can have a more significant impact on the financial performance of the bank.

Meanwhile, HSBC UK said its early-career workers can help it build a “high-performance culture” and “shape the future of banking”.

Chief executive of the UK bank, David Lindberg, said: “Investing in early-career talent is important for HSBC’s future as we build a high-performance culture with care.

“As the world of work changes, we are building the skills our customers and communities need.”

The bank said work experience students will particularly gain experience learning about digital technologies used across the bank and how artificial intelligence tools support people’s day-to-day work.

Recruitment for the 2027 entry-level roles will open from late September.
