Sports.title: Harry's American dream: England captain Kane plans to 'seriously look' at becoming an NFL kicker... and opens door to finishing career in the MLS
Sports.content:
Harry's American dream: England captain Kane plans to 'seriously look' at becoming an NFL kicker... and opens door to finishing career in the MLS

Harry Kane has his eye on a career in the NFL when he eventually stops playing football.

England captain Kane – tipped to be next month’s Ballon D’or Winner - believes he may have ‘five or six years’ left in the professional game and will match Peter Shilton’s all-time appearance record of 125 caps if he plays in all four of his country’s forthcoming Nations League games.

But the 33-year-old revealed on Wednesday that he already has his eye on trying out as an American Football specialist place kicker.

A two-handicap golfer, Kane has given up on his previous ambition of joining the professional ranks but said: ‘That [the NFL] is something I will try and look at a bit more seriously.

‘It all depends on what happens in my career over the next five or six years but the NFL is a lot more realistic than the golf one.

‘I take penalties and it is a very similar pressure and technique. If I did that, in terms of training, I would be closer to that more than any other sport.

Harry Kane says taking penalties could help him succeed as an NFL kicker

‘If I was to do it, it is something I would take seriously. I would take six months to a year to try and practise before. Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that, it might be a thing where you could connect the two seasons.

‘It is in the back of my mind because right now, I am feeling that I want to play as long as I can here.’

Playing in the MLS is also something Kane has not talked about before and it appears the Bayern Munich striker is starting to consider what the back end of his career may look like.

For now, he is concentrating on sorting out the final details of a new contract in the Bundesliga.

Kane was subject of interest from Barcelona in the summer but said: ‘Bayern and I are still talking. We're in good talks, I'll be honest.

‘We're fairly close. There's still some things that we need to iron out. I'm happy there and I think it won't be too long before there's some sort of announcement.

‘I feel really comfortable in the team, with the coach, the environment. Like I touched on a bit earlier, at this level, I want to just be at this level, and push this level for as long as possible.’

Kane, pictured with wife Katie at Oktoberfest in Munich, is talking with Bayern over a new deal

Having just had the season of his life with club and country, Kane revealed a new strict diet has played its part.

‘The biggest thing was after games having a few sweets to eat or something that isn’t good for you,’ he said.

‘But last year, especially, I was ultra-strict. With the World Cup on the horizon, I knew how hot it was going to be, how demanding it was going to be.

‘The fact I took out some of that stuff and then was performing the way I was performing and having my best season ever, it became addictive and I just carried on through the World Cup into this season.

‘Ultimately I think all those little details do add up and when I talk about extracting as much as I can from this period of my career, these are the things that are going to help me.’

Sports.title: How Premier League clubs are exploiting their most loyal fans - the season ticket tricks used by Chelsea and Man United, the subtle ways 'old-school' supporters are being swapped out for tourists, 'hospitality' rip-offs and why the worst is yet to come
Sports.content:
How Premier League clubs are exploiting their most loyal fans - the season ticket tricks used by Chelsea and Man United, the subtle ways 'old-school' supporters are being swapped out for tourists, 'hospitality' rip-offs and why the worst is yet to come

The railing that once hoisted the Holmesdale Fanatics flag at Selhurst Park has gone. The distinctive and raucous Crystal Palace ultras group? Disbanded.

The flagpole remained in place for the first home game of the season, just 24 hours after the group announced their dissolution, but had vanished by the following match.

Selhurst has felt a little lifeless ever since. The ceaseless noise from the 400-man section behind the goal in the Holmesdale Road End is no more.

When Daily Mail Sport asked the Holmesdale Fanatics for an explanation, they declined and redirected us to their initial statement, where they criticise the ‘draconian restrictions’ imposed on supporters.

Those restrictions extend well beyond Selhurst Park. Across the country, the football fan experience is changing, replaced by a game that is increasingly commercialised and gentrified.

Daily Mail Sport has spoken to insiders across the Premier League and beyond, industry experts and, most importantly, loyal supporters themselves to uncover just how the modern-day fan is being exploited – and why the worst may yet be to come...

Crystal Palace's distinctive and raucous Holmesdale Fanatics group has disbanded, leaving Selhurst Park a little lifeless

It is a sign of the wider exploitation and disenfrachisement of old-school, matchgoing supporters

Times are tough for football fans of all stripes, but season-ticket holders are feeling the pinch more than anyone. Premier League regulations now restrict those fans from sharing their season tickets with fellow supporters, family and friends.

At the start of the season, digital tickets became mandatory, supposedly to improve stadium security, prevent ticket touting and streamline entry into stadiums.

Manchester United have used digital ticket enforcement to identify what they describe as ‘suspicious activity’ and curb ticket touting, banning 685 season ticket holders as a result. However, fears remain that innocent fans using the ticket sharing system have been caught up in the clean-up operation.

A cynic would argue the new policy presented a fresh opportunity for clubs to squeeze supporters and monetise them sharing their season ticket.

Rather than the trusty plastic card which supporters could hand over to friends if they were not attending a match or wanted to split the cost of a season ticket, fans must now resell their tickets through official club channels – which clubs can make a profit from – or share them using the club’s ticketing platform, with access often commanding a membership fee.

At Chelsea, for example, to share a ticket the recipient must be a member, with prices beginning at £15. Meanwhile, Crystal Palace allow season-ticket holders to share their match ticket with non-members but charge a one-off £50 fee for the privilege.

Manchester United offer a ‘ticket sharing’ membership which allows supporters to receive forwarded tickets from season-ticket holders – charging £30 per person.

There are, in fairness, valid safety concerns behind this development. The Premier League partly introduced the scheme to ensure match attendees can be identified, which helps the enforcement of banning orders and detection of high-risk supporters.

But the self-serving, avaricious clubs have opportunistically commercialised supporters' autonomy over their own tickets.

At Manchester City, season tickets must be used for 16 Premier League home games, ten of which must be attended by the named individual, or the ticket will be cancelled

Across town, United have used digital ticket enforcement to identify what they describe as ‘suspicious activity’ but fears remain that innocent fans have been caught up in the clean-up

Things are unlikely to get better anytime soon. One senior football executive told Daily Mail Sport that clubs view season tickets as a ‘discounted rate’, blocking a conveyor belt of high-spending corporate and tourist spectators attending one-off games that would generate more revenue. They added that clubs could look to reduce the number of their season tickets.

That perspective was echoed by football finance expert and host of The Price of Football Podcast Kieran Maguire, who told Daily Mail Sport: ‘The bigger brands see season-ticket holders as bed blockers because tickets can be sold at a higher price to international fans and those desperate to see their club but who can only manage it once a year due to logistical challenges.

‘If we take the case of Liverpool, Anfield has gone from 44,000 to 61,000 capacity, but there was hardly any increase in season-ticket sales. It is far more lucrative to target the corporate market or the day-fan market as opposed to someone who is a local Red and unlikely to go to the megastore and drink in the ground beforehand because they go to the pub with their mates, sit at the same table and have the same chats.

‘These people, of course, are the bedrock of football fans. For political reasons, clubs won’t want to be seen to be reducing season tickets. But I don’t think we will see an increase going forward unless they are for corporate seats.

‘In some of the more desirable areas of the stadium, the clubs might not convert season tickets that haven’t been renewed into new season tickets despite long waiting lists.'

That shift has already begun, with United relocating around 500 fans sat behind the dugout at Old Trafford to the top of the North Stand to increase hospitality tickets in what United describe as a ‘high value area of the stadium’.

At Manchester City, meanwhile, season tickets must be used for 16 Premier League home games, ten of which must be attended by the named individual, or the ticket will be cancelled. Some fans argued the move breaches the Equality Act as pregnant women, mothers or disabled people could struggle to attend for prolonged periods.

To make matters worse, season-ticket waiting lists are becoming increasingly exploitative. Arsenal’s exceeds 110,000 people, meaning the club would need to turn over every season ticket three times before reaching the bottom. With the current wait time estimated at around 20 years and a £50 deposit required to join, it is difficult to envisage many supporters ever securing one.

There is therefore logic in closing the waiting list – as Liverpool have done – rather than asking supporters to part with their hard-earned cash for a ticket they may never receive. However, clubs' passive income would take a hit. Arsenal say they regularly review the waiting list and would consult supporters on any proposed changes.

Liverpool supporters recently successfully protested ticket price hikes of 3 per cent for three consecutive seasons

English football is shifting towards a matchday experience built around tourists rather than hardcore supporters. Americans fans used to taking in entertainment that goes beyond the game itself

Aside from their wallets being raided, the fan experience is also declining as English football culture shifts towards a matchday experience built around tourists rather than hardcore supporters. American fans, in particular, are accustomed to taking in entertainment that goes beyond the game itself.

Tourism dilutes the home support. At Selhurst Park, people were spotted wearing Erling Haaland Norway shirts in the home end during Manchester City’s 4-1 win over Palace in August.

And when Palace travelled to Craven Cottage earlier this month, Daily Mail Sport observed Chicago Fire and Brazil shirts in Fulham's newly redeveloped Riverside Stand, with some spectators even whipping out their phones to record themselves when the visitors scored. A similar picture is painted weekly across Premier League stadiums.

Fan experience has played a significant role in the breakdown in relations between Palace and the Holmesdale Fanatics. The fan group want an organic atmosphere inside the stadium, while the club have veered towards an artificial one.

Before kick-off, the HF had found themselves competing with Natasha Bedingfield’s Unwritten - among other pop songs - blared over the recently upgraded PA system.

There is an internal directive to ensure the stadium looks attractive on television; hence the introduction of fireworks and pyrotechnics when the players enter the pitch. But manufacturing a look is precisely what the HF stand against.

Perhaps the pomp and circumstance makes football clubs more marketable to international audiences.

The Premier League’s own economic and social impact report from July 2026 boasts that the top flight drew over a million international fans to matches in the 2023-24 season, with a trip-related spend of £903million. Those numbers are projected to rise continuously.

The Premier League say the top flight drew over a million international fans to matches in the 2023-24 season, with a trip-related spend of £903million

Palace's Holmesdale Fanatics want an organic atmosphere inside the stadium, while the club have veered towards an artificial one

Daily Mail Sport spoke to one US-based neutral who regularly flies over to attend Premier League games. Among the thousands he has spent on tickets already this season, he paid £350 for a general admission ticket to watch Ipswich take on Liverpool at Portman Road, purchased through a third-party reseller.

Clubs discourage buying third-party tickets as they do not receive the benefits besides the money spent in the stadium on merchandise, food and drink – although it does indicate the extravagant prices international fans are willing to pay for a £38 ticket, splashing nine times over the odds.

It has not gone unnoticed at Premier League clubs that World Cup stadiums in the United States were 99.7 per cent full despite extortionate general admission prices. That spells danger for domestic supporters.

Sites like Seat Unique and Sportsworld have partnerships with Premier League clubs including Manchester City, Manchester United and Everton and market padded seat packages suitable for tourists. For Manchester City’s Champions League match against Paris Saint-Germain next month, Sportsworld are selling a £279 padded seat package which non-members can purchase – the only requirement is they are not in away colours.

'Westview' at Stamford Bridge is similar. The package ranges from £225 to £625 per game depending on the prestige of the fixture for a padded seat and a market hall style concourse with no food or drink included.

It is barely a hospitality package, besides sitting in a swankier area of the stadium. Simply put, Westview allows Chelsea to sell extortionately priced tickets to non-members, enabling the club to benefit directly from the tourist trade. These visitors are also likely to spend money on food and drink and visit the megastore.

Some Premier League clubs have even been spotted bringing the megastore to fans, with merchandise staff now carrying trays of baseball caps and scarves around the pitch and concourses to cater to the tourist market.

The Premier League needs to captivate an international audience but it should not come at the expense of ordinary fans.

Last year, the Football Supporters' Association said: ‘Football is becoming a luxury good for some, pricing out working-class communities, young supporters and families who represent the future heartbeat of the game. Record broadcast revenues – the 2025-28 deal is worth £12.25billion – and packed corporate hospitality sections tell us that financial sustainability does not depend on pricing out traditional supporters.’

Yet the cheapest ticket for a Category A game in nine of the 20 Premier League grounds exceeds £50, while general admission season tickets range from £380 to £3,192. Newcastle offer the cheapest season ticket, and Fulham’s is the most expensive.

Coventry City are one of the few clubs that have looked out for their supporters in recent years

‘Football is becoming a luxury good for some, pricing out working-class communities, young supporters and families who represent the future heartbeat of the game,' say the FSA

Although the outlook for fans appears bleak, there are rays of positivity to cling on to. Coventry City deserve praise for rewarding loyalty. In 2023, the club committed to giving supporters who bought a season ticket a free one should they reach the Premier League. This season, some 5,000 fans are benefiting from that scheme.

The £30 price cap for away fans has been extended until the end of the 2027-28 season – providing good value for the most loyal supporters.

And despite the widespread rip-off, fans can still fight back. Liverpool supporters had success at the end of last season after the club announced season ticket price hikes of 3 per cent for three consecutive seasons. But a protest at Anfield – where supporters raised yellow cards – prompted the club to reconsider, raising prices for this season and freezing them for 2027-28.

In light of the European Super League debacle, Premier League clubs created fan advisory boards to ensure that supporters' concerns were heard. Now, however, those bodies must stop being symbolic – and ensure English football remembers its most loyal fans represent the heart of the game.

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez transfer statement made as Man City warning issued to Premier League rivals
Sports.content:
Enzo Fernandez transfer statement made as Man City warning issued to Premier League rivals

Enzo Fernandez won the Club World Cup and the UEFA Conference League during his time with Chelsea before moving to Man City during the summer transfer window

View 2 Images Enzo Fernandez has made an instant impact at Manchester City (Image: (Matt McNulty/Getty Images))

Enzo Fernandez has been told he has taken Manchester City from possible Premier League challengers to definite contenders. City spent an eye-watering sum revamping their midfield during the summer, with Fernandez’s British record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea completing their business on deadline day.

‌



The Argentine won the Club World Cup and the UEFA Conference League during his time in London and he has already made an immediate impact at the Etihad. And former City defender Danny Mills, speaking via BestBettingBonuses.co.uk, believes the transfer was a game changer for his old club and has called on people to stop going on about the fee.

‌



“I think the Enzo Fernandez signing was really, really important," he said. "(Ayyoub) Bouaddi is a very, very good player, very talented, but he's very, very young.

‌



“And it's difficult to go through a full season if it was just him and (Elliot) Anderson in there. You'd be thinking, can they survive the whole season? Is there enough creativity in that midfield?

“Suddenly you throw Enzo Fernandez into that, and you've got the likes of (Mateo) Kovacic, incredibly experienced, to drop in and out as well. Suddenly you're going, well, actually, this is now. And this is why I said the Enzo Fernandez signing is a game-changer for City.

“So if you did lose him, you've got to try and replace that, which is difficult. But he's fit, he's strong, he's robust. We've seen this time and time again.

“He's scored an obscene amount of goals already this season. So if something did happen, I'm sure there would be a plan, and I'm sure in January they would go again if needed.”

Sports.title: 'Let football fans have a pint — it’s time to scrap this outdated drinking in stands ban'
Sports.content:
The ban on drinking alcohol in the stands is horribly outdated.

And it is great that the United Kingdom has a real football fan as a Prime Minister who is ready to change the law which is so unfair on supporters. Everton fan Andy Burnham is right to speak up and push for supporters to be able to enjoy a pint within sight of the pitch.

You can have a drink at cricket and it is time football fans were allowed to do the same. Times change and it is wrong for football fans to be treated as second class citizens.

In my experience, if you treat people as grown ups - then they will behave like adults. Of course we should be sensitive. Just as we have been in the reintroduction of safe standing. Do it sensibly and, as Burnham suggests, even on a trial basis. Fans will prove him right.

‌



View 2 Images Football's drinking restrictions date back to the hooliganism of the 1980s (Image: PA)

Harry Kane defends Declan Rice after Arsenal star explained England drop out READ MORE :

Harvey Elliott enduring second loan nightmare as Liverpool star branded 'overweight' READ MORE :

No one can forget the booze and drug fuelled scenes outside Wembley ahead of the Euros final in 2021. It has to be policed but being able to drink in your seat would actually ease the binge drinking culture which exists at football games before and at half time.

We have moved on from the bad old days of hooliganism in the 1980s which led to this ban in the first place. Football has a new generation of fans and stadiums are generally safer, there is a different vibe within grounds and it is time to move on.

The other compelling argument which emerged in Tracey Crouch’s independent review into football back in 2021 was that League Two and National League clubs lose up to an estimated £100,000-per-year in sales because of the ban.

‌



This is an important change for all levels of the game - and it is great that we have a PM who understands and respects football fans.

Sports.title: Mike Tindall's dad dies as England rugby icon shares tragic Royal Family heartbreak
Sports.content:
Mike Tindall's dad dies as England rugby icon shares tragic Royal Family heartbreak

The former England international shared the sad news on a podcast

View Image Mike Tindall has announced the death of his father (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Mike Tindall has revealed that his father, Phil Tindall, has died at the age of 80. The former England Rugby Union star shared the news on a podcast he co-hosts.

‌



Speaking on The Good, The Bad & The Rugby, which he co-hosts alongside James Haskell and Alex Payne, he said: "Unfortunately, my dad passed away last week."

‌



His father was captain of Otley Rugby Club in West Yorkshire in the 1970s, with Tindall thanking them for their tribute over the weekend, when a minute's silence was held.

‌



"But thank you very much to Otley Rugby Club for it," he said. "That little moment, I got to watch it. Someone recorded it, sent it to me, and then they wrote a little thing in the programme as well, which I read."

BBC Sport confirms further cuts as furious staff left weighing up strike action READ MORE :

Referees attacked by rugby fans as security rushes to shield them from projectiles READ MORE :

Tindall, who is a member of the royal family through his marriage to Zara, the daughter of Princess Anne, has been open about his father's 20-plus-year battle with Parkinson's disease.

Speaking back in May, he said: "My dad is not doing great at the moment. Parkinson's is brutal and there is no let-up from how it attacks the body and changes people."

‌



He added: "After 23 plus years of the disease, it has quite honestly left him a shell of what he once was, which is why I don’t want anyone else to see a parent or loved one suffer and have their quality of life decline so massively."

Phil was diagnosed with the disease in 2003, the same year that Tindall was part of the England team to lift the Rugby Union World Cup.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast earlier this year, he said that the impact of the disease wasn't apparent until much later: “I wouldn’t have known until…I don’t think I really noticed until the late 2000s probably," he said.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

“That is something I look…not judge myself on…it’s easy in hindsight let’s look back and what would I have done differently.

"I’d have been on him more about exercising, staying stronger but the research in that time probably wasn’t where it is now, where it’s so easy to find what you should be doing, or notice all the signs like shuffling, freezing, quietness of voice, impatience, whatever it may be.”

Article continues below

The 47-year-old has been a patron of the charity Cure Parkinson's since 2018. He has spent years raising money and awareness as the search for better treatments continues.

Sharing memories of his late father, Tindall reflected on an injury shortly before marrying his mother, Linda.

“He got married in 69, broke his leg the week before, went down the aisle in a cast," he said. “I mean, it sort of all went wrong. He had to retire at 27.”

Sports.title: Fellow boss calls for Tonda Eckert to be hit with 'severe' punishment for Spygate plot
Sports.content:
Fellow boss calls for Tonda Eckert to be hit with 'severe' punishment for Spygate plot

Tonda Eckert will discover his punishment from the FA on Thursday having been charged with misconduct for his role in the Southampton Spygate scandal last season

View 2 Images Tonda Eckert is about to discover his fate (Image: Matt Watson/Southampton FC via Getty Images)

Southampton manager Tonda Eckert deserves a "severe" punishment from the FA for the Spygate scandal, according to Cambridge United boss Neil Harris.

‌



Eckert will discover his fate on Thursday at an FA hearing, having admitted giving the order for a junior member of staff to spy on three rival clubs' training sessions. Southampton were chucked out of the Championship play-off final in May and docked four points this season by the EFL.

‌



But now Saints are braced for further punishment, with the FA set to announce its decision on Eckert, having charged him with misconduct back in July. The 33-year-old has pleaded for forgiveness in a four-hour meeting with the FA, but could be given a hefty ban.

‌



"[I'm talking] on behalf of myself but probably also every other manager in the Football League and a lot of fans as well," Harris told BBC Radio 5 Live.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"What happened is bordering on disgraceful. Listening to their CEO (Phil Parsons) saying they've been punished enough, the football club; I agree - Southampton Football Club and the fanbase and the workforce have been punished hugely.

"Tonda has owned it and said it was his decision to spy and send a junior member of staff. He's owned it and the club have decided to stick with him.

"The manager should get a huge ban, in my opinion, as a senior football man in this country. He's gone way across the mark of cheating. We don't do that in this country. There's no place for it in the game over here and it deserves a ban.

‌



View 2 Images Tonda Eckert was behind Southampton spying on rival club's training sessions (Image: Matt Watson/Getty Images)

"I've seen a couple of bits recently saying it should be two or four-game ban. We're talking about basically cheating and trying to gain an advantage on the opponent.

"So, as you can tell, I feel quite strongly about it - and it's not just me, it's every manager in the Football League that agrees. I think whatever punishment he gets needs to be severe and it needs to be stamped down on. It can't happen again."

‌



Saints chief executive Parsons told the BBC that he felt the club had "taken enough" from the EFL's punishment for what it called a "contrived and determined plan" to spy on Oxford United, Ipswich and Middlesbrough. That is the belief of ex-Southampton striker Charlie Austin.

“I think we should just move on," he told The Sun. “The punishment has been done. They got taken out of this game, which is worth millions.

“Eckert is a young coach. He made a mistake, he’s admitted he’s made a mistake, and he’s learned from it. Just let him get on with his career now. It’s ridiculous this has been dragged out further.”

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo vows to carry on playing for Portugal and targets 1,000-goal landmark
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo vows to carry on playing for Portugal and targets 1,000-goal landmark

Cristiano Ronaldo has decided to keep playing for Portugal at the age of 41, despite suffering huge disappointment at the World Cup and facing increased criticism over his performances

View 2 Images Cristiano Ronaldo is still going at the age of 41 (Image: Fadel SENNA / AFP via Getty Images)

Cristiano Ronaldo has hit back at his critics and vowed to carry on playing for Portugal as he nears 1,000 career goals.

‌



Ronaldo's future in international football was in doubt following the World Cup, but the 41-year-old is playing on after Jorge Jesus replaced Roberto Martinez as manager. Ronaldo has 146 goals in 233 appearances for his country and is approaching a personal landmark.

‌



The Al-Nassr striker sits on 979 career goals for club and country ahead of Portugal beginning their Nations League campaign against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night. While he has denied that his decision to continue playing for Portugal was driven by his own goal tally, Ronaldo did admit he'd like to reach four figures while on international duty.

‌



Portugal were dumped out of the World Cup by bitter rivals Spain in the last 16 and the 1-0 defeat did give Ronaldo pause for thought. Asked if he considered retiring, he replied: “Yes I did.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"Of course, I’m always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I’m a thinker. You have to think. This is why you see me here now. It means I will continue.

“I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I’m able to help the national team to reach what they want, and will finish when I feel like I’m not doing anything here.

“I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football. This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.”

‌



View 2 Images Jorge Jesus has taken over as Portugal boss (Image: Patricia de Melo Moreira / AFP via Getty Images)

The veteran forward now wants to help bring through the next generation. “I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired… in 10 years," he joked.

“I’m happy with myself. It doesn’t matter if I play tomorrow, if I rest the next game, for me the most important thing is that I feel good.”

‌



Ronaldo's place in the starting XI has become a hot topic of debate in Portugal. He insists that it doesn't bother him. "I said it quite often at home with my friends. I’ve been playing football for so many years, I have been welcome almost everywhere, apart from a few exceptions," Ronaldo said.

“I feel the Portuguese fans like me, but I do understand that some TV channels want to criticise me – they’ve tried to kill me, but only with a shotgun.

“They are dying for me not to come to the national team anymore, but I can still move away from it. Anyway, I am used to it. For over 20 years I have been doing this, but my memories are with people who love me.”

Sports.title: 'I'm not fine with Ronnie O'Sullivan - I don't want anything to do with him'
Sports.content:
'I'm not fine with Ronnie O'Sullivan - I don't want anything to do with him'

Ali Carter and Ronnie O'Sullivan have had a strained relationship, despite being friends as teenagers

View 2 Images Ronnie O'Sullivan has had a strained relationship with some of his rivals over the years (Image: Tai Chengzhe/VCG via Getty Images)

Ali Carter has admitted that he wants nothing to do with Ronnie O’Sullivan, despite the two being friends early in their careers. The duo used to train together at Witham Snooker Bowl.

‌



Carter credits O'Sullivan for helping him to win a championship, but then claims that their friendship went downhill. The two have come up against each other 29 times in their careers, with O’Sullivan winning 25, but some of those matches haven’t been without incident.

‌



Speaking on the Talking Snooker podcast, Carter said: “Me and Ronnie, we used to practise together, as a 17-year-old at Witham Snooker Bowl. We played every single day.

‌



Ali Carter reveals phone call with Ronnie O'Sullivan's dad during cancer treatment READ MORE :

“That was what led up to winning the Benson & Hedges Championship in 1999. That was a big tournament then and if it wasn’t for him getting me prepped up, I probably would never have won that tournament.”

However, despite that early friendship, Carter outlined how things changed. “So, after spending a lot of time with Ronnie, and he probably knew at the time how good I was, I just felt that when we went to tournaments, he wasn’t really the same toward me,” he said.

“Looking back, I probably took it personally. I think he’s like that with everyone, it wasn’t just me. But I’m not everyone, am I?

‌



“I can only speak from my own perspective. So, I just thought, well, if he can’t be bothered to talk to me, then I can’t be bothered to talk to him. That’s fine. We both know where we stand then.”

View 2 Images Ali Carter has spoken about his relationship with Ronnie O'Sullivan. (Image: Tai Chengzhe/VCG via Getty Images)

There was, however, an incident during the 2018 World Championships in Sheffield in which the two appeared to shoulder-barge during their match. Carter remembers an apology from O’Sullivan over the incident, but then recalled how their relationship soured again.

‌



He said: “We were at the Novotel in York, and he was with Damien Hirst and all his cronies, and I was having breakfast. Ronnie came over to me, he said, ‘Listen, I’m really sorry about what happened in Sheffield’.

“Then lockdown happened and all the tournaments were in Milton Keynes, so I played Ronnie O’Sullivan in the semi-finals of the [2020] Northern Ireland Open at Milton Keynes.

“I’d done an interview with Alan McManus before and he said, ‘It’s always a needle match between you and Ronnie.’ I said, ‘No, not at all. He came up to me in the Novotel in York and he apologised and I apologised. It’s all water under the bridge.’

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

“So, anyway, he beat me, then the next tournament, I’ve come out of the tournament office. He must have seen my interview and he’s gone, ‘I never apologised to you. That was your fault.’

“I said, ‘What? So I just made it up then, did I? That you come up to me in York and apologised?’ He went, ‘Yeah, you did,’ and then had a little laugh, and that was that.

Article continues below

“You can’t comprehend what’s just happened. Is he getting me at it or what? And I just thought, right, okay, he wants to say that, whatever. The only way I can take myself out of that situation is just have nothing to do with it anymore, not speak to him. It’s pointless.”

Reflecting on their current relationship, Carter added: “I mean, me and Ronnie…we’re not fine, [but] there’s nothing. There’s no relationship there, there’s no hate, there’s no nothing.”

The most recent meeting between the two was in January this year, in the last 32 of the German Masters. That match saw Carter come out as 5-3 winner.

Sports.title: Harry Kane defends Declan Rice after Arsenal star explained England drop out
Sports.content:
Harry Kane defends Declan Rice after Arsenal star explained England drop out

Declan Rice was one of five players to pull out of the England squad for the four Nations League games in the current international break, but Harry Kane understands his reasoning

View 2 Images Harry Kane received a message from Declan Rice (Image: Julian Finney/FIFA via Getty Images)

Declan Rice “reached out” to Harry Kane to explain why he pulled out of England duty.

‌



Arsenal midfielder Rice was one of five players, along with Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford, Robbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento, to withdraw from the squad for the Nations League fixtures, with Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner called up as replacements.

‌



Kane was highly critical of nine players pulling out in November 2024 by insisting “England comes before everything” but was more sympathetic this time.

‌



Palmer missed the World Cup and had played the whole 90 minutes of Chelsea ’s last four Premier League games, but Rice struggled in the World Cup because he played 69 games for club and country last season.

Sports.title: Harry Kane opens up on true impact of England's World Cup heartbreak vs Argentina
Sports.content:
Harry Kane insists England must put the “hurt” of the last World Cup behind them. Kane admits the pain of losing to Argentina last summer was even worse for him personally than missing the penalty against France in the 2022 quarter final.

Three Lions captain Kane admitted they did not show their “true selves” against Argentina in the semi-final but says they must use that as motivation in the future.

England start their Nations League campaign against world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday and Kane wants to start a new chapter after the pain in the United States.

Kane said: “You have no choice. You have to move on. I am so passionate about England, especially because I have been on this journey now. I have been to the finals, I have been to semi-finals and been so close.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

“Each one hurts in a different way. This one hurt, for sure. More than any other one. I would probably say even more than when I missed a penalty in Qatar because of the manner that it happened. It was not us as a team.

“It was not the team we wanted to be or said we would be. Sometimes you maybe go against your beliefs and it feels 10 times worse than losing your way when you accept it, take it on the chin and move on. It is tough and it will still be tough.

‌



“But leading up to the next major tournament for example, they are feelings that if you use them in the right way, you can use them to motivate you and you can say ‘I can go one step further’. And that is what we need to try and do.”

The disappointment comes from England having it within their grasp. They were 1-0 up against Argentina, they were on top and yet let it slip in the dying minutes against an ageing team which was not as good as when they won it coup years previously.

But Kane also explained the questions in their minds about where they went wrong and also how they can improve in the longer term.

Kane said: “I think those are the questions that we need to kind of discuss amongst ourselves and answer ourselves, as players and as coaching staff ‘how how can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more in those moments?’

‌



View 4 Images Kane consoles Jude Bellingham after England's defeat to Argentina (Image: Getty Images)

“It's something that we haven't quite been able to do in latter stages of tournaments against the bigger nations and the better nations.

“And it may be a mixture of things - it may be personalities. It may be mentality. It may be just the direction and how we want to play in those games. I think it's conversations that we need to have as as a group and team.”

Incredibly, England will have played the last three world champions in their last three games by the time they finish Saturday’s showdown with Spain.

‌



They lost to Argentina, they beat France in the third place play-off and then face Spain. It is a big test for Thomas Tuchel’s men and Kane says it will also act as part of the “healing process.”

Kane said: “It kind of is. But you have to heal while getting on with it. In life in general, whenever there's like big major events in business or in sport, you have time to process it, you have time to talk about it.

View 4 Images Kane is now back in the England camp for the first time since the World Cup (Image: Getty Images)

“In football, you don't have that. In football, before you know it's the next one, and now we're focused on Nations League, so it's a hard balance because you're trying to get over it and learn from it, but also we play the world champions on Saturday and it's a big, important game.”

‌



England boss Tuchel welcomed the group back to St George’s Park with a team meeting, every member of staff was also welcomed into the room with a clear message that they cannot let the disappointment of the way the summer ended distract from their progress.

Kane added: “The general messaging is that we continue what we've been building. I think sometimes after a tournament, it's easy to say we start fresh or it's a new start, but I don't think it is that.

“I think it's a continuation, he’s been here for two years. A lot of the squad have been together and at the World Cup, so let's continue what we've done because we have done a lot of good things.

“It’s easier said than done, but if we can get better at that I think we'll show an even better version of ourselves. So that was kind of the general meeting really. We're still going to talk about the summer and talk about good and bad. That will happen naturally over the next year.”

‌



Heartbroken Kane could not bear to watch the World Cup final - even though he was in the same city. He flew from Miami after the third place play-off straight to New York to see his family, play golf and relax after the campaign.

But Kane admitted he did not watch Spain defeat Argentina and made himself busy by hitting the golf course before going on a family holiday.

View 4 Images Kane was left heartbroken after England's defeat to Spain (Image: Getty Images)

Kane said: “I didn’t watch it. Funnily enough, I was in New York playing golf, I flew straight to New York straight after the third and fourth play-off, spent a couple of days there, would like to say hiding in New York but New York was the busiest place in the world at that point.

‌



“But to be honest, I have got some friends there, I was out and about and whether it was on the golf course or restaurants, the support and the amount of people that came up to me and said how proud they were of England and me and the team.

“Those are the moments that you start to appreciate everything you have been through. And a lot of Americans as well, the amount of impact it had in America and with their sports as well, although I wasn’t in New York for the reason I wanted to be in New York.

“It was a nice eye-opener of there is stuff to be proud of and you have got to hold your head up high and move on, it was quite a nice couple of days just switching off.”

Kane said the best medicine after the World Cup heartbreak was just enjoying some much-needed family time.

‌



He added: “The first time I saw them, they were so excited to see me. It does bring you straight back to that world. I am playing football with my son out on the grass, going out on the trampolines with my daughters, back to being a dad.

“Sometimes it is hard to make that switch but whoever is in the room who is a dad knows it happens naturally. They are the most important things to get back to enjoying that life.”

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
