World.title: Trump says Canada is 'destroying itself' with immigration. Ministers say that's bogus
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at Canadian immigration policies on Wednesday, saying the country is "destroying itself" by allowing "millions" of people into the country without proper security checks — comments federal ministers say are ill-informed and grossly inaccurate.

In a social media post, Trump claimed that Canada is letting too many people in and those who are coming are "essentially unchecked and unvetted" and that's "causing problems that will soon be too big to handle."

All prospective residents go through a multi-step screening process jointly led by Canada's border, security and intelligence agencies. The number of recent arrivals is far fewer than the "millions" the president cited.

"It is a Liberal takeover that will end very badly," Trump said in his latest broadside against Canada.

After a post-COVID surge in new arrivals, the Liberal government led by Prime Minister Mark Carney has slammed the brakes on immigration, curtailing the number of temporary residents, particularly students. That followed the Trudeau government lowering its immigration targets in the fall of 2024.

According to federal figures compiled by the parliamentary budget officer, the number of permanent residents admitted last year returned to pre-pandemic levels with about 328,000 new additions.

The number of temporary residents has plummeted from a peak of 789,000 newcomers in 2023 to a net loss of 382,000 last year.

Statistics Canada data released on Wednesday shows that population growth is at a decades-low level with a year-over-year increase of 189,425 people. That is the lowest annual population growth since 1944-45, the agency said.

That 0.5 per cent annual growth rate is roughly the same level reported in the U.S. under Trump's leadership, according to U.S. Census Bureau figures.

"Let's put some facts on the table," Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York when asked about Trump's comments.

WATCH | Minister responds to Trump comments: Minister says immigration increases Canadian prosperity following Trump comments | Duration closed caption 1:22 Asked about U.S. President Donald Trump's social media post claiming Canada's immigration polices have led to 'big unemployment,' Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the government has since 2024 reduced immigration levels to 'stabilize' supports for all Canadians.

"Canada has had a revised immigration policy since 2024 and we are certainly ensuring our immigration levels, including temporary foreign workers, are reduced in order to stabilize the supports that are available to all Canadians," Anand said.

She said Canada has deliberately curtailed immigration and restored some "stability" to the system to make more homes and health-care services available to the people who are already here.

Rather than something that is "destroying" Canada, Anand said overall immigration has "led to increased Canadian prosperity, especially from an economic standpoint," but the government recognizes that past immigration levels were too high.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser, who was immigration minister during a period of particularly high migration during and after the pandemic, said Trump's claim that people are coming in unvetted is bogus.

"Obviously that's not an accurate depiction of Canada's immigration system," Fraser said. "We scan for security purposes every application for a person seeking to come into this country."

Still, some advocates in this country have said the government needs to scrutinize incoming foreign students more closely. Some alleged Bishnoi gang members have entered Canada on student permits.

Since the Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed and Trump imposed another round of tariffs that are deeply unpopular stateside, the president has been seized with Canada and its leadership.

On Monday, Trump claimed the U.S. would buy potash from Belarus over Canada, even though the Russian-aligned dictator who runs that country says it has none to sell the Americans. Trump later walked back those comments.

Last week, as Carney signalled he wanted Canada to draw closer to the European Union through an "alliance for the future," Trump dismissed that proposed alignment as "laughable."

And he said Canada has been a "terrible trade partner," even though it was his administration that launched a trade war designed to destroy key sectors of the Canadian economy and seems uninterested in the North American trade deal he negotiated in his first term.

World.title: Cineplex may be going up for sale, company says in announcement of new CEO
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Cineplex is considering a potential sale, the company revealed in a statement announcing former Landmark Cinemas head Bill Walker as its new CEO, adding that while the board is confident in the company's future prospects, it is evaluating all avenues.

"The Board has initiated a Strategic Review to evaluate opportunities to enhance and maximize value for all shareholders," a memo on Walker's appointment said Wednesday.

"As part of the Strategic Review, the Board will consider a range of alternatives, including, but not limited to, a potential sale of the Company."

Goldman Sachs and TD Securities have been engaged as co-financial advisers for the strategic review, the company says.

According to Cineplex, the company is the largest cinema chain in Canada, operating more than 1,600 movie screens across nearly 170 movie theatres nationwide, and employing more than 10,000 people in its theatres and entertainment venues.

The last time Cineplex was up for sale was in 2019, when the company agreed to a $2.8-billion buyout by U.K.-based Cineworld Group PLC. However, the deal fell through .

Cineplex was last up for sale in 2019, but the $2.8 billion takeover by Cineworld was cancelled. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

Former CEO Ellis Jacob will serve as a special adviser to the board during the strategic review.

Phyllis Yaffe, chair of Cineplex's board, said that Cineplex has a "strong market position [and] portfolio of leading entertainment assets."

"However, we believe the Company's current market valuation may not fully reflect the strength of its business and long-term prospects," Yaffe said.

Walker previously led Landmark Cinemas, Canada's second-largest theatre exhibitor, and oversaw its sale to Kinepolis in 2017.

He said in the statement that he supported the strategic review, and that "regardless of the outcome," his focus would be on "driving operational excellence, delivering exceptional guest experiences and superior outcomes for shareholders."

World.title: Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Southwestern Mexico braced for coastal flooding and mudslides Wednesday after Polo, a powerful Pacific cyclone, became a major hurricane. Forecasters also warned that Hawaii could face another onslaught of harsh weather later in the week.

Hurricane Polo, an "extremely dangerous" storm, is expected to skirt Mexico's Guerrero state, submerging coastal areas with 10 to 15 centimetres of rain through Thursday, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami. Guerrero has been repeatedly pummelled by hurricanes in recent years.

Polo, which was swirling a few hundred kilometres off the coast Wednesday afternoon, was not expected to make landfall, meteorologists and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said. Rain and strong winds had already started to pummel the coast, with waves crashing onto the normally pristine beaches.

Tropical storm conditions including torrential rain and extraordinary wind were also expected along the Pacific coast of Michoacan and Colima states through Thursday.

I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before | Duration 3:17 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a 'super' El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this 'super' El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

At its peak, Polo was a Category 5 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 290 km/h. It was a Category 4 by Wednesday afternoon, but still packing sustained winds of up to 230 km/h.

"Fluctuations in intensity are expected, but Polo is expected to remain a very powerful major hurricane during the next few days," the hurricane centre said.

LISTEN | Experts discuss what could transpire in months ahead: What on Earth? 25:02 Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?

Concepción López Villegas was busily bolstering her seaside restaurant in Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán, against the expected onslaught of rain.

Strong waves were already hitting some beaches and López Villegas said she feared the storm could destroy the small business she worked decades to build.

"We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed."

The hurricane centre warned that Polo's deluge could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, in particular in Guerrero.

The region most under threat from the hurricane is rural and mountainous, scattered with a few small tourist towns and ports. Much of the area is marked by poverty and residents routinely complain authorities abandon them to fend for themselves during natural disasters.

Mexico's government has called for evacuations in some areas and set up shelters for those affected. Thousands of military and Red Cross personnel have been deployed to the region as a preventative measure.

A partially submerged boat is seen in Acapulco Bay as strong waves and winds caused by Hurricane Polo were evident in Acapulco, Mexico, on Tuesday. (Francisco Robles/AFB/Getty Images)

Phil Klotzbach, research scientist in the department of atmospheric science at Colorado State University, attributed Polo's rapid intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, which has fuelled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods elsewhere.

In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said.

"There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said.

Mexican National Guard members on Tuesday warned beachgoers and tourists in Acapulco, Mexico, of the potential dangerous effects from Polo. (Javier Verdin/Reuters)

Separate hurricane could hit Hawaii

A tropical depression about 845 kilometres south-southeast of Hawaii's capital, Honolulu, could be a tropical storm by the end of the day and a hurricane by Thursday.

The hurricane centre advised the island chain to monitor the system, which was projected to drop 38 to 51 centimetres of rain on Big Island, raising the possibility of flooding and mudslides.

The centre of the cyclone was expected to close in on the islands by Friday or Saturday.

While wind and rain were mainly expected on Maui and Big Island, Kauai's electric co-operative urged residents to prepare for "the possibility of prolonged power outages," and to store non-perishable food and potable water.

Over 100 Kauai households remain without power from Hurricane Lowell, which passed west of the island on Sept. 7.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's primary utility, said crews would return to at-risk areas to help residents prepare for the coming storm.

World.title: Is it unprofessional to bring iced coffee to a job interview? Gen Z is being dragged for it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The list of acceptable items to bring to a job interview might include, but isn't limited to: your CV, your portfolio, your winning personality, your best foot forward.

But what about your iced latte? That's the debate currently raging online after a job recruiter recently called out Gen Z for showing up to corporate interviews "with iced coffee, iced latte, in hand" in a now-viral TikTok video.

In the video, which has been viewed more than 420,000 times since it was posted last week, U.S. recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen says she believes showing up with an iced beverage comes across as too casual, "like it's just a stop in your list of errands for the day."

"It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks and now you’re stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing," Wehniainen said.

"Don't just waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand."

The video has divided generations and the internet, with some agreeing that bringing a beverage to a job interview is unprofessional and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.

"It's not about the f--king coffee,"someone posted on Threads. "It's about reading the room, being able to be part of a community and society, compromise, and tolerate discomfort," they added.

It's about basic etiquette, someone else commented on Reddit.

"Arriving at an interview with a beverage for only yourself would be just as impolite as if the interviewer were drinking coffee but didn’t offer you a beverage," they added.

Conversely, how a company reacts to a beverage is a litmus test, others argued.

"In 2026 being YOU is a competitive advantage, and any environment that tries to micromanage something as small as whether or not you brought coffee to an interview is NOT a place you will thrive," marketing professional Zoë Hartsfield wrote on LinkedIn Tuesday.

"N o wonder 58 per cent of Gen Z has a side hustle or runs their own company."

WATCH | How did the Gen Z job market get so bleak?: How did the Gen Z job market get so bleak? | Duration closed caption 5:25 Gen Z graduates between the ages of 15 and 24 are facing the highest unemployment rate the country has seen in decades, apart from the pandemic. CBC's Paula Duhatschek breaks down what’s behind the surge and what it could mean for a whole generation of Canadians.

Generational divide?

The iced coffee debacle isn't the first time Gen Z has been dragged over etiquette and other so-called soft skills. Last year, the term "Gen Z stare" entered the lexicon, which describes the "blank, expressionless" look that the younger generation gives to older generations, particularly in customer service settings, according to Know Your Meme.

And like the "Gen Z stare," some argue the iced coffee debate touches on deeper issues, like how young adults and teens are coping with the lingering effects of COVID-19 lockdowns while facing the worst youth unemployment rate in decades and having to navigate AI's impact on entry-level jobs and recruitment processes.

Gen Z largely came of age during the isolation of the pandemic, tend to prefer digital communication and report higher rates of anxiety than previous generations. Recent surveys have shown that some managers are hesitant to hire younger workers, citing a lack of soft skills like communication and collaboration.

But is the younger generation really bringing iced coffees into job interviews?

Allison Venditti, a Toronto-based human resources expert, says she can count on one hand the number of times it has happened to her, and that's no different to how often it happened 15 years ago.

"We just have TikTok to hear about it now," Venditti, founder of Moms at Work, an advocacy group for working mothers, told CBC News.

"Most folks, Gen Z or otherwise, take the recruitment process seriously and come well prepared and do a great job."

WATCH | Is the Gen Z stare for real?: Is the ‘Gen Z stare’ for real? | Duration 1:55 According to a recent debate on TikTok, Gen Z has been blankly gazing into the middle distance instead of speaking, especially when interacting with older generations. CBC’s Ashley Fraser breaks down how real this phenomenon is and what could be behind it.

Is there a middle ground?

That said, Venditti says she does have some iced coffee horror stories, like the time someone brought one in to an interview and accidentally dumped it all over themselves and their papers.

"We spent about 15 to 30 minutes cleaning it up. We also had to find a new room to do interviews as it was sticky. It was awful for all involved," she said.

But maybe there's a middle ground, others argued.

If you do bring an iced beverage into a job interview, don't swirl it around, slurp, put it on the interviewer's desk or hold it in your right hand, since that will make it wet when you shake hands, says Benjamin Chipman, a branding and marketing specialist based in New York City.

"You maybe have one sip that you get to take throughout the entire interview, because that is your opportunity to think a little bit when they are asking you a question," he said in a video posted to LinkedIn.

Which is better than responding with a Gen Z stare, some might argue.

Regardless, the short answer to whether bringing an iced coffee into an interview is unprofessional, is "yes," Venditti says.

"Would you bring a sandwich? No? Then don't bring that, either."

An embattled for-profit plasma centre in Winnipeg is now officially suspended from collecting the blood component, after Health Canada cited concerns about its "quality management system" in the wake of a donor's death last year.

The federal agency suspended Grifols's Taylor Avenue plasma centre licence "effective immediately," the regulator announced in an email Wednesday afternoon.

Advocates have been calling on the federal government to crack down on the company after CBC News reported two people died in the past year after donating plasma at Grifols clinics in Winnipeg, including the Taylor location.

Grifols had already temporarily shut down collection at the rest of its Canadian centres last month, citing " unfounded attention" on paid plasma collection in Canada.

"Grifols had not effectively implemented some corrective and preventive actions and, overall, it failed to demonstrate that the Taylor Avenue site has implemented an effective quality management system," Health Canada said Wednesday.

A spokesperson for the Spain-based company said the licence suspension has no impact on its current operations, since collection had already been paused.

The company is working with Health Canada on a reopening plan for its collection centres, the spokesperson said in an emailed statement sent Wednesday.

As of Sept. 1, the company has acquired full ownership of its Canadian operations, the spokesperson wrote, and since then it has been retraining staff and strengthening its procedures.

Fatal cardiac arrest during donation

Grifols operates 17 centres in Canada that pay people for their plasma, including two in Winnipeg.

The now-suspended Taylor Avenue centre is where Rodiyat Alabede, 22, suffered a fatal cardiac arrest while donating plasma on Oct. 25, 2025.

Katherine Lanteigne, an advocate for Alabede and her family, said she was shocked Health Canada didn't suspend Grifols's licences across Canada, noting the agency has found issues during inspections at other locations, including Grifols locations in Regina and Calgary, and its Oakville, Ont., head office.

"The same activities that are happening at the Taylor site are happening other Grifols sites countrywide," she said.

Lanteigne said the only path forward is a police investigation into Alabede's death.

"My biggest fear is that they will not be held accountable in the appropriate way," she said.

WATCH | Winnipeg Grifols centre's licence suspended by Health Canada: Winnipeg plasma collection centre's licence suspended: Health Canada | Duration closed caption 1:01 Health Canada announced Wednesday it has suspended the licence of the Grifols plasma collection centre on Taylor Avenue in Winnipeg, saying it failed to address deficiencies found by the health regulator during a recent inspection. That's the same location where a 22-year-old woman suffered a fatal cardiac arrest while donating plasma last year.

The federal regulator initially inspected the Taylor Avenue site roughly a month after Alabede died and found multiple deficiencies it directed Grifols to fix.

After inspecting it twice more over the summer, Health Canada warned Grifols it could suspend the company's licence if the issues weren't addressed.

Health Canada said it proposed suspending Grifols's licence on Aug. 13 and gave the company "an opportunity to be heard."

That same day, Grifols announced it was pausing plasma collection at all of its Canadian locations. It described the pause as voluntary and proactive.

Before the pause and suspension, virtually all of Grifols's locations were already under the regulator's scrutiny.

After its head office in Oakville failed an inspection , Health Canada slapped new terms and conditions on its licence for "recurring, systemic deficiencies" that applied to 16 of its centres.

The Winnipeg Innovation Drive site, officially known as Grifols Canada Plasma II Inc., was left out because it operates under a separate licence.

Health Canada said it will work with Grifols as it tries to restart operations and implement corrective action plans.

"Prior to resuming operations, Health Canada will verify Grifols's compliance with our regulatory requirements and we will not hesitate to take further action if needed," the agency's email said.

After the two deaths in Winnipeg, Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara previously said a ban on paid plasma donation in the province was one option on the table.

In an emailed statement Wednesday, the minister said "all options remain" around paid plasma collection in the province, and said "this latest development will be part of that consideration."

The minister said they expect Grifols to fully address the identified deficiencies before collection resumes.

World.title: Trump greets Xi on tarmac as Chinese leader arrives for state visit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday, where he was met with a rare planeside greeting from U.S. President Donald Trump, who was there to welcome his counterpart instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House.

Trump's decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far he is going to honour China's leader as he made his first state visit to the U.S. capital in more than a decade.

A 30-metre-long red carpet was unfurled at the bottom of the staircase placed at the door of Xi's plane. A 21-person honour guard was arrayed on the sides of the carpet and Trump and first lady Melania Trump stood near a staircase on the side of the plane, where they greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, with handshakes.

Two American children presented bouquets of yellow-colored flowers to Xi and his wife. The welcome ceremony also included a flyover by two B-1 bombers, platoons from each military service, and a presentation of the flags and anthems of both countries.

Trump and his wife spoke inaudibly to their counterparts. Trump, who wore gloves and an overcoat though it was a relatively warm 17 C outside, removed one of his gloves to shake hands with Xi. At one point, he slapped Xi on the back and said something to him that was inaudible.

The salutation kicks off a three-day visit that's expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump's May visit to China.

But it is also a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan.

U.S. senator critical of 'lavish welcome' for Xi

Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend, all while giving him a pass on many issues.

WATCH | China, the U.S. and concerns about AI: Why U.S. and China may have to co-operate on AI guardrails | Duration closed caption 2:42 Chinese and U.S. economic officials have begun talks ahead of a meeting between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping, where AI safety is expected to be a top issue.

Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." Wicker said during a speech Tuesday in the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader "based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party."

Wicker archly suggested a list of topics that Trump could discuss with Xi at the state dinner, such as "the purposes of China's massive military buildup, or about China's clear support for Iran."

He said that "during every minute of dialogue" Trump should keep in mind that "his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbours and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. and China must interact at the highest levels because the countries are "the two largest economies in the world" and "probably the two most powerful militaries in the world."

"The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It's outrageous. We have to," Rubio told reporters Wednesday while he was in New York.

Match of pageantry for Trump

Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new "work-of-art" helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not.

Trump on Wednesday was looking to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. While Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump, a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing.

A plane carrying Xi and wife Peng is seen taxiing at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Wednesday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

A military honour guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present. The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional paint colors of the presidential plane.

First lady Melania Trump said earlier Wednesday her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrived in the Washington region because "they have a great relationship."

"He's coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect," she said of Xi and his wife during an interview on Fox News Channel's Fox & Friends.

The long red carpet recalled a similar extra-long one the U.S. laid out for Russian President Vladimir Putin when he touched down at a U.S. Air Force base in Alaska last summer for a summit aimed at trying to find an end to Russia's war in Ukraine.

When Putin arrived in August 2025, he shook hands with Trump while both grinned. They then took the unusual step of climbing into Trump's limo to share a ride to the building where they were holding talks.

On Wednesday at the end of the arrival ceremony, Xi and his wife climbed into their own car, and the Trumps retreated to theirs.

Trump is seen arriving at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, where he greeted Xi. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Trump's airport ceremony for Xi will be followed on Thursday by more formalities, including an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Before a black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk, the two leaders are expected to dive into the weighty issues behind closed doors, even as expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs.

On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries.
