World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: Prague Taxi Drivers Could Be Tested on Czech and Local Geography
World.content:
Prague taxi drivers could soon be required to demonstrate their knowledge of Czech and the city’s geography.

The Chamber of Deputies approved the change on Wednesday as part of an amendment to the Road Traffic Act. The legislation does not automatically introduce testing in Prague or other Czech cities. Instead, it would give municipalities the authority to impose such requirements.



Under the amendment, municipalities could test taxi drivers on their legal rights and obligations, their Czech language skills to the extent necessary for the job, and their knowledge of locations within the municipality that are relevant to taxi services.

The bill now goes to the Senate.

What the new rules could mean for taxi drivers

The issue has been debated in Prague for some time, particularly as the taxi industry has changed with the rapid growth of app-based services.

Pirate Party leader Zdeněk Hřib introduced a more detailed proposal in May. That version included specific provisions defining what drivers could be required to know and what would fall outside the scope of the tests.

For example, the proposal said drivers should not be expected to demonstrate encyclopedic knowledge of Prague’s landmarks. Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik of the SPD, however, argued that the Pirate Party’s proposal had legal shortcomings.

A shorter amendment submitted by ANO MP Patrik Nacher ultimately became the version approved by the Chamber of Deputies.

Supporters of the change say taxi driving has increasingly become a profession with few formal qualification requirements beyond holding a driving licence.

The explanatory report accompanying the legislation argues that the sector has attracted foreign workers who may have limited knowledge of Czech, local traffic rules and the city in which they operate.

Critics, meanwhile, have raised concerns about the potential impact on fares. They argue that additional requirements could increase the cost of entering the profession and eventually lead to higher prices for passengers.

No English requirement in the legislation

The approved amendment refers specifically to knowledge of the Czech language. It does not introduce an English-language requirement, even though some taxi drivers in Prague also have limited English skills.

The legislation would apply to taxi drivers regardless of whether they operate independently or through digital platforms such as Uber and Bolt.

Foreign nationals make up roughly half of Prague’s registered taxi drivers, reflecting the sector’s long-standing reliance on foreign workers and recently arrived migrants.

World.title: More Than 250 People Fall Ill in Salmonella Outbreak at Prague School
World.content:
More than 240 children and 10 adults have developed gastrointestinal symptoms in connection with a suspected Salmonella outbreak at a school in Prague’s Újezd nad Lesy district.

Masaryk Elementary School, which has around 1,100 pupils, is being temporarily closed while health authorities investigate the source of the infection. The school’s kitchen and cafeteria will also undergo thorough disinfection.



Salmonella has so far been confirmed by laboratory tests in four children, according to Petra Batok, a spokesperson for the Prague Public Health Authority. Officials are continuing to investigate how the infection entered the school.

The first cases were reported earlier this week. The largest number of illnesses has been recorded among upper-level pupils and children attending Montessori classes. Classes for those groups were cancelled on Wednesday, while all pupils have been given Thursday and Friday off.

Food samples taken from the school cafeteria have been sent for laboratory testing, with results expected on Friday.

The final number of people affected is not yet known. Health officials are collecting additional information through questionnaires completed by parents and adults who visited the cafeteria.

The Prague public health authorities have described the incident as an epidemic.

Prague emergency services have received 55 calls from people reporting gastrointestinal symptoms in connection with the outbreak.

Twenty patients were transported to hospitals for treatment, while another 24 were examined and treated without being admitted. The remaining people received medical advice by telephone.

Salmonellosis is usually contracted by consuming contaminated food. Common sources include eggs, insufficiently cooked meat, unpasteurized milk and foods containing raw or unpasteurized eggs. Symptoms generally appear between 13 and 36 hours after infection.

World.title: Prague Metro and Tram Disruptions Planned for September 28 Weekend
World.content:
Prague commuters should expect changes to metro and tram services from Saturday, September 26, through Monday, September 28, as maintenance work affects Metro Line C and tram routes in Libeň.

Metro Line C will be suspended between Pražského povstání and Chodov for the entire long weekend. Trains will continue running between Letňany and Pražského povstání, while the southern section between Chodov and Háje will operate as a shuttle service.



Four stations will be affected by the closure: Pankrác, Budějovická, Kačerov and Roztyly. Passengers can use replacement bus XC, which will run between Pražského povstání and Chodov via all four stations.

Hundreds of railway sleepers to be replaced

The closure will allow Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) workers to replace several hundred wooden sleepers with concrete ones.

Once the work is completed, around 17,000 of the approximately 20,000 original sleepers between Florenc and Kačerov will have been replaced.

DPP said the work is scheduled during long weekends because the materials used to secure the new sleepers need more time to harden than a standard weekend allows.

Tram services suspended in Libeň

Tram services will also be disrupted between Palmovka and Ke Stírce from early Saturday morning until 6 p.m. Monday.

Several lines will operate on modified routes. Tram 3 will run via Těšnov, Vltavská, Strossmayerovo náměstí, Výstaviště, Nádraží Holešovice, Hercovka, Ke Stírce, Kobylisy and Ládví before terminating at Sídliště Ďáblice.

Line 10 will run from Palmovka via Balabenka and Arena Libeň jih to Nádraží Libeň, while lines 24 and 95 will terminate at Palmovka.

Replacement bus X3 will operate during the day between Palmovka, Bulovka, Ke Stírce and Kobylisy. Night service will be provided by bus X95, which will continue to Vozovna Kobylisy.

Passengers using Prague public transport over the long weekend should allow extra travel time and check the latest DPP information before travelling.

World.title: Czech Man Jailed 13 Days After Protest on Moscow’s Red Square
World.content:
A judge at Moscow’s Tverskoy District Court sentenced a Czech man to 13 days in jail on Tuesday for staging a protest on Red Square.

Identified as Michal Plamenek, the man was arrested for holding up a sign in English next to Lenin’s Mausoleum on Sunday afternoon, the court’s press service said in a statement.



No details were provided as to what was written on Plamenek’s sign, but the court press service said a judge ruled that the inscription was “aimed at discrediting the Russian Armed Forces.”

Police officers arrested Plamenek because Red Square directly adjoins the Kremlin, where protests are banned. He allegedly refused to listen to a request by officers to accompany them to a police station and resisted arrest.

A judge found Plamenek guilty on three separate administrative counts of discrediting the Russian military, violating protest rules and disobeying a police officer.

He was also fined a total of 60,000 roubles, around CZK 15,000.

The Czech Foreign Ministry said its embassy in Moscow has been providing the detained man with consular assistance from the outset. It declined to comment further because of the sensitivity of the case.

World.title: Heating Season Starts Across Czechia as Temperatures Fall
World.content:
District heating plants across the Czech Republic are beginning to supply heat as temperatures drop, with conditions for the start of the heating season now being met in much of the country.

Some plants have already begun providing additional heat during the colder morning and evening hours. The first systems to respond were mainly in mountainous parts of northern and western Czechia and in the Vysočina region.



Other heating plants are expected to gradually start operating in the coming days, depending on local temperatures and weather forecasts.

Since 2010, district heating systems have generally started supplying heat after September 20, although the exact timing varies considerably from year to year.

If temperatures rise again in late September or early October, heating can be suspended. Under the standard rules, heating is normally interrupted when the average outdoor temperature exceeds 13°C for two consecutive days and the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue to rise.

Last winter was colder than average

The previous heating season placed greater demands on heating systems than the years immediately before it.

According to figures from the Czech District Heating Association, the season was 4.9 percent colder than the previous year. It was also 3.2 percent colder than the average of the preceding 15 years.

The colder conditions translated into higher demand for heat, particularly during periods of sustained low temperatures.

Heating costs could increase next year

Households are not currently expected to face a direct increase resulting from a recent change in the interpretation of a fuel tax exemption, but some other users of district heating could see higher costs.

The issue concerns combined heat and power (CHP) generation. This year, the state changed how an existing fuel tax exemption is interpreted, limiting its application to the amount of heat supplied to households.

Heating companies say the change could increase annual heating bills for institutions such as hospitals and schools by tens or even hundreds of thousands of Czech crowns.

World.title: Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague’s Roxy Club
World.content:
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.

Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.



A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.

Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.

More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.

Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.

The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.

The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.

The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.

Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

World.title: Prague and the 15-Minute City? Only for One in Seven Residents
World.content:
In the first year of the Friendly City Index, Prague ranked second among Central and Eastern European metropolises.

Yet only 13.82% of residents can reach most daily destinations – work, schools, shops, or healthcare – within 15 minutes. The best metropolises in the region remain closer to “30-minute cities.”



Young Czechs are closest to the ideal: 34% of those aged 18–24 said they can reach everyday destinations within 15 minutes. Middle-aged people, especially 45–54, scored the worst at 14.7%.

Smaller Czech cities outperform Prague. Olomouc (36%), Ostrava (29.7%), and Brno (21.8%) all ranked better in their categories. Compact urban structures and shorter distances explain much of this advantage. Polish cities also dominated the rankings, including Krakow, Szczecin, and Lublin.

Among metropolises, Warsaw leads with 15.9%. In other categories: Krakow (30.3%), Split (44%), Rijeka (53.3%), and Zadar (53.6%). Riga ranked worst at 9.8%, while Zagreb scored only 20%.

The smaller the city, the better the accessibility

Around 10–15% in metropolises, 30% in large cities, 40%+ in medium-sized cities, and over 50% in small cities. Even cities with metro systems like Prague or Bucharest show little improvement, confirming that compactness and urban structure matter more than infrastructure alone.

Transport habits

In Central and Eastern Europe, 46% rely on cars and 27% on public transport. In Czechia, the split is nearly even: 42.6% drive, 42.4% use public transport. Among 18–24-year-olds, more than half (51.1%) rely on public transport. Alternative mobility options such as bikes, scooters, and carsharing remain marginal.

Urban planner Peter Bednár explains: “The point is not that all journeys must be short, but that most daily activities can be done without a car. Achieving this requires higher density and a mix of functions. Without enough services and destinations nearby, the most practical walk still leads to the parked car.”

About the index

The Friendly City Index is an international survey on quality of life and urban development. In 2025, it covered 54 cities in nine countries with 4,500 respondents, including 500 in Czechia. The study was carried out by Syno International in partnership with Bolt.

World.title: Hungarian police raid Fidesz-linked think tank over suspected misuse of public funds
World.content:
Hungarian police raided a company linked to the pro-Fidesz Centre for Fundamental Rights as part of an investigation into suspected financial mismanagement. The operation has sparked a strong reaction from opposition party Fidesz, which has condemned the investigation as politically motivated.

Hungary’s National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) announced on 23 September that it was investigating suspected criminal mismanagement involving a publicly funded company associated with the Centre for Fundamental Rights (Alapjogokért Központ), a conservative think tank closely linked to Fidesz.

According to the official police statement , the company allegedly paid a former foreign official, currently subject to an international arrest warrant, more than HUF 3.5 million gross per month despite minimal actual work.

Police seize documents and question witnesses

Investigators searched the company’s Budapest premises, its accounting firm and the former official’s last known Hungarian address. Officers seized contracts, invoices, payroll records and other documents, while also collecting data from the company’s servers. Several witnesses were questioned.

Photo: Police.hu

The investigation is being conducted against an unidentified perpetrator. Police said the seized materials would be examined to establish the circumstances of the payments and determine whether criminal wrongdoing occurred.

If you missed it: PM Péter Magyar accuses prosecutors of ‘protecting mobsters’ in escalating immunity row

Fidesz names former Polish minister and condemns raid

Although police did not identify the foreign official, Fidesz named former Polish Deputy Justice Minister Marcin Romanowski in its subsequent statement.

Romanowski served in Poland’s previous Law and Justice government and is wanted by Polish authorities over allegations involving the country’s Justice Fund. He faces allegations relating to 18 offences, including participation in an organised criminal group suspected of causing losses to state assets.

Romanowski was granted asylum in Hungary under Viktor Orbán’s former government. He is wanted by Polish authorities over allegations concerning the management of the country’s Justice Fund.

In a statement reported by Hungarian News Agency MTI , Fidesz described the searches as politically motivated and without legal basis.

The party accused Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s Tisza government of using law enforcement authorities against political opponents. It also maintained that Romanowski’s employment was lawful and that he had received appropriate payment for his work.

Centre for Fundamental Rights responds

Following the searches, the Centre for Fundamental Rights maintained that it had operated in accordance with the law since its establishment, including in its cooperation with foreign researchers.

In a Facebook statement, the organisation said:

“We are ready to cooperate with the authorities on any matter, as a lawful procedure can only establish that we have complied with all legal requirements.”

The centre also highlighted its international and regional partnerships, maintaining that these activities served Hungary’s interests. The criminal investigation remains ongoing, and yet no determination of criminal liability has been announced.

World.title: Hungarian ambulance service apologises after celebrating rescue of man buried that same day
World.content:
Hungary’s National Ambulance Service (OMSZ) has publicly apologised after sharing a Facebook post celebrating the resuscitation of a man who had subsequently died. His wife revealed that her husband’s funeral was taking place on the very day the organisation published the story.

Hungary’s National Ambulance Service updated its earlier Facebook post with an apology on Wednesday, 23 September, following criticism over its account of a man’s emergency treatment.

The organisation had published the story on Monday, highlighting the efforts of paramedics who repeatedly resuscitated a patient in his forties. However, the man’s wife commented on the post, explaining that her husband had died and that he was being buried that day.

The ambulance service initially edited the post for reasons of respect for the deceased and expressed its condolences to the family. On Wednesday, it added a further update containing a public apology.

In the statement, the organisation wrote:

“We regret that the post in this form may have caused additional pain to the family, and we therefore apologise. In light of the lessons learned from this incident, we will review our practices for presenting individual patient cases on social media.”

Wife discovers ambulance service’s Facebook post on husband’s funeral day

The man’s wife responded to the ambulance service’s original Facebook post, revealing that her husband had died on 6 September. She explained that the family was holding his funeral on the same day the organisation published its account of the emergency.

The original post praised the medical team’s efforts and expressed hope that the patient would recover, without mentioning his subsequent death.

Following the woman’s comment, OMSZ amended the post and offered its condolences. However, the initial revision did not include an apology, which was only added in the 23 September update.

How paramedics fought to save the man’s life

According to the ambulance service’s account, the emergency began at a family home in Pest County, where a woman noticed unusual gasping sounds coming from the bedroom.

Her husband, who was around 40 years old, had been resting, but she was unable to wake him. She immediately called emergency services.

An emergency dispatcher guided her through checking his breathing and starting resuscitation while an ambulance and an emergency response vehicle were sent to the scene. When paramedics arrived, they took over treatment, with an advanced life-support ambulance later joining the operation.

The man was transported to hospital while resuscitation efforts continued. During the journey, his circulation returned several times before collapsing again, requiring paramedics to perform chest compressions and use a defibrillator.

Despite the repeated cardiac arrests, the emergency crews managed to hand the patient over to hospital staff with his circulation restored. Although the paramedics had successfully restored his circulation during the emergency, this did not mean that he had recovered or survived in the longer term.

Following the incident, the National Ambulance Service has apologised to the family and announced that it will review its approach to sharing individual patient stories on social media.

If you missed it: Two suspects arrested over fatal Budapest stabbing

World.title: Half of Hungarian workers have changed careers – and money is a growing factor
World.content:
Half of Hungarian workers have changed careers at least once, while four in ten now work in a completely different field from where they started. New research reveals which sectors workers are most likely to leave and what is driving Hungarians to seek new career paths.

A new representative survey of Hungarian workers found that 54% of career changers would have stayed in their previous profession for a higher salary, while 40% said better management and a more positive workplace atmosphere could have persuaded them to stay, according to a study published by Profession.hu.

The research found that half of respondents had changed careers at least once, with 40% now working in an entirely different field and industry from where they originally started. A further 30% had seriously considered changing careers but ultimately decided against it. Only one in five workers said they had never considered such a move.

Higher salaries are becoming increasingly important for career changers

One of the survey’s main findings is that financial considerations have become more influential in career decisions over recent years.

In 2022, 42% of career changers said they would have stayed in their previous profession if they had been offered a higher salary. By 2026, that figure had risen to 54%.

According to Blanka Dencső, market research and business development expert at Profession.hu, salary remains a decisive factor in job and career changes across all generations.

However, money is not the only factor. Better management and workplace conditions could have persuaded 40% of career changers to remain in their former profession, while 30% cited greater professional recognition.

Related: How to find a job in Hungary in 2026: Salaries, job sites and what foreigners need to know

Which sectors are Hungarian workers most likely to leave?

The survey identified significant differences between industries. IT and technology, healthcare and social care, and manufacturing tend to retain professionals relatively well. Although employees in these sectors may change positions, they are less likely to leave their industry altogether.

By contrast, workers in finance and insurance, agriculture, hospitality and tourism are more likely to move into an entirely different sector.

According to Profession.hu, hospitality and tourism have consistently ranked among the three sectors experiencing the largest declines in job s over the past year.

Besides the shrinking number of vacancies, pay may also be an important consideration. According to figures updated by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) in September, accommodation and food service activities had the lowest average earnings in Hungary in July 2026.

How long does it take to find a new job in Hungary?

One of the biggest questions for anyone considering a career change is how long it might take to secure a new position. Profession.hu examined the time between starting a job search and taking up a new position, meanwhile KSH measured how long people who were still unemployed at the time of its survey had already been looking for work.

According to the Profession.hu survey published in March , the average time between beginning a job search and starting a new position had fallen to three months and 22 days, compared with slightly more than five months a year earlier.

However, the KSH’s latest figures, paint a more challenging picture for unemployed jobseekers.

Between May and July 2026, unemployed people in Hungary had been looking for work for an average of 12 months. Furthermore, 34.7% had been searching for more than a year, an increase of 5.5 percentage points compared with the same period a year earlier. The figures illustrate how differently job searches can unfold for people moving between positions and those who remain unemployed.

Rising costs and economic uncertainty are also driving career changes

Changing careers is not always simply about finding better opportunities. The broader economic environment can also influence workers’ decisions.

Therefore ising prices, inflation and economic uncertainty played a role in the decisions of 36% of career changers. Profession’s research also found that career changes were particularly common among workers with secondary-level qualifications and those living in smaller settlements. Among these groups, 56% and 60%, respectively, had changed careers at least once.

The findings suggest that changing careers is increasingly about adapting to shifting economic and labour market conditions, rather than simply pursuing a new professional direction.

World.title: Hungary set to get another public holiday: Christmas Eve bill submitted
World.content:
Hungary could soon have 12 official public holidays instead of 11, as lawmakers from the governing Tisza Party have submitted legislation to make Christmas Eve a permanent day off. If approved, the change could take effect before Christmas 2026, while most shops would be required to close on 24 December.

A bill to make Christmas Eve an official public holiday was submitted to the Hungarian Parliament on Wednesday, 23 September, by three lawmakers from the governing Tisza Party, Hungarian News Agency MTI reported.

According to the legislative proposal published on Parliament’s website , the measure is intended to strengthen work-life balance and allow more people to spend Christmas Eve with their families.

The proposal describes Christmas Eve as a day of “togetherness, peace, love and consideration for one another, regardless of religious belief”, while also recognising the Christian origins of Christmas and its particular significance for believers.

The bill also calls for shops to remain closed on 24 December, with certain exceptions, to allow as many retail employees as possible to enjoy the festive break with their families.

What would change for workers in Hungary?

Under the current Labour Code, Hungary has 11 statutory public holidays. Christmas Day and Boxing Day, on 25 and 26 December, are already included, but Christmas Eve is not.

The proposed legislation would add 24 December to that list, creating three consecutive statutory public holidays over Christmas. This issue has been debated for years, trade unions have repeatedly called for Christmas Eve to become an official day off, while several major retail chains have already voluntarily closed their stores on that date.

Before taking office, Prime Minister Péter Magyar also pledged that a Tisza-led government would introduce Christmas Eve as a public holiday.

Most shops would close on Christmas Eve

Under the current rules, shops may generally remain open until 2 PM on Christmas Eve. The proposed amendment would instead require most retailers to remain closed throughout the day.

However, several exemptions would remain. The following establishments would still be permitted to operate:

Restaurants, cafés and other hospitality establishments;

Hotels and other accommodation providers;

Flower shops and confectionery stores;

Petrol stations;

Shops located at railway stations, bus terminals, airports and petrol stations.

Essential services, including healthcare, public safety, transport, energy and utilities, would continue to operate under the existing rules governing work on public holidays.

How many public holidays does Hungary have?

Hungary currently has 11 statutory public holidays. If the proposed amendment is adopted, Christmas Eve would become the 12th, creating three consecutive public holidays from 24 to 26 December.

The number of actual days off varies from year to year, depending on weekends and the arrangement of working days.

For a detailed look at next year’s holiday calendar, including six long weekends, read our earlier guide: Hungary public holidays 2027: six long weekends to plan for.

World.title: Two suspects arrested over fatal Budapest stabbing
World.content:
A Budapest court has ordered the detention of two men suspected of involvement in a fatal stabbing in the city’s popular nightlife district. Both men have previous criminal convictions and allegedly attempted to hide the weapon and their clothing after the attack.

The Buda Central District Court has ordered the two suspects in the Akácfa Street killing to be held in pre-trial detention for one month, according to a statement from the Budapest-Capital Regional Court, as reported by HVG.

A 40-year-old man is suspected of murder, while his 48-year-old accomplice is being investigated for attempted grievous bodily harm.

What happened in Budapest’s Akácfa Street?

According to an official statement from the Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office , the incident took place during the early hours of 18 September near the intersection of Akácfa Street and Dob Street in Budapest’s District VII. The area is part of Budapest’s lively Jewish Quarter, a popular nightlife district known for its ruin bars, restaurants and clubs.

The two suspects allegedly became involved in an argument with a 36-year-old man, which escalated into a physical confrontation.

Investigators believe the younger suspect pulled out a long decorative dagger while his companion assaulted the victim. The 40-year-old allegedly stabbed the victim in the chest after he had fallen to the ground. Despite efforts by emergency medical personnel, the victim died at the scene.

The suspects subsequently fled, changed clothes and attempted to conceal the weapon. During the investigation, officers initially detained another 40-year-old man on 19 September, but he was subsequently released after investigators established that there were no grounds for reasonable suspicion against him.

Eventually Police confirmed that both men were arrested in Budapest’s Csepel district on the evening of 20 September.

If you missed it: British tourist says he remembers nothing of brutal Budapest assault – VIDEO

Suspects may have used drugs

The court considered several factors when ordering the men’s detention, including their previous criminal convictions, other ongoing proceedings and the risk that they could flee or commit further offences.

According to the court’s statement, the available evidence also raised the possibility that the suspects had consumed drugs. Investigators believe the two men involved other individuals in concealing the dagger and their clothing, raising concerns about potential interference with evidence.

The court concluded that pre-trial detention was necessary to address these risks.

One suspect appeals detention ruling

The man suspected of murder and his defence lawyer accepted the court’s decision, making the detention order final in his case. However, the second suspect, who is being investigated for attempted grievous bodily harm, has appealed the ruling. His case will be reviewed by the Budapest-Capital Regional Court.

The criminal investigation remains ongoing, and neither suspect has been convicted in connection with the killing.

Read more from us: Hungarian billionaire Jellinek and former state asset manager chief arrested

World.title: Budapest’s House of Terror Museum is free to visit this week – Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
Budapest’s House of Terror Museum has reopened after a week-long closure, offering free admission to all visitors during its first week back. The reopening follows the dismissal of the museum’s long-serving director, Mária Schmidt, and a demonstration outside the institution. Here is everything you need to know before visiting.

The museum reopened on Tuesday, 22 September, at 10 am. According to Hungarian news agency MTI, considerable public interest greeted the reopening, with a long queue forming outside the building.

Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr announced that admission would be free for everyone during the museum’s first week after reopening, while a professional review of its exhibition continues. The existing exhibition remains accessible to visitors throughout the review.

“During the first week after reopening, admission to the museum will be free for everyone, so that anyone who wishes to see the exhibition, which has sparked heated debate among experts, can do so. We are working to ensure that the House presents the complexity of the past and different perspectives in a credible way, providing a genuine space for confronting history,” Zoltán Tarr wrote on social media.

What can visitors see at the museum?

Opened in 2002, the House of Terror documents Hungary’s experiences under the Nazi and communist dictatorships of the 20th century. Its permanent exhibition explores the Arrow Cross regime, the Soviet occupation and communist rule, including political persecution and the activities of the secret police.

The building itself is also historically significant: Located at 60 Andrássy Avenue, it served as the headquarters of the Arrow Cross Party before being taken over by the communist political police. Today, its exhibitions commemorate the victims of both dictatorships.

For international visitors, the museum offers English-language guided tours for groups of 10 to 30 people, subject to advance booking. English-language audio guides are also available for individual visitors.

According to the museum’s official website, regular admission prices are:

Full-price ticket: HUF 4,000

Reduced-price ticket: HUF 2,000

English-language audio guide: HUF 2,000

English-language guided tour: HUF 20,000 per group (10–30 people).

However, admission is free for everyone during the museum’s first week after reopening, giving visitors the opportunity to explore the exhibition without paying the usual entrance fee. The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday, from 10 am to 6 pm, meaning visitors can take advantage of the offer during the remaining days of this week, through Sunday, 27 September.

If you missed it: Fuel prices in Hungary buck EU trend – but diesel is now climbing fast

Demonstration held after House of Terror museum director’s dismissal

The reopening follows a political dispute over the museum’s future. On 15 September, the government terminated the appointment of long-serving director Mária Schmidt, temporarily closed the institution and announced a review of its operations and exhibition.

The decision prompted a demonstration outside the museum on Sunday, 20 September, organised mainly by Orban supporters and right-wing public figures. Several hundred people gathered on Andrássy Avenue to protest the decision, with opposition Fidesz politician Tamás Menczer and singer Feró Nagy also taking part.

Schmidt addressed the crowd, defending the House of Terror museum’s work and criticising the government’s decision. She argued that the institution’s presentation of Hungary’s 20th-century history should not be changed, while other speakers expressed concerns about the planned review.

Although the government had already announced that the museum would reopen, the organisers proceeded with the demonstration. The professional review remains ongoing, but the existing exhibition will stay open to visitors in the meantime.

World.title: EU moves to unlock €4.2 billion in frozen funds for Hungary
World.content:
The European Commission has proposed unlocking €4.2 billion in frozen EU funds for Hungary, marking a major development in the long-running funding dispute between Budapest and Brussels. The move could also restore full access to Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe for Hungarian students and researchers, following reforms introduced by the country’s new government.

According to the European Commission, Hungary has adequately addressed the previously identified rule-of-law concerns that could have put the European Union’s budget at risk, MTI reported.

“Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union’s financial interests. Today, we are proposing to unlock €4.2 billion and reopen the doors of Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe to Hungarian students and researchers. I am glad that they will once again fully benefit from the opportunities our Union creates. This shows that reforms deliver results.” – said Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission.

The proposal would make €4.2 billion in suspended cohesion policy funding available to Hungary, although it must first receive approval from the Council of the European Union. The proposed €4.2 billion release forms part of a broader €16.4 billion package of previously frozen EU funds for Hungary. As we earlier reported, Prime Minister Péter Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced in May a political agreement aimed at unlocking the funding.

EU funds for Hungary: What has changed?

The European Commission’s decision follows a series of reforms introduced by Hungary’s new government, led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

According to Brussels, Hungary has taken steps to tackle corruption risks, improve transparency in public spending and strengthen oversight of EU funds. The government has also introduced stricter rules to prevent conflicts of interest and expanded the powers of the country’s Integrity Authority.

Another important development was Hungary’s decision to join the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, which investigates crimes involving EU funds.

After reviewing the reforms submitted by Hungary on 9 September, the Commission concluded that the concerns behind the funding restrictions imposed in 2022 had been sufficiently addressed.

If you missed it: PM Péter Magyar accuses prosecutors of ‘protecting mobsters’ in escalating immunity row

Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe could reopen to Hungarian universities

In December 2022, the EU prohibited new funding commitments involving Hungarian public-interest trusts and institutions maintained by them. The restrictions affected the participation of several Hungarian universities in the Erasmus+ student exchange programme and the Horizon Europe research programme.

If the Council approves the Commission’s proposal, the affected institutions would regain full access to both programmes, allowing their students and researchers to participate in EU-funded opportunities again.

The restrictions did not apply to every Hungarian university, but specifically to institutions covered by the measures concerning public-interest trusts.

What happens to the remaining frozen EU funds for Hungary?

Wednesday’s announcement concerns the financial restrictions imposed under the EU’s rule-of-law conditionality mechanism. It does not mean that the entire €16.4 billion package has now been released.

Hungary is also seeking access to €10 billion in recovery funds, with the Commission’s assessment of that request still ongoing. Meanwhile, approximately €2 billion in cohesion funding remains blocked over separate concerns involving the asylum system, child protection legislation and academic freedom.

The next step lies with the Council of the European Union, which has one month to decide whether to lift the measures imposed in 2022, although the deadline may be extended in exceptional circumstances. The decision requires a qualified majority of member states.

Until the Council adopts the proposal, the affected funds for Hungary remains subject to the existing restrictions.

Read more from us: Boycotts and institutional warnings dominate Hungarian parliament session

World.title: PM Péter Magyar accuses prosecutors of ‘protecting mobsters’ in escalating immunity row
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has accused the Prosecutor General’s Office of protecting alleged criminals after prosecutors publicly rejected his criticism of their work. The escalating dispute follows a decision to seek the suspension of the parliamentary immunity of Magyar and two opposition MPs, with the prime minister questioning why the three cases were announced together.

The confrontation continued late on Tuesday, when Magyar responded to a statement from the Prosecutor General’s Office in a comment on Telex’s Facebook page.

“Was this written by some comedian? When you’re protecting mobsters, you’re not so sensitive, you little rascals. The sun will rise soon, and you won’t be able to carry on your shady dealings in the dark,” the prime minister wrote.

Magyar’s remarks came after prosecutors rejected his accusations against the organisation and its staff, insisting that their decisions were based solely on the law and professional considerations.

Péter Magyar questions the prosecution service’s impartiality

The prime minister continued his criticism on Wednesday morning in a separate Facebook post, questioning the prosecution service’s claim that legality and impartiality were its only guiding principles.

“Really? What about the gold convoy case, the MNB foundations, the Rogán-linked bailiff mafia and the alteration of investigation documents? Are you familiar with the term aiding and abetting?” Magyar wrote.

His remarks referred to several investigations and alleged corruption cases involving figures or institutions associated with the previous Orbán administration.

Prosecutor General’s Office rejects the accusations

According to MTI, The Prosecutor General’s Office issued a statement late on Tuesday in response to Magyar’s earlier video message, rejecting his criticism of the organisation and its employees.

“As a participant in the administration of justice, the prosecution service always strives for lawful and proper cooperation with the executive branch. However, this does not mean that it will remain silent in the face of statements that seriously criticise the organisation or its staff,” the statement said.

Prosecutors welcomed Magyar’s stated willingness to facilitate the smooth conduct of criminal proceedings. However, they stressed that legality, impartiality and equality before the law were the only standards governing their constitutional duties.

According to the statement, requests to suspend MPs’ parliamentary immunity are prepared on a strictly legal and professional basis, independently of any political or other considerations.

The office also acknowledged that prosecutors were not infallible but maintained that their decisions were guided by the law and their conscience, regardless of the identity of the suspected offender or victim.

“The Prosecutor General’s Office rejects statements questioning this on behalf of all prosecutors,” the statement concluded.

Related: Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Péter Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

What sparked the dispute over parliamentary immunity?

The confrontation began after the Prosecutor General’s Office requested the suspension of the parliamentary immunity of three politicians: Prime Minister Péter Magyar, Fidesz MP Balázs Hankó and Christian Democrat MP Miklós Seszták.

Magyar’s case relates to a 2024 incident in which he allegedly threw another man’s mobile phone into the Danube following a confrontation at a party. The other two requests concern separate investigations involving alleged financial misconduct.

In a video posted on Facebook on Tuesday evening, Magyar called on the Hungarian Parliament to suspend his immunity without delay. However, he criticised the prosecution service for announcing the three requests together.

The prime minister described the move as the “last pathetic attempt” by what he called the “Polt-era prosecution service” to downplay the change of government.

He accused prosecutors of attempting to equate alleged corruption involving tens or hundreds of billions of forints under the former Orbán administration with what he described as a repeatedly failed political character assassination attempt against him, launched in 2024.

The Prosecutor General’s Office has rejected the suggestion that political considerations influence its decisions.

World.title: Kosovo Court Orders MPs to Elect President by October 6
World.content:
A Kosovo parliament session, September 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Constitutional Court on Wednesday ordered MPs to elect a new head of state by October 6 to avoid new snap elections – which would be the fourth parliamentary polls in two years.

The order comes ten days after the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, filed a complaint, alleging that parliament had exceeded the deadline for its inauguration.

“The 60-day deadline for the election of a President started on August 8 and will expire on October 6,” the court said.

The court rejected the PDK’s request to halt the work of parliament in the meantime and declare the vote on a new government unlawful. It declared parliament already inaugurated and ordered MPs to elect the fifth and final deputy speaker “as soon as possible”.

On September 14, the PDK complained to the court that the inauguration of parliament a day before had violated the rules, while one day later it asked the court to assess whether the parliamentary vote that re-elected Albin Kurti as Prime Minister was valid.

The PDK claims Kurti’s ruling Vetevendosje party violated the 30-day deadline to inaugurate parliament and that the assembly cannot be considered inaugurated until all five deputy speakers are elected.

Prior to this submission, the PDK withdrew its candidate for the post of deputy speaker, while four others were elected. The court has now ruled that parliament must elect the PDK candidate.

Kurti was re-elected Prime Minister by MPs at a session boycotted by the opposition parties. A narrow majority of 62 MPs out of 120 voted for Kurti’s new cabinet. Eight MPs from the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista voted against.

If parliament fails to elect a new President by October 6, new elections will be called within 45 days.

In late August, Vetevendosje’s Kurti and the head of the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, Lumir Abdixhiku, agreed on Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, for the President’s post.

But Sejdiu withdrew from the race on September 14, following disagreements within the LDK parliamentary group over his candidacy.

For a vote electing the President to be valid, at least 80 out of 120 MPs must be present in the chamber. If the first two rounds of voting fail, the third round requires only a simple majority of MPs to elect the President – but at least 80 of them still need to present in the chamber.

Kosovo has been without a President since April 4, when Vjosa Osmani’s five-year term ended. Parliament speaker Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje is serving as Acting President.

Opposition parties had claimed that Vetevendosje may have been preparing the ground for snap elections to be held at the end of December, when many members of the Kosovo diaspora, which mostly supports Kurti, come back to Kosovo for the holidays. However, under the new ruling, any snap elections would have to be held by mid-November.

Perparim Gruda, an MP from the PDK, said that the court’s verdict shows that “the constitution cannot be adapted to the interests of the moment”.

“Vetevendosje could not shift the constitutional deadlines according to its political interest and push the country towards elections on December 27, as it intended,” Gruda said.

World.title: Bulgarian PM Pledges to Sharply Limit Gambling Adverts
World.content:
Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Wednesday announced a new bill targeting the gambling industry including a near-total ban on s.

Drafts to Bulgaria’s Gambling Act are being prepared with the goal of limiting the wide presence of betting and gambling adverts across the country – often endorsed by Bulgarian celebrities and entertainers – as well as curbing addiction issues.

Billboards and posters promoting such activities will now be prohibited. Bright, flashing, illuminated signs and promotional window displays on casinos and gaming halls will also be banned, as Radev complained that “our towns and villages have come to look like Las Vegas”.

“We don’t want gambling to have this everyday presence in the eyes of Bulgarian citizens. We don’t want this aggressive way of advertising, which corrupts young people and children,” Radev told the Ministerial Council.

The law amendments will require foreign operators licensed in Bulgaria to register their financial activities locally, ensuring they pay taxes and remain subject to state control.

Radev has also talked about a new taxation model for casinos and gaming to reflect real financial outcomes, accompanied by stricter anti-money laundering and tax evasion measures. Taxes on online gambling will increase, with a portion of the revenues directed to sports and education.

“Whoever operates on the Bulgarian market, and profits from it, will pay taxes here and be subject to full oversight by the Bulgarian state,” Radev added.

Logos and gambling adverts will now be only allowed on official club jerseys and sports halls.

The law change is expected to be widely supported in parliament, where Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria has a majority of seats, following a landslide election win in April.

Opposition parties have also called for law changes. The opposition Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change parties earlier this month called for law amendments and criticised governments for not acting on accepted regulations from 2024, when the Gambling Act was created.

In 2024, advertising was prohibited online, on radio and on TV – but this only prompted saw an increase in the visual presence of gambling on billboards, street posters and banners on buildings.

“Gambling has turned into an epidemic. We accepted amendments in 2024 that also introduced serious limitations but these regulations are not being followed, nor is the state implementing sanctions,” MP Bozhidar Bozhanov of Democratic Bulgaria, which has promoted such bans for years, said on September 9.

World.title: Andrija Mandic: Montenegrin Speaker’s Journey from Serb Firebrand to EU Advocate
World.content:
If Montenegro’s parliament votes on Thursday on whether to keep Andrija Mandic as its speaker, the man at the centre of the dispute will be defending a political career that has taken him from the forefront of the country’s Serb nationalist camp to one of Montenegro’s highest constitutional offices.

The immediate trigger for the vote is the message of condolence he sent to the son of former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted by the United Nations tribunal in The Hague of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and who died recently aged 84.

Mandic has acknowledged sending the condolences. Opposition parties have used the gesture to demand his removal as speaker, with the vote scheduled for September 24.

The episode has renewed attention to a question about how much Mandic has changed in his politics and the language with which he presents himself.

World.title: Netanyahu Lawyer Part of Operation to Build Israeli Drones in Serbia
World.content:
In Serbia’s business registry, the company name ‘SDS Technologies’ appeared within hours of the factory’s opening, not as a new firm, however, but as the new name of a company previously called CUPA Enterprises. The very same day, September 17, Amir was formally appointed as a director of SDS.

Vucic said previously that ownership of the drone venture would be shared equally by Serbia and Israel.

The ownership structure of SDS Technologies, however, does not reflect this.

SDS is in fact owned by London-registered CUPA Limited, itself majority-owned by Greek national Athanasios Ramos. On September 21, four days after the factory opened, CUPA Limited changed its name to Blue Liberty International Ltd.

Elbit System, the designer of the drones, told BIRN it “collaborates with local companies in several European countries as part of localisation processes and efforts to tailor its offerings to customer needs”. It denied any link to SDS, however, or to Amir. It stressed it does not own, nor is a partner in, any drone facility in Serbia.

Lawyer representing Netanyahu before Supreme Court

BIRN reporters first visited the Makis factory site several months ago, for an exclusive story about Serbia’s plan to open a drone factory with Elbit.

Situated alongside several other businesses and warehouses, the factory gates were branded with the name SDS Technologies. At the time, there was no such company in Serbia’s business registry.

Today, SDS Technologies has three directors: Greek national Maria Kardamaki, Lebanese-born US citizen George Antoine Elghossain, and Amir.

Since last year, Amir has been representing Netanyahu and his government before the Supreme Court in five petitions against the government’s decision to dismiss Ronen Bar as head of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security service.

According to Haaretz’s reporting, Bar had warned Netanyahu of a potential attack on Israel in a phone call before the Palestinian militant group Hamas struck on October 7, 2023, triggering Israel’s devastating war in Gaza.

Israel’s state prosecutor argued that Netanyahu’s removal of Bar was unlawful, given the conflict of interest arising from the fact Shin Bet was investigating the alleged involvement of Netanyahu associates in the paid promotion of Qatari interests in Israel, so-called ‘Qatargate’.

One of those associates is Srulik Einhorn, who has also advised Vucic.

Amir declined to answer questions about his involvement in SDS Technologies and the new drone factory in Serbia.

World.title: Bosnia Presidency Head Slams Serbia at UN Over Mladic Glorification
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnian Presidency Chairman Denis Becirovic at the UN. Photo: Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The chair of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s three-member state presidency, Denis Becirovic, accused Serbia’s leaders on Tuesday of violating international standards by systematically glorifying convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic on the global stage.

Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, the Bosnian leader issued a stark warning that persistent ethno-nationalist ideologies threaten stability in the Western Balkans. He argued that the honours paid to the former Bosnian Serb general at his Belgrade funeral this month prove that Serbian leaders have not abandoned their expansionist wartime ideology.

Becirovic – the Bosniak member of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s presidency – noted that international judicial bodies have firmly established that genocide occurred on Bosnian soil in the 1990s, making the attempted rehabilitation of its perpetrators an unacceptable assault on international law.

“The convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic is not a hero, but a judicially proven war criminal,” Becirovic stated from the UN podium.

“The institutional glorification of this criminal is an anti-civilisational act. It represents a direct alignment of Serbia’s state leadership with one of the worst executioners in European history, proving they have not abandoned the ideology that leads to aggression,” he added.

The address made political waves back home, where Bosnian Serb political officials condemned the speech. The Serb member of the state presidency, Zeljka Cvijanovic, accused Becirovic of presenting his own personal opinions rather than those of the state.

“Becirovic’s address at the UN General Assembly was a unilateral, private performance that completely bypassed constitutional procedures,” Cvijanovic told media.

“By using this international platform to spread hate and manipulate facts about regional relationships, he has further damaged internal trust and demonstrated that he does not speak on behalf of the entire state,” she added.

Bosnian Serb leaders reject international courts’ definition of the Srebrenica massacres as genocide and see Mladic as a war hero.

Concluding his remarks, Becirovic urged the UN and international organisations to take concrete measures against political figures in the Balkans who systematically honour war criminals at official levels.

He said ensuring legal accountability and defending the historical truth established by international tribunals remains the only path to long-term regional peace.

Mladic, who commanded Bosnian Serb forces in Bosnia’s 1992-5 war, was convicted by a UN tribunal of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws and customs of war. He died in the UN Detention Unit in The Netherlands aged 84 while serving a life sentence.

World.title: As Geopolitical Competition Intensifies, the EU’s Balkans Policy Must Adapt
World.content:
With its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia’s aggression towards European security architecture has opened a new chapter in the history of geopolitics.

Given the changing role of the United States in international affairs, the diffusion of power through the rise of middle powers, and China’s assertiveness as a peer competitor, the contours of the international order will see increased volatility, competition and uncertainty.

In this multipolar, multi-ordered world, small actors such as the countries of the Western Balkans will pursue ad hoc alliances and engage in transactional foreign policy with multiple powers in parallel.

World.title: Albania ‘Not Ready for the Risks’ as AI Enters the Electoral Arena
World.content:
Artificial intelligence has already entered the electoral arena all around the world. From fake audio recordings of candidates to videos making politicians appear to utter words they never said, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly used to discredit political opponents, shape voters’ perceptions and influence their electoral behaviour.

Albania is no exception. From last year’s general elections to the marathon anti-government protests known as the “Flamingo Revolution”, AI has been widely used to produce online political content, often in harmful forms.

During the 2025 parliamentary polls, disinformation campaigns targeting political actors were orchestrated through anonymous pages and spread across digital platforms. During the ongoing “Flamingo Revolution” protests, BIRN has identified dozens of cases in which AI was used to disseminate false information, which was then amplified through anonymous social media pages and accounts.

World.title: Hungarians and Czechs Cool on Ukraine’s ‘Carpathian 8’ Ambitions
World.content:
More amenable partners

Poland, on the other hand, as Ukraine’s strongest ally in the region, was represented by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and showed the clearest interest in the C8 format.

For Poland, the appeal of the C8 appears to lie in the overlap between security and cross-border infrastructure. Projects presented at the summit included a 216-million-dollar industrial park and multimodal terminal on the Polish–Ukrainian border, designed to handle up to more than 2 million tonnes of cargo annually, as well as a 441-million-dollar plan by Ukrainian Railways to establish a low-cost passenger operator using European-gauge trains, with connections from Uzhhorod, Lviv and Kovel to EU cities including Warsaw.

Together with cooperation on missile defence and the longer-term reconstruction of Ukraine, these plans give Warsaw several concrete reasons to remain involved, say experts.

The summit also gave Warsaw and Kyiv an opportunity to inject new momentum into relations that have been strained in recent months. Tusk said he had come to demonstrate solidarity with Ukraine and discuss bilateral cooperation, including Poland’s participation in the European anti-ballistic missile initiative. After talks with Zelensky, the two leaders confirmed that Poland would join the coalition, and Tusk said Poland’s absence from the initiative when it was launched in Paris in July had been the result of “a certain misunderstanding”.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic – who will be the prime ministerial candidate for the ruling coalition in the snap election to be held on October 25 – made an appearance in person, which analysts say is in keeping with the strategy he has been following over the last few months that included a bilateral meeting with Zelensky in Belgrade and a multilateral forum in Kyiv.

“I assume it has something to do with the elections approaching in Serbia, as Vucic now needs to show his more pro-Western face to keep support coming from the EU. He will not communicate it much at home, but will use his presence vocally when talking to EU counterparts,” AMO’s Cermak told BIRN.

Indeed, Vucic suggested as much during the summit, when he presented the initiative as his personal commitment to Serbia: “I am doing all of this to further ensure stability and peace for our citizens and for Serbia.”

Vucic said that Serbia has traditionally relied on the countries of the former Yugoslavia and also looked toward the West: “We were wrong: I believe that expanding and strengthening our relations within the broader Carpathian region will mean a great deal for Serbia.”

By way of example, Vucic noted that the opening of the Belgrade–Budapest high-speed railway would further facilitate connectivity, while Serbia is also working to establish other better links with Romania, such as making progress in talks on the construction of the Timisoara–Belgrade motorway as well as connecting the two countries’ electricity transmission systems.

Vucic also noted how 50 per cent of Serbian exports now go to Romania, Hungary and the Czech Republic, while trade between Serbia and Ukraine has increased by 42 per cent (though he did not specify the period to which this increase referred). The Serbian Chamber of Commerce told the weekly Vreme in August that Serbian exports to Ukraine increased by 92.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, largely due to electricity exports.

Romania was represented by President Nicusor Dan at the summit, where he signed a memorandum of understanding with Ukraine aimed at improving connectivity between the two countries by opening 10 new border crossing points and also upgrading infrastructure.

Dan also said that protecting the rights of national minorities could be one of the priorities of the C8 initiative. “This format can make use of the linguistic and cultural wealth of the region, making the protection of the rights of national minorities a priority,” Dan said in his speech at the summit.

According to Dan, the C8 could also become an additional tool for the European integration of EU candidate countries.

World.title: Croatia Needs to Keep Investing in Nautical Tourism
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Croatia must keep investing in its nautical tourism sector as 2.7 million overnight stays are recorded so far in 2026.

In the first eight months of this year, over 431,000 charter guests visited Croatia, who recorded more than 2.7 million overnight stays. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that Croatia must continue investing in nautical tourism in order to maintain competitiveness, while also resolving the issue of concessions that are expiring for individual marinas, it was said at the conference Nautical Tourism of Croatia 2030.

The country currently has 216 nautical tourism ports and other facilities for berthing and accommodating vessels, with almost 19 thousand berths. Minister of Maritime Affairs Oleg Butković emphasised that the key challenge remains seasonality, since the highest traffic and revenues are realised in July and August. The goal is to develop a year-round business model and additional content that would attract nautical tourists outside the main season as well.

According to his words, the Croatian Government should soon adopt decisions on the extension of concessions for individual existing concessionaires who have the documentation ready. The process, he said, is being prepared in cooperation with the ministries of tourism and finance and the European Commission. At the Croatian Chamber of Economy they emphasise that for further investments it is necessary to ensure legal certainty and a competitive business framework.

Concessionaires say they are ready to continue investing in marinas and charter, while the sector is at the same time being pressed by rising operating costs and a shortage of quality labour. The Ministry of Tourism and Sport highlights the green and digital transition as important directions of development.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Harshly Criticises “Out of Control” Croatian Prices
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – President Zoran Milanović has harshly criticised “out of control” Croatian prices, saying that time flies and things are getting “worse and worse”.

President Zoran Milanović is participating in the Lider conference Day of Big Plans, which is being held at the Westin hotel in Zagreb. Index reports that the conference discusses the macroeconomic and economic challenges and circumstances coming in 2027. “Time flies, and things are getting worse and worse. Not only in Croatia, but everywhere around us, things are slowly slipping out of control. The UN and the international system of collective security are being mocked by their biggest financiers,” Milanović said at the beginning, reports N1.

“the international order has ceased to exist”

“The international order has ceased to exist. Every sanction – a bilateral sanction – anyone’s, without UN verification is illegal. On the surface, the numbers have all advanced, GDP per capita, often a very deceptive piece of data about prosperity behind which great inequality is often hidden. Purchasing power parity is such that the differences aren’t too great in relation to some countries that we once looked at with envy,” the president stated.

“Average salaries aren’t small… However, what can be bought with that money? Croatian prices have completely spun out of control, we can only hope that things will start to eventually calm down,” he said. The worst thing, the president says, is that no one specific can be blamed for that situation, neither the governor, nor the finance minister, nor the prime minister, but one has to look at the surrounding countries, much larger than Croatia.

on the topic of europe

“The European Union and Europe as a continent have been in regression for the last hundred years, with flashes of progress that occurred after the great wars into which Europe dragged the whole world. Europe is in a cycle of shrinking into itself. Nothing that comes from Berlin or some other European metropolis should be taken either too seriously or not seriously,” Milanović said.

“Europe has some very serious problems with energy that it hasn’t managed to solve for decades already, but the moment that is said out loud, you are immediately labelled extreme left, extreme right, pro this, pro that, but that is not the way we can talk and plan, that is not a conversation at all,” the Croatian president clearly states. We have to build a nuclear power plant, Milanović said, adding that when one country attacks another, the whole world gets a bill to pay.

on america and iran

The president also commented on the situation between the USA and Iran. “It’s a symptom of the disease of large systems and large empires when people no longer want to sacrifice themselves for that system,” he stated.

“The European Union is not democratic and when I say that, I don’t necessarily mean that that makes it bad in itself, on;y that it is not democratic – people are appointed to the highest and most important positions by processes that are not democratic, and more and more people see and feel that and that is why more and more of them vote the way they vote,” Milanović warned.

World.title: “Revolutionary” New Croatian Road Toll System is, Of Course, Delayed
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – The so-called “revolutionary” new Croatian road toll system is delayed, which comes as a surprise to absolutely nobody.

Croatian Motorways still haven’t selected who will create the application and everything else needed for the upcoming Croatian road toll system. Poslovni reports that the project is worth around €160 million and we’re yet to have any idea when it will finally start functioning. All drivers on Croatian motorways should be able to drive without stopping and messing around with tolls and ENC’s as of March, but this “revolutionary” move has, of course, stalled. An unexpected problem has appeared in the development of the application into which every driver would have to enter their data and card details, reports klikni.hr.

Because of an appeal lodged by a company among whose owners is also a firm registered at the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, with its seat in Zdenci, Croatian Motorways have hit a roadblock (no pun intended). Portals with cameras are already being installed on the motorways, but the web portal, mobile app and integration data buses – that is, the part of the system with which drivers will directly interact – is still far from realisation. To make the irony greater, that part of the work is estimated at “only” €330,000 excluding VAT.

appeals, delays and issues – a true croatian saga

Let us recall, at the end of May Croatian Motorways awarded that job to a consortium of bidders consisting of the Zagreb companies Bos Projekt and Infinum and the British AMR CyberSecurity. The Zagreb company Abysalto appealed against the decision, and the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures back at the end of July partially accepted its claims and annulled the selection decision.

HAC now has to re-evaluate the bids. According to data from the court register, Abysalto has three members of the company: the firm King ICT, Stipo Matić and the firm Novčić više. Matić is, at the same time, the president of the supervisory board of Abysalto. Novčić više is registered in the register of the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, and its seat is in Zdenci, a municipality in the east of Virovitica-Podravina County that had a mere 1,453 inhabitants when the last census was carried out. In the list of activities of that company, IT is not mentioned. It is registered, among other things, for the production of pellets, biomass and biogas, forest management, energy distribution and waste transport.

The sole founder of the company from Zdenci is King ICT, and the director is Stipo Matić, which means that the same owner appears in Abysalto both directly and through the company registered in Bjelovar. The share capital of Abysalto was increased in the middle of last year from €7,000 to €5.3 million, and in the same period part of the assets of the company Omega software was also transferred to the company.

the clock is ticking and time is running out

Time for the new Croatian road toll system of toll collection is rapidly running out. The development of the software and application takes six months, and the company responsible for implementation would like to start testing as early as January. The situation is all the more complex because even after HAC reselects the contractor a new appeal is possible, and with it further delays in the realisation of this job.

Transport Minister Oleg Butković despite the standstill claims that the system will start on time. “We’re sticking to that deadline, everything is proceeding at its own pace,” Butković said rather vaguely. From Croatian Motorways they state that all activities are being carried out according to the legal deadline, but they do not deny that it is a complex project in which the appeal deadlines in public procurement procedures must also be respected.

World.title: As Many as 40% of Croatian Retirees at Risk of Poverty
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Another horrendous statistic for the country as as many as 40% of Croatian retirees are formally at risk of falling into poverty.

Just over the border in neighbouring Slovenia, 27 percent of retirees over the age of 65 are at risk of poverty, and in Norway, just nine percent are in the same category, the report states. Poslovni reports the shameful statistic that around 40 percent of Croatian retirees over the age of 65 live at risk of poverty, according to recent Eurostat data. Only Latvia and Lithuania have a higher share, while the European Union average is 19 percent.

Melita Čičak, acting director of the Pension System Directorate, warned in an interview for Dnevnik Nova TV about the difference in the length of working service between Croatia and other countries.

“All of these countries that are ahead on this list have significantly longer service; for example, in Slovenia the average service is 38.9 years, while in Croatia it’s 32 years,” she said. According to the data presented, the average pension in Croatia has risen by 113 percent since 2016 and now amounts to €764. That is laughable given that the staggering rise in the cost of living is burdening everyone, particularly retirees, who allocate a large part of their income to their most basic needs.

“Inflation always hits retirees first. We know that they’re unfortunately a social category and that they spend the largest part on healthcare, utilities, on medicines,” said economist Petar Vušković. The report also warns about the rise in heating and fuel prices, which further pressures retirees. Speaking about people remaining for a longer time in the world of work, Čičak concluded: “We haven’t yet decided to raise the age for acquiring the right to a pension like other countries, but through other mechanisms we encourage longer remaining in the world of work.”

World.title: Croatia’s Končar Presents Hybrid Electro-Diesel Train at InnoTrans
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia’s well known Končar has presented its impressive hybrid electro-diesel train at InnoTrans in Berlin.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that Končar officially presented its latest step forward in Croatian industry in the field of urban mobility and infrastructure at the world’s largest transport technology fair, InnoTrans in Berlin. The train is an ultra-modern hybrid (bimodal) electro-diesel train intended for long-distance transport.

After it was put into regular service on the Zagreb – Split route a week earlier in cooperation with the customer HŽ Passenger Transport, the second train from this series has now also been presented to the international public. With the global premiere of its latest solution for more modern, more comfortable and more sustainable passenger transport, Končar has once again confirmed that the knowledge, competences and technological solutions developed in Croatia compete on equal terms with the biggest names in the European railway industry.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Among the most visited parts of the fair was the outdoor exhibition area with 3,500 metres of track, on which 130 exhibitors from 17 countries of the world exhibited a total of 113 vehicles, including the latest generations of trains, locomotives and vehicles with alternative propulsion systems.

Precisely in such an international environment Končar is presenting technological solutions developed and produced in Croatia for the 10th time, confirming its position among the relevant European manufacturers of modern rail vehicles and advanced solutions for sustainable urban mobility. After two years ago it was the only one at InnoTrans to present a battery train, which then also became the first such product in commercial use in Europe and one of the first such products in the whole world, Končar has also displayed its new bimodal electro-diesel train at one of the most attractive positions on the outdoor exhibition area of the fair – on 75-metre-long tracks.

At the same time, the latest solutions for railway infrastructure, electrification, urban mobility and traffic digitalisation were presented on the spacious indoor area, further emphasising the ability of the domestic company to independently develop and deliver integrated technological solutions for the transport systems of the future.
