publishing all of the inspection body’s 2024 monitoring results;

holding parliamentary hearings involving representatives of the inspection body and the Economy Ministry, as well as scientists and MPs.

Inspection body: ‘No banned pesticides detected’

The inspection body said it was unacceptable to “mislead the public with unfounded and panic-inducing headlines”.

It also responded to the opposition MP’s claim that “what is banned in Brussels and Washington ends up on the plates of our elderly parents and children”. The body’s experts said some pesticides may be banned in one country while being permitted in another:

“Armenia is a party to the Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions and, in accordance with its international obligations, prohibits the registration, import and use of pesticides covered by these conventions. No banned pesticides were detected in the products tested in our country.”

Expert commentary

Food safety expert David Pipoyan recalled that industry experts had raised concerns about food quality a year earlier, but the Food Safety Inspection Body had dismissed their claims as defamatory.

“Last year, this same body denied everything at a news conference, saying there had been no violations. This year, it published — effectively hid — this appalling report on a little-known platform,” he said.

According to Pipoyan, if 47 out of every 100 samples tested were contaminated, this would mean that roughly every second purchase could potentially involve a contaminated product. In other words, he said, consumers would face a 47% chance of buying fruit or vegetables contaminated with pesticides.

Pipoyan said the problems went beyond the risk of consuming products containing carcinogenic substances:

“If you look at the range of pesticides being used, you can find neurotoxic substances, as well as pesticides that affect children’s health.”

He stressed that the report’s findings pointed to an ongoing risk for all consumers. In Pipoyan’s view, the publication of such a report in other countries would inevitably have led to those responsible for quality control being held accountable.

Social media reaction

Social media users also expressed outrage over the situation. Here are some of their comments:

“Every day you pay money to eat poison. And then you wonder why Armenia has ranked among the world’s leaders in cancer cases for decades.”

“This shows complete disregard for the health of the country’s own people.”

“We are demanding not token legislative ‘initiatives’ and justifications, but strict, genuine laboratory controls — from the fields to the shops.”

“Agricultural producers, are you happy with what you are doing? Let’s say there are no controls. But what about your conscience? Don’t you understand that you are committing a crime by poisoning people?“

“I’ve been saying it: we eat poison every day. Meanwhile, environmentalists are only concerned with shutting down mining operations. Environmentalists, what do you have to say now?“

“Whatever you feel like eating, pray first and then eat.”

“Everyone who doesn’t care about people’s health should be held accountable.”

World.title: Abkhaz experts discuss Georgian opposition’s proposals, EU stance on conflict resolution
World.content:
The EU on Abkhazia

Statements by Western officials and initiatives of the Georgian opposition surrounding the status of Abkhazia are once again drawing attention to the region. Abkhaz analysts commented on attempts to intensify Abkhazia’s isolation and evaluated the roles of the EU, Russia, and internal Georgian forces in this process.

Key arguments:

The Abkhazian question is being used by the Georgian opposition as a tool in their struggle against the ruling Georgian Dream party. Attempts to harden their stance and achieve the withdrawal of recognitions, as seen in the case of Nauru, are aimed at accusing the current government of a lack of patriotism and of making concessions to Moscow.

The European Union leadership’s focus on the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia is driven not so much by concern for peace as by a desire to weaken Russian influence and maintain levers of influence over Georgia amid a crisis in bilateral relations.

A peaceful or forceful “return” of Abkhazia to Georgia is an unacceptable paradigm for Abkhaz society. Pressure from the EU and Georgia only destroys trust and narrows the possibilities for a diplomatic settlement.

Here are the questions posed to the experts and their responses.

Why would the Georgian opposition, which already faces plenty of problems in its relations with the authorities, choose at this moment to step up efforts toward the further isolation of Abkhazia, following the successful outcome with Nauru?

Respondent 1

It is difficult to judge the motivation of the Georgian opposition in this matter. I can only assume that, as always, the issue of Abkhazia and the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict serves as a bargaining chip in domestic political processes. Regarding Abkhazia, Georgian Dream behaves with more restraint than previous Georgian authorities, at least at the level of public statements. In contrast to it, and as if to demonstrate greater patriotism, the opposition—which lacks broad support among the population outside of Tbilisi—speaks out much more harshly. Apparently, in its largely ineffective struggle against the current government, the Georgian opposition has decided to weaponize the issue of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, or as they call it, the “Abkhazian question”.

At the same time, other voices are also being heard within the Georgian opposition. For example, Nika Gvaramia recently gave an interview in which he called on Georgian society to move past the traumatic memories of the past. In his view, conflicts should not act as weights tied to Georgia’s feet on its path toward the European Union.

Thus, within opposition circles, there are proponents of both a forceful “return” of Abkhazia and those who advocate for its “peaceful return”. Another matter entirely is that few in Georgia understand that for the Abkhaz people, peace and a “peaceful return” are by no means the same thing. In Abkhazia, such an approach is perceived as achieving the same end by hook or by crook.

Instead of trying to turn back the clock and forgetting everything we went through in the recent past, we ought to accept reality and seek common ground on issues of mutual interest. And such issues do exist, considering that we are neighbors.

To speak of returning Abkhazia, whether by peaceful or violent means, belongs to an entirely different paradigm. The Abkhaz people will resist either of these two options. However, at least a mindset focused on peaceful solutions makes it possible to maintain stability. Unfortunately, if circumstances develop in a way that favors Georgia, those parties advocating a forceful solution will gain the upper hand.

Respondent 2

I believe that the situation surrounding the revocation of recognition by Nauru undoubtedly emboldened Georgian super-patriots. But it also seems to me, paradoxical as it may sound, that the more liberal, pro-democratic forces in Georgia—meaning the current opposition, parts of which were once in the Georgian leadership—have always been and remain more hardline, nationalistic, and hawkish regarding frozen conflicts.

We have always paid attention to this hawkish rhetoric, which was heard back during Mikheil Saakashvili’s rule. On the one hand, he seemed to democratize Georgia’s governance system, but on the other, he approached conflict resolution in a way that was entirely unliberal and disregarded human rights. The current demands of the opposition appear to be a continuation of that policy.

Another factor relates to the fact that relations between the European Union and Georgia—specifically the ruling Georgian Dream party—have deteriorated so sharply that the European Union has no remaining levers of influence over processes taking place inside Georgia. Since the EU is deprived of the ability to affect Georgia’s internal political matters, it compensates by responding to this narrative to cater to the Georgian opposition, which Europe views as pro-democratic and liberal.

Respondent 3

The Georgian opposition raises this issue with a tactical objective: to demonstrate that the current government lacks principle regarding the problem of Georgia’s territorial integrity and is willing to compromise on it. In doing so, it heightens the level of friction between Western countries and Ivanishvili’s government by framing the latter as conduits for Moscow’s global agenda.

In reality, the approach across the entire political spectrum in Georgia toward relations with the former autonomous entities is identical: restoring the territory of the Georgian SSR either by force or through diplomacy.

Respondent 4

In my view, the Georgian opposition has quite a few problems not only in its relations with the government, but also in internal relations within itself; there is no single, clearly defined leader there, and it appears to me to be fragmented and non-united.

The “Coalition for Change” consists of several parties and is headed by a council of four leaders. That is to say, the Georgian opposition has problems with the authorities, within itself, and with the European Union as well.

To both questions, I would answer the same way: the appeal to Ursula von der Leyen lies within the perspective of Georgia’s domestic political problems and its relations with the European Union.

We see that the Georgian opposition has been protesting for a very long time, people are taking to the streets, but these protests yield no visible results; in my view, Georgia’s tilt away from the European Union towards Russia is growing, public support for the Georgian opposition is falling, and its ratings are falling too.

We often hear that the Abkhazian issue currently sits on the periphery of the international agenda and is virtually invisible against the backdrop of other crises. Why, then, do we see such active support from the European Union for the initiative demanding that Syria revoke its recognition of Abkhazia?

Respondent 1

There are two factors here. One is that Abkhazia is indeed at the very bottom of their agenda, if present at all. Russia and Georgia, however, are present. Therefore, the issue of revoking recognition represents, on the one hand, a policy of countering Russia, and on the other, a step toward trying to regain Georgia’s loyalty. Ursula von der Leyen’s support for the Georgian opposition’s demand on such a sensitive, patriotic issue also serves to bolster the position of opposition forces within Georgian society.

On the whole, the fact that against the backdrop of highly acute global and regional problems, the President of the European Commission finds time for the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia reflects political bias and the double standards associated with such bias, which, unfortunately, have always been displayed toward us by Europe and the international community at large.

It would be appropriate here to ask von der Leyen a question: if EU representatives claim to be committed to a peaceful resolution of the conflict, what does revoking Syria’s recognition have to do with it? How does it bring us any closer to peace? If anything, it does the opposite. Such steps certainly do not help the negotiation process, the building of trust, or any of the other goals declared by the Europeans. What they certainly do is call into question the EU’s role as a mediator, further shrinking its already dramatically reduced presence in the region.

Respondent 2

It is true that in words we often hear that amid the major wars taking place around the EU, the Georgian-Abkhaz context is irrelevant. In practice, however, whenever decisions are made that restrict the rights of Abkhazia’s residents, EU officials quickly spring into action.

Interestingly, Ursula von der Leyen herself, who intends to address the revocation of Syria’s recognition of the Republic of Abkhazia, appears to be going through a difficult period within the European Union. From news sources, we can see how European Parliament sessions unfold, with MEPs from various countries harshly criticizing von der Leyen’s actions, raising many grievances and questions.

In this situation, it is remarkable that despite serious internal problems and challenges, she finds the time to attend to the requests of certain political forces in a non-EU country, Georgia, regarding pressure on another non-EU country, Syria. We have always noted the European Union’s special attitude toward Georgia—an attitude I would describe as unrequited love.

The European Union contributed greatly to the development of the modern Georgian state and supported the reform of its state institutions. It seems to me that Georgia was forgiven for things that were never forgiven in other countries. What is happening now appears to be the lingering, phantom feelings toward Georgia at a time when its official representatives have ceased to reciprocate.

Of course, the factor of relations between the European Union and Russia also plays a role that cannot be ignored. Here, the EU operates on the principle of “the friend of my enemy is my enemy”. Perhaps that is why they show little concern for how EU decisions will be received by the government and civil society in Abkhazia, how these decisions impact the protection of Abkhazia residents’ rights, or how they might ultimately affect the state of the conflict.

Respondent 3

I think it is premature to speak of overly active support for this issue on the part of the European Commission. Although, on the whole, a moderate level of activity aimed at having Syria revoke its recognition of Abkhazia’s sovereignty would not surprise me. First and foremost, it is an effort to undo political acts of the Assad era and further weaken Russian influence in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The complaints of the Georgian opposition are of minor importance in this context. What is interesting, however, is whether it is truly in the West’s own interest to indulge Georgia, given the country’s systematic and deliberate drift toward the East. That remains an open question, and I doubt I am the only one considering it.

Respondent 4

Against the backdrop of these problems in relations between the Georgian opposition and the European Union, a certain reboot is required. Running slightly ahead and trying to answer the second question about why the European Union needs this, I think that such a reboot is needed for the European Union as well.

The chosen tactic and strategy of the European Union—not to engage in contacts with the Georgian government, but rather to cooperate more actively and closely with the Georgian opposition on the assumption that it will sooner or later manage to take power in Georgia—seems to me not to be working or to be working poorly, and it requires a new impetus. Yet no visible tracks on which success could be achieved are in sight.

By success, I mean the need to boost the rating of the opposition itself among the Georgian population and to raise its status. After the regime change in Syria, the new leadership of that country needs some assistance from the European Union, and the EU holds certain leverage over it.

If, at the request of the Georgian opposition, it manages to achieve some progress on the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia, this could sharply boost the rating of the opposition in general and of this opposition bloc in particular. The exact same thing, in my opinion, is required for the European Union itself, since the previous tactic is not working and the opposition forces in Georgia are not gaining, but on the contrary are losing strength and influence.

The European Union put forward eight or nine conditions to the Georgian government so that it could return to the previous course of relations with the EU; Georgia is not fulfilling these conditions, and what is more, the tilt towards Russia has already turned into a stable trend toward rapprochement between these countries against the backdrop of the war with Ukraine and in the Persian Gulf, where Europe has a great deal of problems.

Naturally, the European Union needs to restore relations with Georgia, especially since Georgia is located in that region and used to be a partner of the EU, but is no longer one now.

In this context, I allow that the appeal of the opposition bloc to Ursula von der Leyen is necessary for all the purposes I have mentioned.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Sanctions eased in exchange for prisoner: Usmanov removed from list as Aliyev pardons French citizen
World.content:
Aliyev pardons French citizen

On 23 September, Ilham Aliyev pardoned French citizen Martin Ryan, who had been sentenced to 10 years in prison for espionage.

A day earlier, the European Union agreed, at France’s request, to remove Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list. According to the Financial Times, citing diplomatic sources, the two decisions form part of an agreement between Baku and Paris on the release of prisoners.

After years of confrontation over issues involving Armenia, Nagorno-Karabakh and France’s overseas territories, Baku and Paris reached an agreement on specific issues: France secured the release of its citizen, while Azerbaijan secured the lifting of European sanctions against the billionaire it had supported.

From a 10-year prison sentence to a pardon

The French citizen, identified in the pardon decree as Ryan Martin Richard, has been released from serving the remainder of his sentence. Authorities detained him on 4 December 2023, and on 16 March 2026 the Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 10 years in prison.

According to the Azerbaijani side, Ryan, the head of Merkorama, was supposed to collect military and other information for France’s Directorate-General for External Security. Paris rejected the allegations. On 30 July, France’s Foreign Ministry condemned the appellate court’s decision to uphold the sentence, called the conviction arbitrary and demanded Ryan’s immediate release.

The 10-year sentence, which the court upheld in July, was therefore brought to an end in September by a presidential decision. Ryan’s fate took a decisive turn not in the courtroom, but as part of diplomatic negotiations over sanctions.

What did Paris do for Usmanov?

On 14 September, the Financial Times reported that France was seeking to have Usmanov removed from the EU sanctions list in exchange for the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan. Paris and Bratislava called for his sanctions to be lifted and vetoed the extension of the restrictions for another 12 months. The EU initially granted a one-week delay to allow negotiations to continue.

On 22 September, the sides reached a compromise: Mikhail Fridman was also removed from the sanctions list alongside Usmanov, while the remaining individual sanctions were extended for 36 months instead of the previous six. For Usmanov, this means the lifting of the asset freeze and EU travel ban.

The mechanism allowed Baku’s demand to reach the level of European policy. Azerbaijan, as a non-EU country, could not take part in the sanctions decision-making process. However, France’s interest in securing the return of its citizens allowed Paris to pursue this concession within the European Union.

Why is Usmanov important to Baku?

Azerbaijan’s support for Usmanov did not begin in recent days.

On 18 September, a senior Azerbaijani diplomat told Reuters that between November 2023 and March 2025, Baku and other members of the Organisation of Turkic States had sent letters supporting Usmanov to the leaders of the United States and European countries. The diplomat described him as a philanthropist who helps strengthen ties between the West, Central Asia and the Turkic world.

The same diplomat denied reports that Azerbaijan had pressured France. A French Foreign Ministry representative, meanwhile, declined to disclose details, saying the matter concerned national security.

On 21 September, Euronews also reported that Uzbekistan had played a role in reaching the agreement. According to the report, the proposed deal involved releasing two French citizens detained in Azerbaijan in exchange for removing Usmanov from the sanctions list, with Aliyev expected to sign a pardon decree. The EU made its sanctions decision the following day, after which Ryan received a presidential pardon. The events unfolded in the same sequence that Euronews had previously described.

Confrontation from Nagorno-Karabakh to New Caledonia

The political significance of the agreement becomes clearer against the backdrop of relations between Baku and Paris in recent years. France criticised Azerbaijan’s military actions in Nagorno-Karabakh and expanded defence cooperation with Armenia. Baku, in turn, viewed Paris’s military support for Yerevan as interference in the regional balance of power.

Azerbaijan also extended the confrontation to issues sensitive for France itself. The Baku Initiative Group, established in 2023, held events involving supporters of independence for New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Martinique and other territories. Links were established between these movements and Azerbaijani political structures.

When unrest broke out in New Caledonia in May 2024, France accused Baku of interference. Azerbaijan rejected the allegations. Changes to electoral rules and fears among the indigenous Kanak people of losing political influence lay at the heart of the domestic crisis. At the same time, the crisis became a new source of mutual accusations between Baku and Paris.

The current agreement points not so much to a resolution of these disputes as to the sides’ willingness to set them aside in order to achieve specific results. For Paris, the priority was securing the release of its citizen; for Baku, it was securing a decision on Usmanov, whom Azerbaijan had supported for years.

The cost of the concession for Europe

France is not the only party to face political costs from the agreement. Ukraine’s leadership opposed removing oligarchs from the sanctions list. Within the EU, there were also concerns that making exceptions to the bloc’s common sanctions policy for national interests could set a dangerous precedent.

The political outcome of these events is that the release of a prisoner in Baku became part of negotiations over European sanctions against Russia. France secured the release of its citizen, while Azerbaijan brought one of the EU’s most influential members into supporting a billionaire backed by Baku. This points more to diplomacy based on mutual concessions under pressure than to a restoration of trust between the two countries.

Aliyev pardons French citizen

World.title: Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Race time is set, but getting home is anyone’s guess
World.content:
Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix

Sports journalist Anar Khanlarov left his home in Sumgayit half an hour earlier than usual on 21 September to make it to Baku in time for a TV programme. But even that was not enough.

He planned to take the metro from 20 January station to Nizami, then a bus to 28 May, followed by bus No 5 towards State Flag Square. As the İdman TV studio was undergoing renovation, filming was taking place at the Rowing Federation building on the boulevard.

His bus became stuck in traffic near Winter Park. Khanlarov continued on foot towards the Puppet Theatre, hoping to catch another bus from there or, failing that, take a taxi. When he reached the theatre at 20:40, he found that the road towards Bayil was closed. The programme began at 21:00, but Khanlarov did not reach the filming location until 21:25, alternating between walking and running. By then he was sweating heavily, and the production team decided he was not in a suitable condition to appear on air. As a result, Khanlarov did not take part in the programme at all that day.

The main events of the Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix will take place on 24–26 September. But even before the racing begins, road closures and changes to bus routes have brought life in the city to a standstill.

26 bus routes changed, leaving passengers with no real alternative

According to a plan by the Azerbaijan Land Transport Agency (AYNA), 26 bus routes have been changed between 21 and 26 September.

Route No 5, which Khanlarov had planned to take, is among those affected. On one section, the bus runs between Nariman Narimanov metro station and Suleyman Rahimov Street, while on another it runs along a route covering the Salyan Highway, Bibi-Heybat Mosque and the Baku Funicular. Under the new arrangements, it is no longer possible to use the bus to travel from the city centre to Bayil via the usual route. Some stops on this and other routes are inside the restricted race zone. There is no alternative public transport available.

The changes have also affected people travelling into the city from the suburbs. Buses No 149 and 149E from the settlement of Sahil and No 195E from Alat now run only as far as the Lokbatan transport hub near the Bina shopping centre. Passengers travelling to the city centre have to change to another form of transport. Bus No 125 reaches the centre via the ring road through Badamdar.

The transit corridors announced by the organisers are also not an alternative for bus passengers. On 21–22 September, they are open from 07:00 to 09:00 and from 18:00 to 20:00. However, these arrangements do not apply to public transport. Except in emergencies, picking up and dropping off passengers is also prohibited within the transit corridors. By the time Khanlarov reached the Puppet Theatre at 20:40, he says, the evening transit window had already closed.

‘We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes’

Former transport officials have also complained about the traffic jams. Mais Aghayev, former head of the Baku Transport Agency’s press service, wrote on Facebook:

“We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes on the stretch from the Mikayil Aliyev roundabout towards Heydar Aliyev Avenue.”

The congestion has also been acknowledged by the authorities. On the evening of 22 September, the Intelligent Transport Management Centre reported traffic jams on 28 May Street, as well as on the section of Shamsi Badalbeyli Street running from Winter Park towards the Central Bank. These streets are also part of the routes affected by AYNA’s changes to bus services.

Seven schools and universities switch to remote learning

Measures related to the race are not limited to changes to transport. According to the Baku City Education Department, seven schools are holding classes online from 22 to 26 September: Public Schools No 6, 7, 8 and 23, Classical Gymnasium No 160, Lyceum No 132–134 and the Ilyas Efendiyev Elite Gymnasium.

Under an order issued by the Ministry of Science and Education, universities in Baku have also switched to remote learning from 23 to 25 September. The ministry says the measure is intended to ensure continuity of the education process.

The move may reduce the number of daily journeys to schools and universities. However, remote learning creates additional difficulties for working parents: who will look after younger children, and how will families ensure they have the devices and internet access needed for online classes? The switch to remote learning does not mean parents no longer have to go to work. So while it may ease pressure on the transport system, it does not necessarily ease the everyday burden on families.

No indication of how much longer journeys will take

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative party, linked the problem to Baku’s fragmented system of governance in a Facebook post on 14 September. In his view, the key factors are the availability of public transport and journey times. He also argues that any changes to working hours should take into account the school schedules of employees’ children.

Economist Akif Nasirli told Radio Azadliq that the race should be held outside the city centre. In his view, the economic benefits of the event should not be used to justify restrictions on residents’ freedom of movement:

“People have the right to move freely in their own country, in their own capital.”

AYNA’s traffic management plan for the race, published on 19 September, lists alternative streets that drivers can use. However, it provides no information on actual bus frequencies along the altered routes, how much additional time journeys will take, or how much time passengers may lose when changing between separate sections of disrupted routes.

For residents, it is not enough simply to know which street a bus will take. They need to know when to leave home, where they will have to change and whether they can get to work on time. Without this information, the burden of adapting to the route changes — and the consequences of any resulting delays — falls on passengers themselves.

World.title: Why Georgia closed 10 schools days into new academic year
World.content:
School closure in Georgia

Ten state schools in Georgia were closed during the first three days of the new academic year. Some of the buildings are due to be demolished and rebuilt, while others will undergo repairs.

The decision followed assessments by the National Forensics Bureau, which found that the school buildings were in a state of disrepair and unsafe for use.

One of the schools is in Tbilisi, while the others are located in different regions across the country.

For the first week after the closures, the schools switched to remote learning. During this period, the Education Ministry and school administrations are expected to urgently find alternative premises.

All 10 schools are likely to be temporarily accommodated in neighbouring schools, with classes held in two or three shifts and lesson times shortened. If any of the alternative schools are too far away, school buses will be provided.

More than 4,000 pupils and around 400 teachers are now waiting for the ministry to decide where they will be relocated and which shifts they will study and work in.

his is not unprecedented. In recent years, thousands of pupils across Georgia have been studying in temporary, “borrowed” premises, while schools that were demolished have yet to be rebuilt.

How events unfolded and what the decisions were based on

The closure of all 10 schools followed the same pattern. The start of the new academic year on 15 September was celebrated as usual, with balloons, flags and flowers in school courtyards and classrooms.

Three days later, on the evening of 17 September, parents received messages informing them that the schools were being closed.

Number of pupils and teachers at the closed schools. Source: JAMnews, based on data from the official schools portal.

In all 10 cases, the decisions to close the schools were based on assessments by the National Forensics Bureau dated 10 September 2026. The education minister says the ministry did not receive the documents until 17 September, explaining why the closures were announced at such short notice.

Some parents do not believe that the school buildings are unsafe. They suspect that some of the decisions may be linked to corrupt deals and investors’ interests.

JAMnews examined publicly available documents relating to all 10 schools, including decisions by the Authorisation Council, expert assessments, public procurement records, renovation plans and municipal reports.

We sought answers to several questions: Why were these schools allowed to begin the academic year as normal on 15 September if their buildings had to be vacated just days later? When did the responsible authorities learn about the condition of the schools? And if the buildings were already destined for demolition, why was money allocated for their renovation year after year?

Renovating schools only to abandon them

The documents examined by JAMnews show that concerns about the poor condition of some of the schools had been known for years. In other cases, however, there had previously appeared to be no need even for repairs, let alone demolition.

Some of the schools underwent minor renovation work in recent years, with substantial sums spent on the projects.

For example, according to public procurement records, Public School No 16 in Kutaisi underwent various repairs in 2015, 2017 and 2022. The largest amount was spent in 2015 — around 190,000 lari [about $70,300].

The Kutaisi school made its most recent purchase just three weeks before the start of the current academic year. On 24 August, the administration signed a 2,500-lari [about $925] contract for maintenance of the school grounds, including mowing and removing grass.

Public School No 16 in Kutaisi. The start of the academic year was celebrated with invited entertainers. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

The public school in the village of Misaktsieli underwent major renovations in 2008, while its heating system was completely upgraded last winter.

This is also confirmed by the Mtskheta municipality’s 2025 budget. According to the document, several schools were due to undergo renovation work funded through a targeted transfer from the state budget. The school in Misaktsieli was among them.

The Misaktsieli school continued to spend money on various works and services in 2026. Its most recent contract, signed on 4 September, was worth 12,515 lari [about $4,635] and covered the removal of flooring, plumbing work and the subsequent installation of granite flooring.

The school in the village of Abranlo, in the Kvemo Kartli region, is the smallest of the schools closed in recent days, with around 80 pupils. It too has undergone renovation work in recent years.

Mariko Tsikoridze, a project co-ordinator for CENN in Kvemo Kartli, says three sanitation and hygiene projects were carried out at the school before 2019. Toilets were built, washbasins renovated, and an illegal rubbish dump created by local residents in the school grounds was cleared.

“We brought in six truckloads of soil and built a sports ground. The local authorities were also actively involved at the time,” Tsikoridze says.

The school is now due to be demolished. Its headteacher, Mikheil Jakeli, wrote on social media that, according to the National Forensics Bureau’s assessment, constructing a new building would be preferable to repairing the existing one, prompting the ministry to decide on demolition.

Problems left unaddressed

For some of the schools, JAMnews was unable to find any relevant records in the public procurement system. However, municipal reports and local media articles show that concerns about the condition of these schools had been raised for years.

For example, parents of pupils at Public School No 5 in Khashuri were calling for repairs as early as January 2023, complaining about damaged walls, floors and doors, as well as loose stair railings.

First day of the new academic year at Public School No 5 in Khashuri. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

In municipal reports from the Imereti region, Public School No 2 in Tskaltubo had for years been listed as a building in need of renovation.

Available records for 2022-2026 contain no evidence of major renovation work at the school. However, according to Info Imereti, minor repairs were carried out, including in the summer of 2026.

“There is an assessment stating that the building is not cost-effective to repair. It would therefore be better to construct a new one rather than renovate it,” Mamuka Chkhetiani, head of the Tskaltubo education resource centre, told Kutaisi Post.

Officials knew as early as 2022-2023 that Public School No 3 in Senaki was in a state of disrepair. In 2022, the school’s headteacher, Marine Naneishvili, told Etaloni that the building was due to be demolished.

The Finance Ministry’s 2023 review of investment projects listed the “Construction of Public School No 3 in Senaki”as a separate project, with 12.696m lari [about $4.7m] allocated for it. It is unclear what became of the project.

Public School No 3 in Senaki. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

Reaction at schools

Members of the school communities at two of the 10 schools — in Tbilisi and Misaktsieli — responded to the authorities’ decision with protests, which are still continuing. At the other schools, discontent has largely been confined to social media, where parents have complained about the disruption to both their children’s plans and their own.

“We are in shock” is the most common reaction beneath posts announcing each new school closure.

Two of the three schools closed in the Kakheti region — Public School No 3 in Gurjaani and the school in the village of Velistsikhe — are in Gurjaani municipality. More than 500 children attend the Velistsikhe school, while School No 3 has 148 pupils.

“Congratulations to the school community of Velistsikhe Public School — pupils, parents, teachers and everyone interested in improving our school,” headteacher Nona Menabdishvili wrote on social media alongside the news of its closure.

The post attracted numerous comments, many of them essentially asking: “What is there to celebrate?” Others shared stories of schools elsewhere that have remained closed for years.

Unlike Menabdishvili, Mikheil Jakeli, headteacher of the school in Abranlo, expressed no enthusiasm about the Education Ministry’s decision.

He has appealed to the ministry to allow pupils to complete the current academic year in the old building, subject to appropriate safety measures, “to avoid moving the children elsewhere just days after the start of classes and causing them unnecessary stress”.

‘From positive assessment to demolition’ – story of School No 21

The largest of the 10 schools to be closed is Public School No 21 in Tbilisi, formerly Gymnasium No 6. News of its closure was also the first to emerge.

It is one of the capital’s most prestigious schools. Because of its emphasis on German-language teaching, it is often referred to as the “German school”.

According to a National Forensics Bureau assessment dated 10 September 2026, several problems were identified in the school building, including a risk of plaster falling from the façade, a faulty drainage system, cracks in some areas and damage to reinforced concrete blocks.

The assessment also identified seismic vulnerability as a separate problem, citing the absence of an earthquake-resistant reinforcement belt on the roof parapet and other failures to comply with current seismic standards.

Protest outside Public School No 21 on 18 September 2026. “Don’t demolish the Sixth,” reads an improvised protest banner.

However, the same school had previously received a very different assessment from the same National Forensics Bureau on 15 November 2023, when it underwent authorisation. The assessment said the building required repairs, but gave it an overall “positive” evaluation, and the school was authorised to operate until 2032.

In April 2026, the Authorisation Council carried out scheduled monitoring of the school and, citing the positive assessment, said the building required repairs and gave the school until 2028 to address the problems.

In other words, as recently as spring 2026, official documents still listed School No 21 as requiring repairs rather than demolition.

However, by the time the Authorisation Council made that assessment, a new examination of the school building was already under way.

The Municipal Development Fund had requested the examination on 16 September 2025. An expert inspected the building on 10 December, and nine months later, on 10 September 2026, issued a new assessment.

The building was initially classified as Category III based on the extent of the damage. However, following Georgian government decree No 161 of 22 April 2026, which sets out criteria for assessing whether buildings are fit for use, the damage was subsequently classified as Category IV because of seismic safety concerns.

How could the school have deteriorated so severely in three years that it now needs to be demolished? This is the question being asked by parents. Many suspect corruption. The school is located in a prestigious tourist area, prompting speculation that a private investor may be interested in the site.

Parents fear that the school will be demolished and never rebuilt. They are demanding an independent assessment and say they will not allow the building to be torn down. They also oppose both online learning and the relocation of pupils to other schools.

If we don’t act now, we will lose our school’ – story of Misaktsieli village school

Protest outside the school in Misaktsieli, 18 September 2026.

Irine Kalandadze’s child started first grade this year. He had barely had time to settle into school when his parents were told it was closing:

“He had only been at school for three days and was eagerly looking forward to the next one — he liked it so much. Then suddenly we were told the school was closing. I can’t explain this to my child, and it is very painful for me too. This is precisely the stage when children need to develop a love of school, and now we don’t even know where or how he will study.”

The school in Misaktsieli serves five villages in Mtskheta municipality and has more than 500 pupils.

Parents say lessons will be held online for the first week after the closure, after which the children will be transferred to the school in the village of Tsilkani. But that school has capacity for only 300 pupils, meaning classes will have to be held in several shifts.

Parents do not know for certain whether the Misaktsieli school is due to be demolished or is being closed for repairs. On 18 September, residents gathered in the school grounds and demanded an explanation from the headteacher, who told them that he had not yet seen the expert assessment himself.

Villagers fear there may also be business interests behind the decision: the school is in a popular tourist area, occupies a large site and is surrounded by numerous commercial properties.

“We all want our children to study in a modern school. It’s just that we have seen many examples of how school renovation projects have ended,” Irine says.

Parents are demanding that, if the school needs repairs, the work be postponed until spring. If the building is to be demolished, they want construction of a new school to begin simultaneously on vacant land nearby, with the existing building demolished only once its replacement is ready.

“If we don’t act now, we will lose our school,” Irine says.

The protest is continuing, and parents say they have no intention of backing down.

Not an exception, but a wider trend

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, there are 2,086 state schools in the country.

In 2022, the Education Ministry launched a large-scale reconstruction programme that was intended to cover 800 schools.

Since then, hundreds of schools have closed across Georgia. Two years ago, in 2024, the fact-checking platform FactCheck reported that 21,203 pupils had been relocated to alternative premises.

Based on publicly available data, the number is likely still in the tens of thousands. The Municipal Development Fund, which oversees school reconstruction, regularly publishes updates on the completion or launch of work at schools across Georgia.

For example, in August 2026, the fund announced tenders for the reconstruction of 11 schools. None of the 10 schools closed in recent days appears on that list, suggesting that the overall number of schools currently not operating in their own buildings is considerably higher.

On 18 September, as thousands of teachers, pupils and parents were reeling from the news that their schools were being closed, government officials were holding a high-profile ceremony to reopen the renovated Public Schools No 4 and No 5 in Batumi.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze and other senior officials at the opening of two schools in Batumi. Photo: Municipal Development Fund.

What is actually happening?

Education experts say the situation illustrates systemic problems and a lack of a consistent strategy and long-term vision in the education system.

Education expert Revaz Abkhazava lists the problems created by what he describes as a poorly planned intervention — the reconstruction of schools:

It has disrupted the education process;

It has upended established routines for parents and children, including attendance at after-school clubs and additional classes;

It has shown a complete disregard for teachers’ needs, with low salaries forcing many to work at several schools at the same time;

It has imposed additional costs on the state for transporting pupils to other schools.

“The education system is extremely complex. It consists of many interconnected components. If you fail to see it as a whole, you get what we are seeing now. A single decision does not simply create one problem — it can push the entire system to the brink of collapse.”

Abkhazava says such decisions are the result of experienced and qualified professionals with institutional knowledge being pushed out of the education system.

“School reconstruction is a technical task. It does not require any special expertise. Education management professionals could have resolved this issue very easily.”

The expert also points to problems in communication between state institutions. The process, he says, was not managed in a way that would have ensured the assessments were ready at least a month before the start of the academic year.

Revaz Abkhazava believes the root of these problems lies in the politicisation of Georgia’s education system. He says education should not serve any political party and that safeguards are needed to ensure this, including an education council and teachers’ associations. He also argues that the ministry’s strategy should not change every time a new minister takes office.

“The education system should be as decentralised as possible. The ministry should employ professionals with knowledge and experience in education management and education policy.

“The ministry should focus on evaluation, analysis and research, and make decisions based on them. It should support educational institutions, while those institutions should have the autonomy to make decisions on matters that concern them,” the expert concludes.

World.title: Armenian orphanage worker brutally assaults disabled resident
World.content:
Armenian orphanage worker assaults disabled child

A care worker at the Kharberd specialised orphanage in Armenia brutally assaulted a disabled child who is unable to walk or speak.

The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, which oversees the institution, confirmed the incident and said it had taken place several weeks ago. The care worker was immediately dismissed and is now under house arrest.

“A disabled child was beaten with a mop in a place where they were supposed to receive care and support. In reality, this is the kind of care the child needs to be protected from,” said Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda.

Rights activist questions purpose of such institutions

“If we do not want violence, these institutions should not exist at all. Family-based upbringing and alternative forms of care are possible for all children if the state makes the necessary effort and allocates the necessary resources. The state’s obligations do not begin after a disabled child has been beaten, nor do they end with the dismissal of the alleged abuser or their placement under house arrest,” Hovsepyan said.

Until such institutions cease to exist, however, he says the state is obliged to establish a system that:

“prevents violence and identifies signs of it in a timely manner;

provides safe mechanisms enabling all children to report abuse;

guarantees a proper investigation and the child’s swift recovery.”

Details of the incident

Local media have established further details about what happened at the orphanage. The incident is now known to have taken place on 13 August.

The child who was assaulted has cerebral palsy and is unable to walk independently or speak.

The care worker who assaulted the child had worked at the orphanage since September 2012.

“In room D-1 of the orphanage, the care worker initially struck the resident, F.M., several times. After he fell to the floor, she picked up a floor mop and continued striking him on his lower back, spine and left shoulder blade. As a result, F.M. suffered severe physical pain and emotional distress,” journalists reported.

Child’s condition described as satisfactory

Nver Kostanyan, spokesman for the minister of labour and social affairs, wrote on social media that the orphanage administration had “identified the incident” and immediately reported it to law enforcement:

“The care worker has been dismissed, while it is for law enforcement agencies to determine whether criminal charges are warranted. The child is in good health and continues to receive care at the specialised orphanage.”

Kostanyan said such incidents were a “red line” for the ministry:

“Any instance of violence is unacceptable and will be subject to an appropriate criminal-law assessment.”

Expert opinion

Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda, warns that disabled children often avoid speaking about abuse they have experienced.

“There are many reasons. Among other things, they think they will not be believed, because what they say is often called into question,” he wrote on Facebook.

Hovsepyan stressed that the public only learnt about the abuse at the orphanage after it was reported by the media. The rights activist believes such cases should be closely scrutinised by state bodies, particularly now that there is no mechanism for public oversight.

A group of civil society experts previously operated at the initiative of the Labour Ministry, carrying out regular monitoring of care centres for children and elderly people.

“The monitoring group was disbanded about three years ago. Easily. But its work is not being resumed with the same ease,” Hovsepyan said.

Hovsepyan himself was a member of the group. He recalls that in 2021 it visited the Kharberd specialised orphanage and documented a case of discrimination against a minor in its care:

“At the same orphanage, staff wore gloves when touching a teenager living with HIV who had recently been transferred there. Separate dishes were used for him. His clothes were washed separately. Other children were told to stay away from him. And yet the world has long known that HIV is not transmitted through this kind of contact.”

The orphanage staff themselves told the experts about this because they believed they were ‘doing everything right’.

Following the recent violent assault, Hovsepyan says he is not convinced that conditions at the specialised institution have improved:

“I am also not sure whether all new employees receive the necessary training before they start working with children. Nor am I sure that the state is taking steps to ensure that children are in safe hands.”

World.title: A pair of porcupines, Khrashuna and Khramuna, at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Tbilisi Zoo is home to two Indian porcupines, a female and a male named Khrashuna and Khramuna. Their keepers chose the names for a reason: the porcupines make funny “crunching” sounds when they eat. Khrashuna is the bolder of the two, while Khramuna is more cautious.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: ALL VIDEO

______________________________________________________________________________

Contrary to popular belief, porcupines have nothing in common with either badgers or hedgehogs. Badgers are carnivores, hedgehogs are insectivores, while porcupines are rodents.

Their most distinctive feature is their long, thick quills, which they mainly use for defence. When threatened, their first response is to flee rather than attack. And no, porcupines do not shoot their quills — that is simply a myth. When they sense danger, they

Alongside their varied diet, Khrashuna and Khramuna always have branches in their enclosure. They gnaw on the wood, which helps keep their teeth strong.

Porcupines are nocturnal animals. During the day, especially in summer, they prefer to stay in their shelter. They become active in the evening and start looking for food. That is why visitors who come to their enclosure during the day may see nothing more than a nose or head poking out of the burrow.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Porcupines at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Qld council says costs prevent it hitting recycling targets
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A regional Queensland council is warning it cannot meet state-imposed recycling targets with the growing cost of moving materials hundreds of kilometres for processing.

Each year 10,000 tonnes of household recyclables collected from the Rockhampton region are driven 600 kilometres to a facility on the Sunshine Coast.

Waste services cost the local council $3 million per year with more than one-third of that bill going to transportation fees.

In June, the Queensland government released its waste strategy and set an overall recycling target of 65 per cent by 2035, with major regional communities including Rockhampton expected to halve the amount of waste it sent to landfill.

The Queensland government has set an overall recycling target of 65 per cent by 2035. (ABC News: Ellie Willcox)

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams said his council was struggling to improve recycling rates, especially as fuel prices soared.

"We've done our waste plans and [our staff] are saying that we can't achieve the targets that the state government is putting onto councils," he said.

" It's a really difficult position for councils to be in (because) if we increase the volumes of recycling, it just costs us more to transport it. "

Recyclables from central Queensland households were previously processed at a private materials recovery facility in Rockhampton.

But that was destroyed by a battery fire in 2020.

The council has so far been unable to attract private companies to develop a similar facility.

The council has been unable to find a firm to develop a materials recovery facility locally. (ABC Radio Canberra: Jolene Laverty)

Mayor Williams said the local government spent about $300 per tonne to send its recyclables for processing, compared to about $100 a tonne for councils in south-east Queensland.

"The cookie-cutter approach to increasing recycling really doesn't help when the tyrannies of distance and the cost to transport that material is ever-increasing," he said.

"With the state government wishing to increase recycling locally, there's no real [financial] benefit unless we get some subsidies towards those transport costs."

In a statement, state environment minister Andrew Powell said the government was providing support for recycling in regional areas, with $11 million in new funding for infrastructure.

The government was also designing a new fund to be spent on helping regional councils send recycling for processing.

The state government is hoping a new fund can help regional councils send recycling for processing. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Calls for national reforms

Australian Council of Recycling chief Suzanne Toumbourou said the federal government should never have shelved national packaging reforms, which would have eased the burden on regional communities.

"It's extraordinarily disappointing to see that lack of progress in packaging reform," Ms Toumbourou said.

"We should have had regulatory certainty about the fact that burden would be shared much better across the supply chain and much more responsibility would be placed on producers."

In a statement, federal environment minister Murray Watt said the government's focus was to work with state and territory governments to reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia.

World.title: Trump rolls out red carpet for Xi's US state visit
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

US President Donald Trump has greeted Chinese President Xi Jinping on the tarmac after he landed in the US, kicking off a three-day state visit aimed at smoothing simmering tensions between the superpowers.

Mr Trump and First Lady Melania shook hands with Mr Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan after the Chinese leader descended from his plane at Joint Base Andrews, a US military airfield outside Washington.

The two presidents stood side-by-side as a military band played, before two B-1 bombers staged a noisy flyover.

Xi Jinping and Donald Trump inspected troops after the Chinese president arrived. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The personal airport greeting, a courtesy Mr Trump was notably denied when he visited Beijing in May, begins three days of pageantry that will include another flyover and a state banquet at the White House on Thursday, local time.

Six F-22 fighter jets and six F-16s were lined up on the tarmac in an apparent display of military might as US officials literally rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese leader.

Expectations of any breakthroughs are low, with analysts saying the main aim of the lavish spectacle is to maintain a fragile diplomatic and trade truce between the world's biggest economies.

Mr Xi was accompanied by his right-hand man Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, among others, according to Chinese state media.

Peng Liyuan and Xi Jinping were met by Donald and Melania Trump at Joint Base Andrews. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

But there were no Chinese CEOs in his delegation, two sources told AFP, despite the fact that top US tech bosses, including the leaders of major AI companies, are set to attend Thursday's White House state banquet.

Mr Xi's visit will wrap up on Friday morning, local time, when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.

AI on agenda

When the two leaders sit down for their highly anticipated talks on Thursday, they will be confronting a host of thorny issues led by fears — boosted by warnings from tech CEOs — that artificial intelligence risks wiping out humanity.

But with China and the United States racing for AI supremacy, there are few expectations of any deal to regulate the rapidly advancing technology.

Jonathan Czin of the Brookings Institution told AFP that expectations were low for any concrete results from the meeting but added: "I think there will be some extension of the gentleman's agreement."

Will Trump-Xi summit actually deliver? China watchers are divided over what the Trump-Xi summit will actually achieve. Some dismiss it as political "theatre", while others believe it could bring greater certainty to the global economy.

Analysts said that China had meanwhile begun to look past Mr Trump, whose second term ends in early 2029, and is in many ways playing for time and using the truce to consolidate its position.

Preliminary talks on Sunday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng included discussion of creating a communication channel for AI concerns.

The two men held further "substantive" talks on Wednesday to prepare for Mr Xi's visit, Mr Bessent said in a statement.

The treasury secretary told Fox News that both sides had agreed to extend a tariff trade truce until January 10, 2027.

Xi's visit draws condemnation

Trump's five-star welcome for Mr Xi has drawn criticism from China hawks within his own party, especially amid reports that Beijing supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.

"Our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator," said Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the powerful Senate Armed Services Committee.

The US president however has played down the need to bring up the allegations of Chinese help for Iran, justifying it on the grounds that both Beijing and Washington spy on each other.

For Mr Trump, the state visit is also a chance to focus on pageantry instead of problems at home, where the Iran war's effect on fuel prices has sent his approval rating plummeting to historic lows ahead of midterm elections in November.

American presidents very rarely travel to the airport to greet foreign leaders, although Mr Trump welcomed Russian President Vladimir Putin off his plane in Alaska last year.

The last such welcomes at Andrews, apart from papal visits, are believed to be John F. Kennedy's welcome for British prime minister Harold Macmillan in 1962, and Dwight D. Eisenhower's for Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in 1959.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Historic winery sold to Victorian company with plans to restart production
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

One of Australia's oldest and most renowned wineries has returned to private ownership.

Family-owned Stonier Wines purchased Seppelt Wines from publicly listed wine giant Treasury Wine Estates.

The sell-off is part of Treasury's plan to reduce its portfolio from 76 wine brands to fewer than 30.

The sale includes Seppelt's vineyards and winery at Great Western, in western Victoria, and its Drumborg vineyard near Portland in south-west Victoria.

The company purchased the business for an unknown figure, with the sale expected to be finalised in mid-October.

The Seppelt brand was launched by the Seppelt family in South Australia in 1851, and in 1918 the family purchased Hans Irvine's vineyards at Great Western.

A long time in the making

Stonier Wines is one of the pioneering estates on the Mornington Peninsula and returned to local family ownership in 2022.

Stonier chief executive officer and co-owner Aaron Drummond said he was attracted to Seppelt after having worked in the Great Western wine region at the Mount Langhi Ghiran winery for many years.

Aaron Drummond says his business has big plans for Seppelt. (Supplied: Aaron Drummond)

"It was incredibly exciting to see the potential of the region," he said.

" The quality of what we can produce in the Grampians and Great Western is extraordinary. "

The sale includes the winery at Great Western, which has been largely dormant since 2014, but is expected to be restarted by Stonier.

"The winery facility is a considerable facility that was processing about 8,000 tonnes a year but is currently crushing nothing," Mr Drummond said.

"Our hope is to put a couple of thousand tonnes through that facility."

Stonier will also make commercial use of Seppelt's historic underground cellars, which have been largely a tourist attraction in recent years.

"We want to get them working again," Mr Drummond said.

"They're the most phenomenal natural cooling environment, so it makes sense to us, and so we'll store all our top sparkling wines in them."

"The Drives" in Great Western is the largest underground cellaring system in Australia, covering 3 kilometres. (Supplied)

From corporate to private

Treasury Wine Estates purchased Seppelt in 2011, as part of the acquisition of Foster's Group's entire wine division.

In June this year, the company announced plans to slash its brand portfolio in a cost-cutting exercise.

Seppelt is the first brand to be sold off since that announcement.

Angus Lilley, TWE's managing director for Australia, New Zealand and Europe, said the company was pleased to find a buyer in Stonier.

"Seppelt holds a distinctive place in Australian wine, with a proud history shaped by generations of winemakers, viticulturists and people across the business and its local communities," he said.

"For the people who know and love Seppelt, it's a positive move that keeps the brand in Victorian hands."

Production will resume at the Great Western winery under Stonier. (Supplied: Treasury Wine Estate)

Swimming against the tide

Stonier's purchase of Seppelt comes at a time when the wine industry is under siege from falling global demand, historic oversupply, and low prices.

Mr Drummond said while conscious of those challenges, he was positive about the future of the industry.

"The wine industry is in probably the toughest cycle it's been in for a few decades, but the reality is that if you get the farming right and you get the wine quality right, the premium wine market is going ok, and there is growth," he said.

" It's a bloody risky time, but it's also calculated, and the thing about this brand is it has a heap of love and people want to see it go well. "

He said Stonier was focused on quality over quantity.

"Trying to make more wine doesn't make sense, but making better wine that can compete at a global level and really focusing on fine wine — I think there's a really lovely market for us," he said.

World.title: 'That's why Taliban is scared': Cyclist's incredible journey to silver
World.content:
The easy part for Fariba Hashimi was winning a silver medal in the women's cycling road race at the Asian Games.

The nearly impossible part for the cyclist from Afghanistan was trying to train in her country. To do that, she dressed as a man in a place where women have few rights.

"All the time when I was going to training I was dressing as a guy," she said.

She said she also hid her face to avoid being recognised.

"Because sometimes when they recognised me, they were trying to throw … stone[s] or hitting me," she said.

Hashimi, who is 23, won silver overnight AEST in a time of 2 hours, 50 minutes, 5 seconds, which marked another leg in a journey that began in 2021 when she left Afghanistan, escaping to Italy with the help of former road racing world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.

Hashimi (left) with gold medallist Guo Li C of China and bronze medallist Leung Wing Yee of Hong Kong. (Getty Images: Cen Yunpeng/Xinhu)

"In 2021, when the Taliban moved into my country, I escaped my country because I wanted to follow my dream," she said.

"I want to show the Afghanistan women in the world that … we can have an opportunity."

Hashimi talked about having many dreams for women in Afghanistan, dreams for herself and dreams that might take time to be realised.

"I'm really, really happy and I'm full of emotion. I don't know how I can explain it for you," she said.

"I hope one day I come back in my country and ride the streets of Kabul — and riding with the women side by side to share the same passion.

"And I hope in the future changing some things.

"I think we are really tired of the situation of our country and I hope the Taliban is watching. I know how much one woman can be powerful, and that's why Taliban is scared [of] women."
