World.title: From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers.

If Lachie Weller hadn't requested a trade to Gold Coast, would Andrew Brayshaw be at the club?

What if Adelaide had taken Hayden Young instead of Fischer McAsey in the 2019 draft?

AFL recruitment, especially at the draft, is an element of good preparation and good luck.

The current Dockers list has been described as "pure" from a recruitment point of view, with no father-son selections, no free agents and no players taken with AFL concessions or free agent compensation picks.

The Fremantle squad that trained this week for a grand final has been carefully put together. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it all began in 2016.

"It was pretty clear the list was old, but finishing so high on the ladder in 2015, it's sort of hard to basically finish on top and then enter a rebuild phase," Fremantle's former national recruiting manager Brad Lloyd said.

"We entered [2016] with an old group, which is fine to have an older group, but you need to be getting the results.

"And that wasn't evident through the start of '16."

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

The Dockers were winless until round nine that season, after winning 18 games the year before.

"Some decisions were made to reset again, which ended up in some pretty experienced players finishing up and the club going back to the draft," Lloyd said.

Starting over

Lloyd, who joined the Dockers in 2008, was no stranger to building a list — he was part of the recruitment team which put together Fremantle's 2013 grand final side.

In 2008 and 2009, Fremantle used 23 draft picks to bring together the core of the squad that would be competitive across the mid-2010s.

Ross Lyon coached Fremantle to the 2013 grand final and 2015 minor premiership, but the side fell off a cliff in 2016. (AAP Image: Gary Day)

"We'd had a really good crack at it through '13, '14 and '15, and played in a grand final and in preliminary finals, but couldn't quite secure a premiership," Lloyd recalled.

"We had the oldest list and were now struggling on field [in 2016] and decided to sort of enter another build to get going again."

From career crossroad to grand final When Neil Erasmus runs out onto the MCG on Saturday, it will vindicate his decision to stay at Fremantle after almost leaving a year ago.

Lloyd believed a complete rebuild would take between six and eight years, and Fremantle embarked on drafting and trading in players it thought would deliver success.

It's been 10 years since that decision was made and the Dockers have resolutely stuck to the plan, though it hasn't been without some misses along the way.

The recruitment of Jesse Hogan, Shane Kersten and Cameron McCarthy, among others, didn't pan out, while some talented draftees such as Adam Cerra and Lloyd Meek now ply their trade at other clubs.

Jesse Hogan was traded to the Dockers from Melbourne, but struggled in his time in purple. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

But under Lloyd and long-time recruiter David Walls, the club did bring in Luke Ryan, Andrew Brayshaw and Sam Switkowski, as well as Sean Darcy, who became the foundation of the club's list.

The stand-out draft

The Dockers' rebuild was slowly unfolding as the 2010s ended, but the 2019 draft accelerated it considerably.

Fremantle selected Hayden Young, Caleb Serong and Liam Henry with picks seven, eight and nine, before securing Michael Frederick at pick 61.

Hayden Young overcame injury woes to help launch the Dockers into the grand final. (Getty Images: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Mark Micallef was part of the Dockers' recruitment team that year.

"The 2019 draft was something that we pegged in that we thought could really change the platform of the footy club," he said.

Securing Young and Serong attracted much of the media attention at the time, though Micallef believed the selection of Frederick so late in the draft was equally important.

"You're trying to find the diamonds in the rough and you're looking for guys that could have a trait or an ability that not many others can see," he said.

Michael Frederick was a late pick in the 2019 draft, but has become an integral part of the Freo side. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"We thought Frederick was the right talent. He had a speed skill set that we really, really liked. He had a really good demeanour and a character.

"He had a good talent threshold, but he also had the work ethic and the character to back it up as well. So that's what really makes a back-end pick."

There were several other excellent drafts for Fremantle, including in 2021, which saw Jye Amiss, Matthew Johnson and Neil Erasmus selected, along with defender Karl Worner in that year's Rookie Draft.

Playing the long game

While the players selected by the Dockers in 2019 have become stars of the side, there was another future stud Fremantle wanted but knew they couldn't get in the draft.

Luke Jackson is emblematic of Fremantle's forward planning as they rebuilt an old squad into a flag contender. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Luke Jackson was described as a "unicorn" — a ruck who played like a midfielder — but he was slated to go very early in the draft.

Fremantle thought they could lure him back within a few seasons, and laid the groundwork in the build-up to the draft.

"We knew he was going to the top three, but we actually put a lot of groundwork into him that year saying, 'if you ever decide to come back, we want to be at the club of your choice,'" Micallef said.

"I think you always look at trades and stuff like that and people think it just happens within that trade period, but there's a lot of time and a lot of work and a lot of resources that goes into that [future planning]."

Shai Bolton's arrival at Fremantle was seen as the cream on the cake after a long rebuild. ( Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Jackson and Shai Bolton both eventually returned to Western Australia as premiership players and are now vital cogs in Justin Longmuir's machine.

A special place

While both Micallef and Lloyd have long since moved on to different things, their time at Fremantle remains dear.

"Fremantle was a very special place. They were very good to me personally. Right from Steve Rosich and Chris Bond, the CEO and footy manager, and Steve Harris, who was the president at the time, to [his successor] Dale Alcock," Lloyd said.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It is remote compared to the rest of the AFL, so they don't get a huge amount of turnover of staff.

"When you're watching them celebrate the other day [after the win over Sydney], you just see staff that have been there for decades. It's a very stable club that's operated in their own area.

"You see so many past players in the rooms and they're a very good club at looking after their people.

"I wish them nothing but the best and particularly for the recruiting team that I've worked closely with — David Walls and Dave McMullin and Ed McMullin and that team, wish them well and even their football manager, Joe Brierty."

Lloyd and David Walls (pictured) worked closely together for a decade at the Dockers. (AAP Image: Con Chronis)

Micallef was only at the club for one year, but he's enjoyed watching their success unfold.

"Kudos to the club. They've done an unbelievable job," he said.

"We set a plan and I think they sort of stuck to it, trying to get WA players back, and it worked really well.

"I loved my time at Freo, and Freo has some really special players and people involved in that footy club and even the fans, they just deserve it more than anyone.

"I really hope they get the job done on Saturday."

World.title: Hervey Bay's dugongs make positive start on slow road to recovery
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

An increase in dugong numbers spotted in key coastal areas in south-east Queensland has researchers feeling cautiously optimistic.

James Cook University (JCU) researchers conducted their second round of aerial surveys in Hervey Bay and Great Sandy Strait in 2024 to analyse how the vulnerable species was recovering after major flooding decimated seagrass meadows in 2022.

The joint study with TropWATER released last month reported positive population growth and wider geographic spread due to the revival of seagrass habitats in key zones.

But the low number of calves has raised concerns about whether the local population is truly on the path to recovery.

Australian Marine Conservation Society's Great Barrier Reef campaign manager Simon Miller said the report was an "important" measure for the local dugong population.

According to Christophe Cleguer, the revival of seagrass habitats is likely attracting dugongs to return to Hervey Bay and the Great Sandy Strait. (ABC News: Rachael Merritt)

"Typically these surveys tend to happen every five years, so it was great to see the [federal] government provide funding to do another survey so soon," he said.

Two data-collection methods were used to calculate the dugong population: raw counts and abundance estimation.

The first technique involved observers in the aircraft taking note of the number of dugongs spotted, while the second procedure applied cross-correction factors to the raw data to gain an approximate population size.

These correction factors are applied because "there's a good chance if they're feeding at the bottom, or if the water is too deep and murky, you'll miss them," JCU's principal research officer Christophe Cleguer said.

According to the report, researchers initially counted about 109 dugongs in 2024 — a slight increase on the 103 dugongs noted in 2022.

Simon Miller said the biennial aerial surveys are an important way of keeping track of the dugong population in south-east Queensland. (Supplied: Simon Miller)

The population change also aligned with the distribution of dugongs: in 2022, the marine mammals were mainly spotted in the central portion off Hervey Bay but had spread south towards the Great Sandy Strait in 2024.

"It is likely the result of seagrass on its way to recovery in these inshore areas," Dr Cleguer said.

JCU-TropWATER consulted with the Butchulla people, the traditional owners of the land from Burrum Heads to Rainbow Beach.

Butchulla Native Title Aboriginal Corporation chair Shawn Wondunna-Foley said the importance of protecting seagrass and yuangan –the Butchulla word for dugong — was clearly highlighted in the report.

"When we look after the seagrass, we look after the yuangan, and we look after sea country," Mr Wondunna-Foley said.

Calf concerns

Worries were raised about the small number of young dugongs counted during observations.

Only three calves were tallied in 2024, a decrease from the nine spotted in 2022.

But Dr Cleguer said there were biological reasons behind the low numbers.

While the dugong population is showing positive signs of growth, the low number of calves has raised concerns. (Supplied: Dr Christophe Cleguer)

"There is a time lag for dugongs; they need to recover and get healthy enough to reproduce calves," he said.

The researcher said further monitoring was needed to determine how nutritional stress was impacting their reproductive responses.

Mr Miller said the few calves were a "negative indication" for the dugong population.

"We're not seeing any evidence a lot of dugongs are coming back," he said.

Although Dr Cleguer maintained the belief that the new report showed the population was on the slow path towards recovery, he urged the public to remain cautious.

"We have to consider the counts as one line of evidence to look at population health," he said.

Future cross-collaboration 'beneficial'

JCU hopes to secure funding to conduct a third aerial survey into the dugong population stretching from the southern Great Barrier Reef to Moreton Bay next year.

But monetary constraints and unexpected weather events could cause significant time delays between studies being undertaken.

To avoid these potential gaps, Dr Cleguer said collaborating with local organisations would be "beneficial".

"They could survey using drones or vessels to give us some indication of dugong presence and movement on the local scale that can fit into the bigger picture," he said.

James Cook University is working to obtain additional funding to undertake a third aerial survey of the dugong population from southern Great Barrier Reef to Moreton Bay next year. (Supplied: JCU-TropWATER )

Mr Wondunna-Foley said the opportunity to work with researchers on improving water quality monitoring efforts and building the resilience of seagrass meadows "in a proactive and positive way" would be welcomed.

For people hoping to make a difference on a small scale, Mr Miller said reducing their boat's speed in areas populated by dugongs can have a big impact.

"It's important for people to respect slow zones, paying attention to their surroundings and really keeping an eye out for the incredible wildlife out there," Mr Miller said.

World.title: Police scour bushland near Albury for missing man
World.content:
A 28 year-old man who has been missing for four days was last seen walking away from his home in southern New South Wales without shoes, prompting a major search.

Police are urging anyone who sees Daniel Tranchard-Harry not to approach him, but instead to keep their distance and try talking to him about fishing.

Mr Trenchard- Harry, who has an intellectual disability, left his home on Centaur Road at Hamilton Valley, near Albury, at about 6:30pm on Monday.

He was last seen wearing blue boardshorts and a blue T-shirt and is believed to be on foot.

NSW Police Acting Inspector Troy Martin said Mr Trenchard-Harry was known to enjoy fishing and talking about it could help keep him calm until emergency services arrived.

"If anyone does see him, if you could just talk about fishing with him, if you can just keep your distance while involving him in that conversation, that would be fantastic," he said.

Police have serious concerns for Daniel Trenchard-Harry's welfare. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

More than 50 involved in search

Police, mounted officers, motorbike riders, bushwalkers, specialist dogs and a NSW police helicopter are involved in the search.

Acting Inspector Martin said Mr Trenchard- Harry's home backed onto bushland, but police did not know which direction he had taken.

"He could have gone into the bushland or he could have gone to the main road. We have no exact location at this stage," he said.

Mr Trenchard-Harry's parents raised the alarm after they were unable to find him on Monday night.

"His family are quite upset, quite worried," Acting Inspector Martin said.

"We have a number of police with them at the moment and they're providing the family with support."

Police have ruled out foul play.

Residents around Centaur Road, Glenroy and Burrowes Road, as well as nearby parts of Albury, are being asked to check their properties, backyards, sheds, cars and caravans for any signs of Mr Trenchard-Harry.

World.title: 'Queen of Scones' hangs up apron after reaching volunteer age limit
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

For the first time in nearly 20 years, the Melbourne Royal Show kitchens will be without their 'Queen of Scones'.

Joy Davis, 80, has been forced to retire from her dream role in the kitchen at the show after reaching the age limit for volunteers.

Mrs Davis, known to her fellow volunteers as the 'Queen of Scones', says working at the show was a lifelong dream, and that she is proud of her lasting legacy of baking.

Joy Davis and the CWA celebrate a record-breaking year for scones in 2025. (Supplied: CWA)

Hanging up her apron is bittersweet for Mrs Davis, who helped turn out a record 17,831 scones at last year's show.

"We say that I retired. I retired happily, but I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it," she said.

"The friendship and the companionship and working with other girls from right across the state, city and country, it was a great experience.

" If I had a chance again, a life again, I'd do it again. "

The 2026 Melbourne Royal Show opens today.

Follow the link to: The secret recipe for Joy's scrumptious scones

Living her dreams

Mrs Davis said she always dreamed of following her mother's footsteps and joining the CWA.

She joined the CFA's Traralgon branch in Gippsland in November 1969, but it would take decades to work up to a gig at the show.

Joy Davis has retired as CWA Victoria's chief scone maker. (ABC Rural: Fiona Broom )

"The first year [at the show] I had one day, and I sort of buttered a few scones at the end of the day," she said.

"The next year I went for six days, and after that, each year I've been there the whole time, 11 days."

The art of scone-making caught Mrs Davis' eye, and she enlisted the skills of senior cooks to teach her their secrets.

As older generations retired, Mrs Davis eventually took over the scone scene, earning her regal title.

She said the secret to her success is quality and self-restraint.

"I believe you always use good ingredients and you don't handle them too much," she said.

"You need a good, light hand. I think I'm a bit lucky to have that."

In her heyday, Mrs Davis could bake almost 1,000 scones per day for hungry punters at the show.

In 2012, she started keeping a tally of how many scones the team baked, a tradition that remains today.

"It's fairly long hours," Mrs Davis said. "I think I'm able to continue for a long time because I work at my own pace.

"No rustle, hustle and bustle.

" So that's my advice. Take your time and work at your own pace. "

Joy Davis, 80, and husband Ron, 88, in their home of 59 years. (ABC Rural: Fiona Broom)

Mrs Davis' slow and steady approach has helped turn the show into CWA Victoria's biggest fundraising event each year.

The CWA's culinary team paid tribute to their colleague, who they said generously offered tips and tricks for the perfect scone with patience and a smile.

"She is a true CWA woman who has left a lasting legacy," said CWA Victoria president Marie Vassallo.

" Joy has been a wonderful mentor to hundreds of CWA members over the years. "

Joy Davis's famous scones. (ABC Rural: Fiona Broom)

World.title: ‘Goodnight, my friend’: Slash, Kate Ceberano, Jason Donovan pay tribute to Angry Anderson
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale ‘Goodnight, my friend’: Slash, Kate Ceberano, Jason Donovan pay tribute to Angry Anderson Kayla Olaya September 24, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rock star Slash and Australian music greats Jimmy Barnes, Kate Ceberano and Jason Donovan have led tributes to Rose Tattoo frontman Gary “Angry” Anderson. Slash, the lead guitarist of Guns N’ Roses and whose real name is Saul Hudson, took to social media to remember his friend, who died on Monday aged 79. Anderson’s death was confirmed in a statement shared by his bandmates and family on Wednesday. Australian Rock Legend Angry Anderson, pictured in full voice in 2009. Getty Images “RIP #AngryAnderson. I’m going to miss my good friend; I can’t believe he’s gone. Condolences to his family, friends and band members,” Hudson wrote on Instagram. Guns N’ Roses covered the Rose Tattoo song Nice Boys Don’t Play Rock ‘n’ Roll, and in 2013, Anderson joined the American band on stage during an Australian tour to perform it.



Donovan also paid tribute to Anderson via Instagram, honouring his legacy and contributions to rock – and to the Australian TV soap Neighbours. Anderson’s song, Suddenly, was famously played during the wedding of Scott and Charlene (played by Donovan and Kylie Minogue), which was one of the biggest moments on Australian television. “Angry didn’t just sing rock ‘n’ roll — he lived it. A voice like thunder, a heart that never stopped giving, and a spirit that fought hard for young people and those doing it tough,” Donovan said. “I’ll always be proud that Suddenly became part of our shared story. Rest peacefully, Gary. Your voice, your heart and your legacy will never be forgotten.” Ceberano shared a photo on Instagram of her with Anderson, singers John Farnham and Jon Stevens and actor John Waters from the 1992 Australian production tour of Jesus Christ Superstar .



She said in her post that it had been a nostalgic week for her and the show’s alumni at John Farnham’s tribute concert, with Ceberano sharing a story about how, on her 25th birthday on the 1992 tour, Anderson encouraged her to get a tattoo. “With all the joy of the week replaying Superstar memories with Jon Stevens for our mate John Farnham, it’s with sadness we say goodbye to our friend and co-star @gary_angry_anderson RIP,” Ceberano wrote. “We had all had a massive lunch together ... and you turned to me and said, flushed with excitement, ‘One of the most celebrated tattooists from the Illustrated Man is in Hindley St TODAY! I think you should go up there and make a memory of this moment that will last a lifetime’. I promptly put pen to paper, drew a simple mandala, and we all traipsed up the hill ... where I gave myself over to the famed gal. “I sobered up pretty fast, I can tell you, but to have ANGRY’s smiling mug keeping me company during this ‘rite of passage’ was unforgettable. Thank you and goodnight, my friend.”



In an Instagram post late on Wednesday, Barnes, the legendary rock singer, farewelled his close friend and collaborator. “We lost a good man this week. Angry Anderson sang from his heart with power and conviction,” Barnes wrote. “But don’t let that tough outside fool you. He was a caring soul who loved his family, cared for his friends and stood up for the downtrodden. “Rock in Peace my dear friend.” Australian-American musician and actor Rick Springfield posted a photo, also on Instagram, of Anderson performing in his later years.



“Really sad to learn that Gary Anderson, aka Angry Anderson [has died],” Springfield said. “Another great voice silenced.” Sebastian Bach, the frontman of American rock band Skid Row, took to Instagram to pay tribute to Anderson. “They don’t make them like Angry Anderson any more,” Bach said. “You left us too soon, but that’s because you were too good for us. The most gifted vocalist, lyricist, performer ...” The original yellow Wiggle, Greg Page, also left a comment on Rose Tattoo’s announcement of Anderson’s death.



“His legend and legacy lives on. Rest easy, Angry,” Page said. Anderson suffered a cardiac arrest in late August and was admitted to a hospital to undergo treatment. Loading “It is with great sadness we announce the passing of Gary ‘Angry’ Anderson on the eve of Monday, 21 September 2026, surrounded by his loved ones here in Australia,” the band said in a statement on Wednesday. “Angry was a devoted father, and much-loved bandmate, friend, and member of the wider music and entertainment community. His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas.”



Anderson joined Rose Tattoo in 1976, soon after the band was founded by guitarist Pete Wells, and served as its lead vocalist until shortly before his death. On August 10, the band announced the cancellation of the European leg of its One Last Ride tour after Anderson was hospitalised due to a “medical issue”. It was set to be the band’s final tour after more than five decades of performing live. The band began its European tour in July, and had nine more shows to go when the cancellation was announced. Rose Tattoo were scheduled to return to Australia this month to perform several farewell gigs across the state capitals. World.title: WA news LIVE: Dockers get green light for ‘Wharfie Time’ in grand final
World.content:
The Fremantle Dockers have been given the all-clear to use the club’s famous “Wharfie Time” motivator during Saturday’s AFL grand final against Brisbane.

But there’s a catch: the AFL is allowing the Dockers to use the spine-tingling intro from AC/DC’s Hell’s Bell’s just once after a goal as part of the celebrations.

Loading

9News Perth reporter Paddy Sweeney said the league believed the Dockers and Lions had two of the best game-day fan engagement experiences, which it wanted to be part of what is shaping to be a grand final for the history books.

“Wharfie Time”, which had its genesis in a rousing speech from former Dockers captain Matthew Pavlich, has been deployed twice this season so far.

The motivator, which is played when the margin is tight and the clock is running down, helped lift the Dockers to victory over Hawthorn in round 9, and was also played in the final minutes of the team’s win over Geelong in the semi-final.

It has only ever been deployed at Optus Stadium, with lights and screens blaring into action and the crowd erupting into rapturous support to transform the venue into “Fortress Fremantle”.

World.title: Nine TV and streaming boss leaving after less than two years
World.content:
Nine’s managing director of streaming and broadcast, Amanda Laing, is departing from the business after less than two years in the job. The powerful executive reported to chief executive Matt Stanton and oversaw Channel Nine, free online video platform 9Now, and premium streaming service Stan. Nine sources said she was departing in a move related to a restructure. Amanda Laing has made major cost cuts in Nine’s TV division, which is enduring a tough advertising market. Dominic Lorrimer Laing joined the company, which also owns this masthead, in April 2025. Laing had previously been a senior executive at pay television company Foxtel and had sat on the Australian Rugby League Commission. The move came after a day of change for Nine, which announced on Wednesday that Australian Financial Review editor-in-chief James Chessell was leaving to join independent media site Rampart. He is being replaced by the Review’s editor Cosima Marriner.



Related Article Updated

Media & marketing Financial Review editor-in-chief James Chessell quits to join media start-up During Laing’s tenure, Nine secured a deal to retain the rights to broadcast the NRL, but also made cuts in its television division in response to advertising revenue declining. Those cuts came as part of a strategy to overhaul Nine’s television news broadcasting dubbed “Future News”, in which it streamlined the number of positions it employs with new broadcasting software. The changes prompted a fierce backlash from staff, some of which have joined the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance union for the first time. And while Nine held onto the NRL rights, the sport’s boss Peter V’Landys has previously said that outcome was due in large part to direct negotiations with Nine chair Peter Tonagh.



In its most recent annual results, Nine cut the value of its Total TV business, which includes both broadcast and digital streaming, in its books by $426 million to about $360 million. Nine’s share price dropped to $0.72 on Wednesday afternoon, down almost 40 per cent over the last twelve months. Laing’s section of the company had already been reorganised during her short tenure. Nine created the new position of streaming and television boss for Laing upon her arrival. It was in part an attempt to bring the company’s streaming service Stan closer to the rest of the business and position it more centrally as one of its main growth sectors. Laing previously worked for Nine from 2006 to 2017 before her stint at Foxtel.

World.content:
WorldEuropeAir accident Close call for pilots and homes as RAF jet loses control and crashes Tom Cotterill , Tom Jeffreys and Gareth Corfield September 24, 2026 — 9:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two trainee British pilots were forced to eject from the Hawk T2 aircraft when it encountered a problem shortly after taking off from RAF Valley on the Welsh island of Anglesey on Wednesday morning. Footage of the incident shared online showed the moment the pilots ejected before the jet crashed into the ground and exploded. Emergency services went to the scene, with an air ambulance reportedly landing nearby. North Wales Police said the pilots were being treated for minor injuries after parachuting to safety. North Wales Police confirmed the jet crashed into a field just off the A4080 motorway, north-east of Aberffraw Football Club. The cause is still under investigation. However, multiple defence sources claimed video footage from the moments before the pilots ejected indicated a potential problem with the jet’s controls.



“The several pitch-ups prior to the ejection is very unusual behaviour for the aircraft at that stage of flight. There is definitely something not normal,” one said. The RAF said it had suspended high-speed Hawk fighter jet training as a “precautionary measure”. It said: “Both pilots are receiving medical treatment. Their families are being supported. “The RAF has decided to temporarily pause Hawk T1 and T2 operations, as a precautionary measure, whilst investigations are ongoing.” Richard Owen, owner of Afallon Caravan Park near Rhosneigr, Anglesey, said flaming debris fell just yards from holiday caravans and a family home.



The 88-year-old said he was in the kitchen when he heard the explosion. “It landed just on the other side of the park,” Owen told the Daily Mail. “I went out to take a look. There were little bits of wreckage all around the site. Loading “The tail section must have blown off and landed next to one of the caravans. There was lots of smoke, thick black smoke. I didn’t dare to go too close. I was worried about it exploding.” A witness told North Wales Live he watched the aircraft take off: “I knew straight away that it was in trouble – right on take-off there was an orange flame, and as it accelerated it was basically on fire.



“As it gained altitude the flame disappeared, but it was clearly in trouble. It climbed at an aggressive pitch. It pitched twice violently in the air, and then there were two clear loud bangs. The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened.” Related Article Analysis

UK Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia In the video clip, the Hawk is seen banking upwards twice, then wobbling slightly before the pilots eject from the aircraft. A loud bang is then heard, believed to be from the rockets used to safely blast the pilots away from the stricken aircraft as it nosedives. The T2 jet crashes into an empty patch of scrubland close to houses before exploding in a ball of flames, with black smoke billowing as the inferno engulfs the wreckage. A separate clip online appears to show two pilots floating back down to the ground on parachutes. The Ministry of Defence is working with the emergency services at the crash scene.



An RAF spokesman said: “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way.” Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.” UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting. Getty Images North Wales Fire and Rescue service said the fire was under control. “North Wales Fire and Rescue Service crews and officers attended at an incident involving an aircraft in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey, working alongside colleagues from Royal Air Force, North Wales Police, Welsh Ambulance Service and Wales Air Ambulance. “The fire is now under control. Members of the public are asked to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work safely.”



The Hawk T2, built by BAE Systems, is a two-seater training jet “equipped with advanced avionics and synthetic radar to simulate front-line combat aircraft like the Typhoon”. Related Article ADF Corruption claims haunt fatal Defence helicopter crash The RAF uses it primarily for advanced jet training and preparing pilots for complex tactical environments. The crash is the latest in a series of problems to blight the Hawk jets. In 2022, engines in the fleet of training aircraft were pulled from service after concerns about the risk of in-flight failures. Alec Shelbrooke, a former defence procurement minister, blamed problems with French-made components in the engines. In January 2023, the 28-aircraft fleet was grounded as a precaution after a blade failed during an incident on the runway at RAF Valley. Flying resumed after a pause, but many engines were removed from service while the problem was investigated.



Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, the head of the UK Armed Forces, said in late 2024 that he wanted to replace the Hawk T2 because of the engine and support problems. The crash comes three months after three members of the Royal Navy died when a helicopter went down during a training exercise in Devon, England. Lieutenant Lily-Mae Fisher, Britain’s only female Royal Navy commando, died alongside Lieutenant Commander Chris Gayson and Petty Officer Owen Green when their Merlin Mk4 crashed in a field near Sourton Down in the early hours of June 4. World.title: Xi Jinping lands in Washington with Trump waiting on the tarmac
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Xi Jinping lands in Washington with Trump waiting on the tarmac Michelle L. Price September 24, 2026 — 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday, with US President Donald Trump waiting to welcome his counterpart on the tarmac instead of waiting for him to drive to the White House. Trump’s decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far the US president is going to honour China’s leader in his first state visit to the US capital in more than a decade. US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan at Joint Base Andrews. AP Trump and wife Melania Trump were at the base to participate in an arrival ceremony for Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan. The salutation kicks off a three-day visit that’s expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump’s visit to China in May. But it also is a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan.



Beyond using the visit to try to keep “strategic stability” between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. The two leaders have a packed schedule over coming days. AP Related Article Trump diplomacy Xi to get the rock star treatment as Trump prepares a spectacle He has lavished praise on Xi as a “great leader” and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Republican senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the US Senate Armed Services Committee, criticised the “lavish welcome”, and told the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader “based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party”.



Wicker archly suggested a list of topics that Trump could discuss with Xi at the state dinner, such as “the purposes of China’s massive military build-up, or about China’s clear support for Iran”. He said that “during every minute of dialogue”, Trump should keep in mind that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbours and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US and China had to interact at the highest levels because they were “the two largest economies in the world” and “probably the two most powerful militaries in the world”. Trump appears to be pulling out all stops to impress Xi. AP “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to,” Rubio said in New York on Wednesday. Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, and told reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new “work of art” helicopter landing pad would be ready for the Chinese leader’s visit, although he bemoaned his massive White House ballroom would not.



Trump on Wednesday was looking to match the pageantry he was met with in China this year. In May, Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump but Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. But a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. A military honour guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!” also were present. ‘He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect.’ US first lady Melania Trump The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional paint colours of the US presidential plane. First lady Melania Trump said earlier on Wednesday that her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrived in the Washington region because “they have a great relationship”.



“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said of Xi and his wife during an interview on Fox News Channel’s Fox & Friends. Trump’s airport ceremony for Xi will be followed on Thursday (US time) by more formalities, including an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Melania Trump said her husband and Xi have a “great relationship”. AP Before the black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, the two leaders are expected to dive into weighty issues behind closed doors, even as expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs in the relationship. On Friday, Xi and Peng will return to the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries.

World.title: ‘It’s up to the clubs’: AFL CEO says there’s risk in trading for besieged Swans
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘It’s up to the clubs’: AFL CEO says there’s risk in trading for besieged Swans Jake Niall Updated September 24, 2026 — 8:30am ,first published 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL boss Andrew Dillon says the league will leave it to the clubs to decide whether they wish to trade for any of the five suspended Sydney Swans players amid an ongoing police investigation into allegations of sexual assault against potentially four of the five. Dillon said the AFL still reserved the right to sanction the relevant players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice – for their behaviour at the Pullman following the conclusion of the police investigation. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has opened up in interview for this masthead in grand final week. Eddie Jim But any decision on stand downs – the AFL can stand down players who face criminal charges – would hinge on the nature and severity of any charges. Heeney, Warner, Blakey and Jordon are persons of interest in a police investigation stemming from the night. Three women have alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. No charges have yet been laid, and the players have all denied criminal wrongdoing.



Dillon’s comments were in a wide-ranging interview with this masthead in which he also condemned the abuse of umpires by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass and expressed a desire for the AFL to eventually sell a portion of its media rights to a global streamer like Netflix. Up to clubs to do due diligence on Swans trades He said clubs had to do their due diligence if they were interested in acquiring any of the Swans players and take on the inherent risks. Police have confirmed that Bice is not a suspect and is being treated only as a witness in the investigation. “I think from an AFL point of view, it would be it’s business as usual,” Dillon told this masthead, when asked how the AFL would handle any trades. “So, ultimately, it will be for the Swans, and I don’t know where the Swans are at with the players ... If there’s a club that was looking to acquire one of those players or any others, you do your due diligence, and that’s where that there will be uncertainty for the foreseeable future while there’s a police investigation still going.” Sydney Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney and Nick Blakey. The Age



Dillon said it would be up to the clubs to make their own calls. “Then it’s you do your due diligence, and you understand there’s obviously risks that come. There’s risk with them staying with the Swans, obviously, and there’s risk if they leave,” he said. Dillon, whose initial response to the Pullman episode was one of “disbelief”, said if any charges were laid before the Swans returned for pre-season, the nature of those charges would determine if and when the accused players could come back to the club and train. “It depends what the charges are, depends when they’re laid ... there’s rules at the AFL’s disposal for stand down and the like. There might be club sanctions as well in relation if there was charging as well. So, we’d work with the club and the players’ association and the players looking at the AFL rules ... if that eventuates.” The five Swans returned to the club on Wednesday for exit interviews and met with teammates. This masthead has reported that Blakey has been willing to entertain a trade, while Warner, a restricted free agent next year, has not considered the possibility of moving this year, a well-placed source has confirmed. All five are contracted for 2027 or beyond. Jordon (left), Blakey (rear, second from left) and Heeney (centre) arrive at Moore Park for their exit interviews from the Swans’ 2026 season. George Chan



‘Community standards have changed’ While the AFL does not have an automatic no-fault stand-down policy like the NRL’s, Dillon said there was a threshold for charges that would bring stand downs. “It’s not a published one, but you look at what it is, what’s the nature of the charge, and then what’s the potential severity of the charge.” The AFL had stood down Geelong midfielder Tanner Bruhn, who was charged rape before the charges were dropped last November after a witness admitted to lying in his police statement. Players have been charged with sexual assault offences in the past and been allowed to keep playing because charges were deemed not commensurate with a stand down, but Dillon said community standards had changed. Loading



“The stand-down rule has been in place for a while ... but there are, you know, community standards and other standards change over time,” he said. “So what might have happened back in 2008 or 2012 isn’t necessarily how it would be dealt with in 2026 or 2027. But, you’ve also got a presumption of innocence, and I think that’s a really important part of you know the Australian justice system.” The AFL CEO said of his visceral reaction to the Pullman incident, in which some of the five players were accused of inappropriate touching by topless waitresses who had been in the room in the early hours of that August morning: “First one was disbelieving, as opposed to anger ... I think it started at disbelief, went through a whole number of other ranges of emotions. I think it’s back at disbelief.” Dillon said, based on the information the Swans had, they had “handled it as well as they could have in the circumstances.” The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne where the Swans were staying during their trip to Melbourne for round 23. Simon Schluter



Dillon met Netflix execs Dillon said the AFL was interested in future deals with global streaming giant Netflix, which had broadcast the NFL game at the MCG between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers. The packed MCG before the start of the Rams v 49ers game. Eddie Jim Dillon had met Netflix executives at a dinner, but had no formal engagement yet. “The Netflix strategy is big events that are global in nature. Now I’m not sure that we’re at that level yet … I’d love us to be there at some stage.” Asked if the AFL would look at a Netflix deal in future, Dillon said: “Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s hard to know exactly where the broadcast market’s going to be in 10 or 15 years, but I think the one thing we know it probably won’t look like what it does now.”



Related Article Exclusive

Lunch with Netflix’s ‘queen of screens’ hid a secret about her past. When it came to light, she froze Netflix has rights to a package of marquee NFL games that includes the Melbourne, Thanksgiving and Christmas games. Sicily, Barrass ‘crossed the line’ In the wide-ranging interview covering the 2026 season and key issues, Dillon also said the behaviour of Hawthorn skipper Sicily, teammate Barrass and some Hawk fans in response to umpiring calls late in Saturday’s epic preliminary final had been “far from appropriate” and “really disappointing”, had crossed a line which the club understood. “I think the reactions of the players and some of the fans was not appropriate, far from appropriate, and really disappointing. I understand the emotion because it was an incredible game and it was intense. But there’s also standards, and there’s lines that shouldn’t be crossed, and I think they were in the terms of the two Hawthorn players, and then a number of Hawthorn fans.”



The AFL had selected umpire Hayden Meyer, who paid the holding the ball decision against Jarman Impey that led to the match-winning goal to Hugh McCluggage, as one of four grand final umpires. Dillon confirmed that Meyer’s selection was “absolutely” an endorsement of the holding-the-ball decision, one of three that went against the Hawks in the final minute and a half. The AFL boss said all three decisions were right. Hayden Meyer, who was at the centre of the dramatic finish between the Hawks and the Brisbane Lions, is set to officiate his third grand final. AFL Photos “I think it’s rare that you get almost 100 per cent unanimity on an umpire’s decision, particularly holding the ball. I think the other ones absolutely were there as well. “For a Hawthorn fan and the Hawthorn players to have three of them in 60 seconds, it’s not ideal, obviously, but they were all there, and I think people who talk about putting the whistle away, well, you’re still going to pay the free kick, whether it’s the first minute or the last minute, particularly when they’re clear.” New illicit drugs policy will ‘change behaviour’

World.title: ‘Goodnight, my friend’: Slash, Kate Ceberano, Jason Donovan pay tribute to Angry Anderson
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale ‘Goodnight, my friend’: Slash, Kate Ceberano, Jason Donovan pay tribute to Angry Anderson Kayla Olaya September 24, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rock star Slash and Australian music greats Jimmy Barnes, Kate Ceberano and Jason Donovan have led tributes to Rose Tattoo frontman Gary “Angry” Anderson. Slash, the lead guitarist of Guns N’ Roses and whose real name is Saul Hudson, took to social media to remember his friend, who died on Monday aged 79. Anderson’s death was confirmed in a statement shared by his bandmates and family on Wednesday. Australian Rock Legend Angry Anderson, pictured in full voice in 2009. Getty Images “RIP #AngryAnderson. I’m going to miss my good friend; I can’t believe he’s gone. Condolences to his family, friends and band members,” Hudson wrote on Instagram. Guns N’ Roses covered the Rose Tattoo song Nice Boys Don’t Play Rock ‘n’ Roll, and in 2013, Anderson joined the American band on stage during an Australian tour to perform it.



Donovan also paid tribute to Anderson via Instagram, honouring his legacy and contributions to rock – and to the Australian TV soap Neighbours. Anderson’s song, Suddenly, was famously played during the wedding of Scott and Charlene (played by Donovan and Kylie Minogue), which was one of the biggest moments on Australian television. “Angry didn’t just sing rock ‘n’ roll — he lived it. A voice like thunder, a heart that never stopped giving, and a spirit that fought hard for young people and those doing it tough,” Donovan said. “I’ll always be proud that Suddenly became part of our shared story. Rest peacefully, Gary. Your voice, your heart and your legacy will never be forgotten.” Ceberano shared a photo on Instagram of her with Anderson, singers John Farnham and Jon Stevens and actor John Waters from the 1992 Australian production tour of Jesus Christ Superstar .



She said in her post that it had been a nostalgic week for her and the show’s alumni at John Farnham’s tribute concert, with Ceberano sharing a story about how, on her 25th birthday on the 1992 tour, Anderson encouraged her to get a tattoo. “With all the joy of the week replaying Superstar memories with Jon Stevens for our mate John Farnham, it’s with sadness we say goodbye to our friend and co-star @gary_angry_anderson RIP,” Ceberano wrote. “We had all had a massive lunch together ... and you turned to me and said, flushed with excitement, ‘One of the most celebrated tattooists from the Illustrated Man is in Hindley St TODAY! I think you should go up there and make a memory of this moment that will last a lifetime’. I promptly put pen to paper, drew a simple mandala, and we all traipsed up the hill ... where I gave myself over to the famed gal. “I sobered up pretty fast, I can tell you, but to have ANGRY’s smiling mug keeping me company during this ‘rite of passage’ was unforgettable. Thank you and goodnight, my friend.”



In an Instagram post late on Wednesday, Barnes, the legendary rock singer, farewelled his close friend and collaborator. “We lost a good man this week. Angry Anderson sang from his heart with power and conviction,” Barnes wrote. “But don’t let that tough outside fool you. He was a caring soul who loved his family, cared for his friends and stood up for the downtrodden. “Rock in Peace my dear friend.” Australian-American musician and actor Rick Springfield posted a photo, also on Instagram, of Anderson performing in his later years.



“Really sad to learn that Gary Anderson, aka Angry Anderson [has died],” Springfield said. “Another great voice silenced.” Sebastian Bach, the frontman of American rock band Skid Row, took to Instagram to pay tribute to Anderson. “They don’t make them like Angry Anderson any more,” Bach said. “You left us too soon, but that’s because you were too good for us. The most gifted vocalist, lyricist, performer ...” The original yellow Wiggle, Greg Page, also left a comment on Rose Tattoo’s announcement of Anderson’s death.



“His legend and legacy lives on. Rest easy, Angry,” Page said. Anderson suffered a cardiac arrest in late August and was admitted to a hospital to undergo treatment. Loading “It is with great sadness we announce the passing of Gary ‘Angry’ Anderson on the eve of Monday, 21 September 2026, surrounded by his loved ones here in Australia,” the band said in a statement on Wednesday. “Angry was a devoted father, and much-loved bandmate, friend, and member of the wider music and entertainment community. His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas.”



Anderson joined Rose Tattoo in 1976, soon after the band was founded by guitarist Pete Wells, and served as its lead vocalist until shortly before his death. On August 10, the band announced the cancellation of the European leg of its One Last Ride tour after Anderson was hospitalised due to a “medical issue”. It was set to be the band’s final tour after more than five decades of performing live. The band began its European tour in July, and had nine more shows to go when the cancellation was announced. Rose Tattoo were scheduled to return to Australia this month to perform several farewell gigs across the state capitals. World.title: WA news LIVE: Dockers get green light for ‘Wharfie Time’ in grand final
World.content:
The Fremantle Dockers have been given the all-clear to use the club’s famous “Wharfie Time” motivator during Saturday’s AFL grand final against Brisbane.

But there’s a catch: the AFL is allowing the Dockers to use the spine-tingling intro from AC/DC’s Hell’s Bell’s just once after a goal as part of the celebrations.

Loading

9News Perth reporter Paddy Sweeney said the league believed the Dockers and Lions had two of the best game-day fan engagement experiences, which it wanted to be part of what is shaping to be a grand final for the history books.

“Wharfie Time”, which had its genesis in a rousing speech from former Dockers captain Matthew Pavlich, has been deployed twice this season so far.

The motivator, which is played when the margin is tight and the clock is running down, helped lift the Dockers to victory over Hawthorn in round 9, and was also played in the final minutes of the team’s win over Geelong in the semi-final.

It has only ever been deployed at Optus Stadium, with lights and screens blaring into action and the crowd erupting into rapturous support to transform the venue into “Fortress Fremantle”.

World.title: Nine TV and streaming boss leaving after less than two years
World.content:
Nine’s managing director of streaming and broadcast, Amanda Laing, is departing from the business after less than two years in the job. The powerful executive reported to chief executive Matt Stanton and oversaw Channel Nine, free online video platform 9Now, and premium streaming service Stan. Nine sources said she was departing in a move related to a restructure. Amanda Laing has made major cost cuts in Nine’s TV division, which is enduring a tough advertising market. Dominic Lorrimer Laing joined the company, which also owns this masthead, in April 2025. Laing had previously been a senior executive at pay television company Foxtel and had sat on the Australian Rugby League Commission. The move came after a day of change for Nine, which announced on Wednesday that Australian Financial Review editor-in-chief James Chessell was leaving to join independent media site Rampart. He is being replaced by the Review’s editor Cosima Marriner.



Related Article Updated

Media & marketing Financial Review editor-in-chief James Chessell quits to join media start-up During Laing’s tenure, Nine secured a deal to retain the rights to broadcast the NRL, but also made cuts in its television division in response to advertising revenue declining. Those cuts came as part of a strategy to overhaul Nine’s television news broadcasting dubbed “Future News”, in which it streamlined the number of positions it employs with new broadcasting software. The changes prompted a fierce backlash from staff, some of which have joined the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance union for the first time. And while Nine held onto the NRL rights, the sport’s boss Peter V’Landys has previously said that outcome was due in large part to direct negotiations with Nine chair Peter Tonagh.



In its most recent annual results, Nine cut the value of its Total TV business, which includes both broadcast and digital streaming, in its books by $426 million to about $360 million. Nine’s share price dropped to $0.72 on Wednesday afternoon, down almost 40 per cent over the last twelve months. Laing’s section of the company had already been reorganised during her short tenure. Nine created the new position of streaming and television boss for Laing upon her arrival. It was in part an attempt to bring the company’s streaming service Stan closer to the rest of the business and position it more centrally as one of its main growth sectors. Laing previously worked for Nine from 2006 to 2017 before her stint at Foxtel.



Nine and Laing were contacted for comment. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

Alec Shelbrooke, a former defence procurement minister, blamed problems with French-made components in the engines. In January 2023, the 28-aircraft fleet was grounded as a precaution after a blade failed during an incident on the runway at RAF Valley. Flying resumed after a pause, but many engines were removed from service while the problem was investigated.



Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, the head of the UK Armed Forces, said in late 2024 that he wanted to replace the Hawk T2 because of the engine and support problems. The crash comes three months after three members of the Royal Navy died when a helicopter went down during a training exercise in Devon, England. Lieutenant Lily-Mae Fisher, Britain’s only female Royal Navy commando, died alongside Lieutenant Commander Chris Gayson and Petty Officer Owen Green when their Merlin Mk4 crashed in a field near Sourton Down in the early hours of June 4. World.title: Xi Jinping lands in Washington with Trump waiting on the tarmac
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Xi Jinping lands in Washington with Trump waiting on the tarmac Michelle L. Price September 24, 2026 — 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday, with US President Donald Trump waiting to welcome his counterpart on the tarmac instead of waiting for him to drive to the White House. Trump’s decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far the US president is going to honour China’s leader in his first state visit to the US capital in more than a decade. US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan at Joint Base Andrews. AP Trump and wife Melania Trump were at the base to participate in an arrival ceremony for Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan. The salutation kicks off a three-day visit that’s expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump’s visit to China in May. But it also is a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan.



Beyond using the visit to try to keep “strategic stability” between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. The two leaders have a packed schedule over coming days. AP Related Article Trump diplomacy Xi to get the rock star treatment as Trump prepares a spectacle He has lavished praise on Xi as a “great leader” and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Republican senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the US Senate Armed Services Committee, criticised the “lavish welcome”, and told the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader “based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party”.



Wicker archly suggested a list of topics that Trump could discuss with Xi at the state dinner, such as “the purposes of China’s massive military build-up, or about China’s clear support for Iran”. He said that “during every minute of dialogue”, Trump should keep in mind that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbours and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US and China had to interact at the highest levels because they were “the two largest economies in the world” and “probably the two most powerful militaries in the world”. Trump appears to be pulling out all stops to impress Xi. AP “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to,” Rubio said in New York on Wednesday. Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, and told reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new “work of art” helicopter landing pad would be ready for the Chinese leader’s visit, although he bemoaned his massive White House ballroom would not.



Trump on Wednesday was looking to match the pageantry he was met with in China this year. In May, Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump but Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. But a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. A military honour guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!” also were present. ‘He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect.’ US first lady Melania Trump The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional paint colours of the US presidential plane. First lady Melania Trump said earlier on Wednesday that her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrived in the Washington region because “they have a great relationship”.



“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said of Xi and his wife during an interview on Fox News Channel’s Fox & Friends. Trump’s airport ceremony for Xi will be followed on Thursday (US time) by more formalities, including an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Melania Trump said her husband and Xi have a “great relationship”. AP Before the black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, the two leaders are expected to dive into weighty issues behind closed doors, even as expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs in the relationship. On Friday, Xi and Peng will return to the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries.
