World.title: ‘It’s up to the clubs’: AFL CEO says there’s risk in trading for besieged Swans
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘It’s up to the clubs’: AFL CEO says there’s risk in trading for besieged Swans Jake Niall Updated September 24, 2026 — 8:30am ,first published 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL boss Andrew Dillon says the league will leave it to the clubs to decide whether they wish to trade for any of the five suspended Sydney Swans players amid an ongoing police investigation into allegations of sexual assault against potentially four of the five. Dillon said the AFL still reserved the right to sanction the relevant players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice – for their behaviour at the Pullman following the conclusion of the police investigation. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has opened up in interview for this masthead in grand final week. Eddie Jim But any decision on stand downs – the AFL can stand down players who face criminal charges – would hinge on the nature and severity of any charges. Heeney, Warner, Blakey and Jordon are persons of interest in a police investigation stemming from the night. Three women have alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. No charges have yet been laid, and the players have all denied criminal wrongdoing.



Dillon’s comments were in a wide-ranging interview with this masthead in which he also condemned the abuse of umpires by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass and expressed a desire for the AFL to eventually sell a portion of its media rights to a global streamer like Netflix. Up to clubs to do due diligence on Swans trades He said clubs had to do their due diligence if they were interested in acquiring any of the Swans players and take on the inherent risks. Police have confirmed that Bice is not a suspect and is being treated only as a witness in the investigation. “I think from an AFL point of view, it would be it’s business as usual,” Dillon told this masthead, when asked how the AFL would handle any trades. “So, ultimately, it will be for the Swans, and I don’t know where the Swans are at with the players ... If there’s a club that was looking to acquire one of those players or any others, you do your due diligence, and that’s where that there will be uncertainty for the foreseeable future while there’s a police investigation still going.” Sydney Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney and Nick Blakey. The Age



Dillon said it would be up to the clubs to make their own calls. “Then it’s you do your due diligence, and you understand there’s obviously risks that come. There’s risk with them staying with the Swans, obviously, and there’s risk if they leave,” he said. Dillon, whose initial response to the Pullman episode was one of “disbelief”, said if any charges were laid before the Swans returned for pre-season, the nature of those charges would determine if and when the accused players could come back to the club and train. “It depends what the charges are, depends when they’re laid ... there’s rules at the AFL’s disposal for stand down and the like. There might be club sanctions as well in relation if there was charging as well. So, we’d work with the club and the players’ association and the players looking at the AFL rules ... if that eventuates.” The five Swans returned to the club on Wednesday for exit interviews and met with teammates. This masthead has reported that Blakey has been willing to entertain a trade, while Warner, a restricted free agent next year, has not considered the possibility of moving this year, a well-placed source has confirmed. All five are contracted for 2027 or beyond. Jordon (left), Blakey (rear, second from left) and Heeney (centre) arrive at Moore Park for their exit interviews from the Swans’ 2026 season. George Chan



‘Community standards have changed’ While the AFL does not have an automatic no-fault stand-down policy like the NRL’s, Dillon said there was a threshold for charges that would bring stand downs. “It’s not a published one, but you look at what it is, what’s the nature of the charge, and then what’s the potential severity of the charge.” The AFL had stood down Geelong midfielder Tanner Bruhn, who was charged rape before the charges were dropped last November after a witness admitted to lying in his police statement. Players have been charged with sexual assault offences in the past and been allowed to keep playing because charges were deemed not commensurate with a stand down, but Dillon said community standards had changed. Loading



“The stand-down rule has been in place for a while ... but there are, you know, community standards and other standards change over time,” he said. “So what might have happened back in 2008 or 2012 isn’t necessarily how it would be dealt with in 2026 or 2027. But, you’ve also got a presumption of innocence, and I think that’s a really important part of you know the Australian justice system.” The AFL CEO said of his visceral reaction to the Pullman incident, in which some of the five players were accused of inappropriate touching by topless waitresses who had been in the room in the early hours of that August morning: “First one was disbelieving, as opposed to anger ... I think it started at disbelief, went through a whole number of other ranges of emotions. I think it’s back at disbelief.” Dillon said, based on the information the Swans had, they had “handled it as well as they could have in the circumstances.” The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne where the Swans were staying during their trip to Melbourne for round 23. Simon Schluter



Dillon met Netflix execs Dillon said the AFL was interested in future deals with global streaming giant Netflix, which had broadcast the NFL game at the MCG between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers. The packed MCG before the start of the Rams v 49ers game. Eddie Jim Dillon had met Netflix executives at a dinner, but had no formal engagement yet. “The Netflix strategy is big events that are global in nature. Now I’m not sure that we’re at that level yet … I’d love us to be there at some stage.” Asked if the AFL would look at a Netflix deal in future, Dillon said: “Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s hard to know exactly where the broadcast market’s going to be in 10 or 15 years, but I think the one thing we know it probably won’t look like what it does now.”



Related Article Exclusive

Lunch with Netflix’s ‘queen of screens’ hid a secret about her past. When it came to light, she froze Netflix has rights to a package of marquee NFL games that includes the Melbourne, Thanksgiving and Christmas games. Sicily, Barrass ‘crossed the line’ In the wide-ranging interview covering the 2026 season and key issues, Dillon also said the behaviour of Hawthorn skipper Sicily, teammate Barrass and some Hawk fans in response to umpiring calls late in Saturday’s epic preliminary final had been “far from appropriate” and “really disappointing”, had crossed a line which the club understood. “I think the reactions of the players and some of the fans was not appropriate, far from appropriate, and really disappointing. I understand the emotion because it was an incredible game and it was intense. But there’s also standards, and there’s lines that shouldn’t be crossed, and I think they were in the terms of the two Hawthorn players, and then a number of Hawthorn fans.”



The AFL had selected umpire Hayden Meyer, who paid the holding the ball decision against Jarman Impey that led to the match-winning goal to Hugh McCluggage, as one of four grand final umpires. Dillon confirmed that Meyer’s selection was “absolutely” an endorsement of the holding-the-ball decision, one of three that went against the Hawks in the final minute and a half. The AFL boss said all three decisions were right. Hayden Meyer, who was at the centre of the dramatic finish between the Hawks and the Brisbane Lions, is set to officiate his third grand final. AFL Photos “I think it’s rare that you get almost 100 per cent unanimity on an umpire’s decision, particularly holding the ball. I think the other ones absolutely were there as well. “For a Hawthorn fan and the Hawthorn players to have three of them in 60 seconds, it’s not ideal, obviously, but they were all there, and I think people who talk about putting the whistle away, well, you’re still going to pay the free kick, whether it’s the first minute or the last minute, particularly when they’re clear.” New illicit drugs policy will ‘change behaviour’

World.title: Government puts $40.5 million towards two gas exploration projects
World.content:
The government is putting $40.5 million towards two gas exploration projects, from the government's $200m gas exploration fund.

The funding includes $14.5m to contract Schlumberger New Zealand to provide companies with free access to AI-backed 3d seismic modelling data for the Taranaki, East Coast, and Great South basins over two years; and $21.5m for EnZed Energy's Kaheru project exploring for recoverable gas offshore from Taranaki.

Resources Minister Shane Jones said the projects would help secure New Zealand's ongoing energy needs.

He said the Schlumberger project would make it easier to access and interpret basin-scale data in an industry-standard format which would be "very attractive to international exploration companies deciding where to put their money and effort".

The datasets would be available for free to potential explorers for two years.

He said the EnZed project was aiming to find 182 petajouls of gas, the equivalent of nearly a quarter of New Zealand's current "proven and probable" reserves.

"New Zealanders need access to a reliable energy supply when renewables are unable to meet demand."

Jones also welcomed the release of the 2025 Petroleum Exploration Data Pack by New Zealand Petroleum & Minerals, saying making such data available was one of the most effective ways to showcase resource potential and encourage new investment.

He said 74 additional wells and 31 3d seismic surveys had been added to the data since the last data pack was released in 2018.

World.title: Man found dead in Northland identified as Tau Henare Kopa
World.content:
The identity of a man found dead at a property in Waiomio earlier this month has been revealed.

Police on Thursday said he was Tau Henare Kopa, 35, of Kawakawa, Northland.

They were still working to establish what happened, Detective Inspector Michele Gillespie said.

His remains were found on the afternoon of 7 September.

"At this stage his death is still being treated as unexplained and our enquiries remain ongoing.

"Police extend our condolences to his family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time."

World.title: Government hits pause on council amalgamation plan until after election
World.content:
The Government has told mayors around the country it's deferring decisions on amalgamating councils until after the election.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop and Local Government Minister Simon Watts said they would be taking additional time before deciding which proposals, part of the Head Start local government reform process, should progress to the detailed design stage.

"It is clear from the response we received that there is genuine appetite for change," Watts said.

Eighteen proposals were submitted in August against the Government's objectives for a simpler, more effective and accountable local government system.

"While the overall quality of proposals was high, none came with the unanimous view of the region, and some needed further analysis before they can progress. These are important gaps we must fill in prior to making final decisions."

Particular areas that required further development included ensuring fair and effective representation with streamlined governance, and the transfer and delivery of regional functions, the ministers said.

"Rather than asking councils to commit further time and resources to finalise proposals now, the Government will now work to fill in these gaps over the next few months. Cabinet will consider these proposals in early-2027."

Bishop said the Government remained committed to local government reform.

"The Government continues to expect proposals endorsed by Cabinet to be developed in detail and considered for final approval in 2027, with Head Start changes intended to be in place ahead of the 2028 local government elections."

"Work is also continuing on the backstop process for areas that do not progress through Head Start. Decisions on that process will be informed by lessons from the Head Start pathway, consultation feedback and further advice from officials. We continue to expect decisions on this in early 2027."

Wellington City mayor Andrew Little. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Ministers made promises they couldn't keep - Wellington mayor

But Wellington City mayor Andrew Little said the announcement showed the Government was not serious about the process.

Little, who is also co-chair of the Wellington and Wairarapa Mayoral Forum, said councils across the region put forward strong proposals that met the Government's requirements and would have worked, while spending nearly $250,000 collectively to put forward a proposal before the recent deadline - which was "significant time and ratepayer money".

"Ministers asked us to move quickly. We did exactly that. It is now clear the Government was not ready to follow through, and didn't have enough support around the Cabinet table."

Little said ministers made promises they couldn't keep and have now abandoned the process.

"Wellington ratepayers are entitled to ask why they were asked to pay for an exercise the Government was not prepared to complete.

"At a time when councils are doing everything possible to keep costs under control, facing an arbitrary rates cap that will affect services and facilities that communities rely on, spending nearly a quarter of a million dollars on a process that goes nowhere is unacceptable."

He said the three-month deadline was "totally unreasonable" and criteria continually shifted.

"We met all of the government's requirements to get a proposal in before the deadline.

"The only party that has not thought through their policy is central government themselves. It claims it is wanting to simplify local government, but today it has confirmed it has no plan for how to achieve this."

RNZ / Angus Dreaver

'Communities will not tolerate ratepayer money being spent on unclear processes'

Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) said councils moved heaven and earth to meet an unrealistic deadline for proposals, and now need certainty.

LGNZ president Rehette Stoltz said the Government's inability to decide which proposals will progress has left councils feeling frustrated.

"Councils were put through a rushed process, only for the Government to now acknowledge that the work could not be completed properly in the time available," she said.

"Communities will not tolerate ratepayer money being spent on unclear processes that are repeatedly reshaped after the work has been done. Before councils do more work, they need certainty the goal posts won't be moved again."

She maintained reform should be locally led, not driven from the Beehive.

"Local government reform is too important to be subject to a constantly changing process."

World.title: Labour pledges $4 billion for state houses, school repairs and hospitals
World.content:
Labour is promising to create more jobs by building homes, improving classrooms and repairing hospitals at a total cost of more than $4 billion.

The party says it will deliver at least 6000 additional social housing places over four years, school improvements at more than 2000 schools and hospital improvements, too.

Its allocated nearly $3b for building new state houses, $450 million for school repairs, and $200m toward health.

It also allocated $760m to cover the additional Income-Related Rent Subsidy and operating costs for Kāinga Ora and Community Housing Providers.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins and Labour jobs spokesperson Ginny Andersen made the policy announcement in Hamilton on Thursday.

They pointed to an 11-year high in unemployment and struggling construction businesses, saying the party would get building projects underway and "more Kiwis back on the tools".

Labour jobs spokesperson Ginny Andersen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Hipkins said: "Labour will build the infrastructure New Zealand needs, create jobs and ensure the benefits return to local businesses and communities."

"Right now, homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing. We can do all three while creating good jobs for Kiwis."

He said government funding for a building project saw benefits beyond the worksite, with builders hiring tradies, tradies buying materials, suppliers getting more orders, apprentices getting hours, and local businesses benefiting from workers spending in their communities.

Andersen said unemployment at an 11-year high under National meant Labour wanted to get Kiwis back to work.

"That means building homes, fixing schools and repairing hospitals, not sitting on our hands," she said.

"This is about putting government investment to work - improving public infrastructure, supporting local businesses and giving the construction sector greater certainty."

World.title: Bringing Aotea back to life through a te ao Māori lens
World.content:
Audio player for " The fight against feral cats on Aotea Great Barrier Island " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/te-ao-maori/1549658%2Fbringing-aotea-back-to-life-through-a-te-ao-maori-lens

The fight against feral cats on Aotea Great Barrier Island Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Ko au te taiao, ko te taiao ko au.

I am the nature, and nature is me.

For the people behind an iwi-led conservation project on Aotea Great Barrier Island, that relationship sits at the heart of the mahi.

Tū Mai Taonga is a Ngāti Rehua Ngātiwai ki Aotea-led conservation project working to remove introduced predators and restore balance to the whenua.

They are undertaking one of the largest feral cat eradication operations in the world.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405466986112

Project lead Makere Jenner told RNZ the kaupapa was about protecting native species and healing whānau.

"While we're doing a feral cat eradication to restore the whenua, we also are restoring and healing ourselves. That's a holistic te ao Māori way to do things."

Jenner said being able to bring people home was an important part of restoring the whenua.

Trappers Lyrik Murray (team lead), Phoebe Ngawaka and her younger sister Reneeah Ngawaka. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

"The Tū Mai Taonga project has provided jobs that allow whānau to be able to return home to Aotea who have had to live on the mainland for work and other reasons.

"To be able to come home, reconnect with the marae, reconnect with whānau, reconnect with culture, te reo Māori, and also gives them the opportunity to heal the land with their own hands, is really magical."

For trapper and team lead Lyrik Murray, the mahi had also provided a way to reconnect with a part of her identity.

"For me personally, I didn't grow up with that, Māori, like our culture was beaten out of our family literally, you know, so to work for like an iwi led project and reconnect with that kind of mahi is pretty important."

Tū Mai Taonga team lead Lyrik Murray didn't grow up in te ao Māori and says reconnecting with that part of herself is pretty special. RNZ / Nick Monro

New Zealand added feral cats to the official Predator Free 2050 target species list for national eradication in 2025.

Tū Mai Taonga was currently working from north to south of the island, setting up hundreds of cage traps and cameras across the ngahere.

The first phase of the kaupapa involved cutting around 90 kilometres of tracks through Te Paparahi, a 3414-hectare rugged forest block located at the northern end of Aotea.

Once the number of feral cats was brought down in one zone, the trapping network moved into the next.

The island was estimated to have around 2500 feral cats, while data from the northern area suggested that now, fewer than 15 remained.

A feral cat roams Aotea, captured on one of Tū Mai Taonga's trail cameras. Supplied / Tū Mai Taonga

Jenner said the decision to remove the introduced predators came from an understanding that people were part of the environment too.

"We see ourselves as part of te taiao, as part of the environment, we are protecting, restoring and sustaining the natural environment, so that the environment is able to sustain us."

And that meant taking responsibility for the damage humans had caused.

"It's not the cat's fault that it's here causing damage in an environment, it's our fault. We brought cats here, people brought cats here and so from a te ao Māori perspective, we are a part of the environment and so sometimes we cause damage but we also need to take every opportunity we can to be able to make things right."

Aotea has specialised ecosystems and is home to many native species. RNZ / Nick Monro

Aotea had specialised ecosystems and was home to native species including takoketai, or black petrel, niho taniwha, the chevron skink, and the kākā.

Jenner said those taonga species could not withstand the pressure of feral cats.

"It's important for us to be able to try to make a way to restore balance for them and to make a way for our taonga species to survive."

The human side of eradication

Restoring that balance also meant confronting the difficult reality of killing the animals that threatened it.

For some of the project's trappers, that could be confronting.

Trapper Phoebe Ngawaka remembered her first kill.

"I went and dug a hole and then asked for [my team lead] to bring the feral over, so she did and then I buried it and planted a little tree on top, had me a little karakia ... but it was traumatic, I wasn't happy about it and it's still the only feral that I've caught."

Trapper Phoebe Ngawaka says her mahi restoring te taiao is closely connected to her mahi with rongoā. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

But Ngawaka said the reason behind the mahi was to create a future where native species could safely return to the ngahere.

"It'd be really cool to have our area set up so that it's safe for those natives to come back, like the kōkako, maybe one day the kiwi, and until then, until all the cats are out of the ngahere, then we can't really have them back."

Jenner said the project's trappers were trained to approach the animals with respect.

"We teach our crew when they're onboarded to be respectful of the fact that that is a living thing. We humanely kill, we don't cause undue distress."

Some people have questioned why the feral cats could not be rehomed, but Jenner said that was not feasible given the numbers involved and the difficulty of domesticating feral cats.

Tū Mai Taonga project lead Makere Jenner says pet cats will always be part of life in Aotearoa, but the project's goal is to make responsible cat ownership possible. RNZ / Nick Monro

Keeping Aotea's pets safe through manaakitanga

While the project targets feral cats, it also recognises the importance of companion cats to Aotea whānau.

Aotearoa New Zealand is one of the world's biggest domestic cat owners, with around 40 percent of homes owning at least one cat.

Unwanted pets made their way into becoming what's referred to as stray cats - the cats which lived close to humans often surviving on scraps.

Feral cats were the truly wild cats, generations removed from their domestic roots and having had no human interaction. It's these cats even the SPCA accepts should be killed due to the risk they pose to wildlife.

As part of the Safe Cat programme, pet cats could be collected by the Cat Taxi and taken to the vet for desexing. RNZ / Nick Monro

Through the project's de-sex drive and Safe Cat programme, free microchipping and desexing was available on Aotea, while pet owners could register their cats in the island's "Cat-alogue".

Collars and ear-tipping could help identify pets, while a "cat taxi" took animals to the vet and brought them home.

Auckland Council conservation advisor Annamarie Clough said keeping pets safe was an important part of the programme.

"Feral cat control is important, but on the other hand, we recognise the importance that companion cats play in households, so we really want to keep them safe while we're undertaking feral cat control."

Seventh-generation Aotea resident Judy Hale. RNZ / Nick Monro

Seventh-generation Aotea resident Judy Hale has four cats. She used the free desexing service, saying she could not have otherwise afforded the procedure and travel costs.

Petrol and diesel at the time of RNZ's visit was over $4.44 a litre.

"I was very lucky that we had this available for us, you know, because there's no way as a pensioner that I could have afforded to have had my cat spayed, so it would have been more kittens.

"And gone are the days you could get rid of them yourselves."

This intitative was an example of how the island's approach was looking after the people and pets who called Aotea home, while protecting the wider taiao, she said.

Tū Mai Taonga project lead Makere Jenner says while they're doing a feral cat eradication to restore the whenua, they are also restoring and healing themselves as a people. RNZ / Nick Monro

For future generations

Te toto o te tangata he kai, te oranga o te tangata he whenua.

While food provides the blood in our veins, our health and wellbeing are drawn from the land.

Jenner said success would not only be measured by how many cats were removed, but by whether future generations grew up knowing abundance as normal.

"My generation has grown up, with the northern bush on Aotea particularly, being absolutely silent, ghostly silent, sadly silent," she said emotionally.

"Particularly sad for the generation before me, who got to experience the remnants of abundance up there. And that generation, my mum's generation, witnessed that peter away at almost nothing.

"Our ambition is for our tamariki, for our future generations, for their normal to be that abundance that two generations ago had."

World.title: Papuan civilians shot in latest security forces violence in Yahukimo
World.content:
Reports filtering out from West Papua say six civilians were shot by Indonesian security forces last week in Yahukimo Regency.

Human Rights Monitor reports that military and police personnel opened fire at a group of Indigenous Papuan civilians near Samboga Village last Friday while returning from a gold-panning site.

Six young men aged between 19 and 28 were shot, including two who were critically injured, although it took several days before they were evacuated to hospital.

This comes as Indonesian security forces have been running a joint operation to pursue guerilla fighters with the West Papua Liberation Army, or TPNPB, in this mountainous region of Papua.

A human rights defender in the region told RNZ Pacific that the latest attack has been condemned by both religious and tribal leaders.

Yahukimo Fellowship of Churches spokesperson Reverend Atias Matuan said the conflict is between Indonesian forces and the TPNPB and should not involve targeting unarmed civilians.

A local church was also raided as part of the military and police operation.

A local tribal chief Alipia Yalak has also pleaded with Indonesian security forces to gain some cultural understanding and differentiate between Papuans who carry arrows and bows or other traditional weapons for hunting and fishing from pro-independence guerillas.

He said if actions by the Indonesian military and police continued to create civilian casualties, the state and the TPNPB should negotiate a peaceful solution.

Meanwhile, the Regent of Yahukimo Didimus Yahuli has urged state security forces not to use extra-judicial killing when detaining criminals

The Papua Tribune reports him saying law enforcement must follow the correct judicial process, starting from arrest, examination, to court verdicts so that perpetrators can serve their sentences in correctional institutions while getting the opportunity to repent.

He said it is wrong for security forces to arrest then simply kill a suspect.

World.title: V'landys steps down as Racing NSW boss to secure firmer grip on NRL
World.content:
Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman is set to be made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.

V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.

His resignation looms as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.

Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.

But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.

When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.

At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.

In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.

Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.

Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.

V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.

He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.

"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."

In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.

Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.

"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.

"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.

"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."

Waterhouse says right time to move on

Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.

Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.

The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.

Australian horse trainer and businesswoman Gai Waterhouse. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.

"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."

Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.

"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.

Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.

"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Excitement, nerves as Dockers hold final home drill before grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Thousands of Fremantle Dockers fans have packed out the club's headquarters to watch the team train for the last time in Western Australia before they head to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

It has been 13 years since the Dockers last made a grand final, and the open training session in Cockburn saw so much demand that the team ticketed the event.

All 3,000 tickets were sold.

Long-term supporter Katie said the Dockers' success this year had special significance for her and her son Finlay.

Katie wants the Dockers to win for her son Finlay. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Finlay was just six weeks old when the 2013 grand final was held. Two years later, he developed cancer, and relapsed a year later.

"It's 10 years now since his relapse," Katie said.

"So it's his year and it's the Dockers' year, and all he wants is the Dockers to win on grand final day … that's his celebration."

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox and his teammates at the open training session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Imogen Somerville, who has also supported the Dockers "her entire life", described the event as overwhelming.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It was really cool to be able to get down here," she said.

"It was like five bucks to get in, which was awesome, so couldn't miss out on that."

Doing the right thing

Fans cheered the team on the field, then posed for photographs with their football heroes, who signed jerseys, posters and autographs.

Thousands of fans thronged to the event. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it was not just the public who were in the stands — past players, the club's chief executive Simon Garlick and Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti also attended the session.

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

Lee Spurr, who played in the 2013 grand final, said he felt "nothing but proud" to see his club back in the running for the flag.

"I was pretty nervous watching the prelim, but now that they're there, I feel like I'm almost playing. My phone's been blowing up," he said.

After experiencing the lead-up to the AFL's biggest week, Spurr said it was important for the players to turn off their phones and stick to preparation.

Former Dockers grand finalist Lee Spurr advises the team to lock in ahead of the game. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"My advice would be don't get caught up in doing too much, " he said.

" This week's about doing the process, doing what's right and preparing. "

Pure excitement

Superstar ruckman Luke Jackson said he loved having the fans participate in the club's biggest week.

Several Dockers said they loved having their fans take part in the session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"Just pure excitement. Can't wait to get over there and can't wait to play on Saturday in front of all these fans. It will be good fun," he said.

Jackson was in his second AFL season when he won his first premiership with the Melbourne Demons in 2021 in Perth.

He said he was looking forward to playing at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where the Dockers will face the Brisbane Lions.

Dockers defender Jordan Clark (left) talks to coach Justin Longmuir at Fremantle's open training session in Cockburn. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Defender Jordan Clark was also excited, and grateful, to see the fans.

"They support us through thick and thin, as they have done for the last 30 years," he said.

All the tickets for the training event were sold. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"So they're pretty happy with this moment and they rightly deserve to be, so it's pretty special when we get this support."

With no chance of making the training session, dozens of Dockers fans 1,600 kilometres away flocked to Broome airport today to catch the only direct flight to Melbourne before Saturday.

David Leslie, who goes by Docker Dave, has followed the team since its inception said his faith had been “restored” after their stellar final performances against Swans and Geelong.

The last direct flight to Melbourne from Broome this week was packed with Dockers fans. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

"We are going to flog the lions," he said.

World.title: Heeney 'extremely thankful' after addressing entire Swans club on return
World.content:
Sydney Swans forward Isaac Heeney says he is "thankful" for the opportunity to address his teammates and the club for the first time since he and four other players were suspended.

Heeney and his fellow banned teammates arrived at Swans HQ in Moore Park for their exit meetings on Wednesday evening after Sydney's 2026 season came to an end last week.

"It was really nice to address the whole club," Heeney said in a short statement.

"Extremely thankful they could give us their time and understanding … so yeah, it was really good."

Heeney (right) and Warner (centre) were the only banned players to speak to reporters at Swans HQ on Wednesday. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

It is Heeney's first public comment since he and four teammates — Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice — were suspended by the club for a breach of standards last month.

Warner and Bice arrived at Swans HQ first before Heeney, Jordon and Blakey arrived as a group shortly afterwards.

Warner was questioned by reporters on whether he would apologise to his teammates and said: "I don't know, we'll wait and see."

The banned players were met at the door by Swans executive general manager of football, Leon Cameron. Blakey, Jordon and Bice did not speak.

Sydney's season came to an end last week after it was defeated by Fremantle in the preliminary final. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Heeney polled a team-high 26 votes at the Brownlow Medal on Monday evening, well short of medal-winner Nick Daicos's record total of 47.

No decision has been made by Sydney on the playing futures of the five suspended players beyond this season.

Warner and Jordon are contracted through 2027 while Heeney and Bice are contracted through 2028. Blakey's contract with Sydney runs through the 2031 season.

An undermanned Swans side shocked grand finalists Brisbane in a qualifying final earlier this month before being beaten by Fremantle in last week's preliminary final.

World.title: Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object
World.content:
If we're ever going to solve that old question about unstoppable forces and immovable objects, the best way might be letting Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew run straight into each other.

The Penrith and Newcastle wingers will go head-to-head in Sunday's preliminary final with collisions that promise to rock the foundations of Stadium Australia.

Between them they boast a little over 200kg of prime Samoan beef, forged by pumping ludicrous amounts of steel in one case and fuelled by a truly startling quantity of Coke Zero in the other.

With a grand final berth on the line they will do what they do best: taking the ball and smashing into each other and anything else that gets in their way.

To'o has long been counted as one of the NRL's top wingers. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

They'll do it returning kicks, they'll do it early in sets, they'll do it close to the line to try and barge in and score and they'll do it over and over again until one of them is grand final bound.

Nobody can do all those things, grand finals included, like To'o, which is why he's the best winger of his time, but having played against Marzhew since the two's junior days he'll readily admit to taking some inspiration from the Knights wrecking machine.

"He's someone I like to base my game on, he's really strong and a big part of their team. I'm honoured to battle it out with my uso Greg," said To'o.

"It's our job to put our body on the front line and get the set started. It doesn't matter if it's one person in front of you, or two or three or four or five, just go as hard as you can."

Marzhew has enjoyed one of the best years of his career in 2026. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Likewise, Marzhew has looked to To'o plenty of times before and this season has the Panthers legend covered for tries (24 to 16), line breaks (27 to 21) and tackle busts (124 to 112), although To'o has him beat for average run metres (194 per game to 188)

Marzhew's form has earned him Newcastle's player's player award and he believes the challenge of taking on players like To'o has brought out the best in him.

"Penrith are one of my favourite teams to play against, they have so many representative players and I'm getting to go up against one of the best wingers to ever do it," said Marzhew

"I pride myself on that kind of stuff [big carries]. I try to excel with it because it's what the boys expect of me, if the crowd gets on top that's the cherry on top."

Fighting against greater numbers and winning is To'o's specialty. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's been doing it for so long now it's hard to imagine a time when To'o didn't relish the contact but he did have to learn to love it.

"When I was a bit younger, I was a bit shorter than I am now, I wouldn't say I was scared but there was that feeling that I might get knocked around," said To'o.

"I don't know if that counts as scared, I guess it pretty much does.

"It wasn't until my old man said, 'You're running it straight and getting knocked down or you're coming off and going home.'

"So I decided I'd run it straight. That was probably under-13s, I just dialled in and decided."

For Marzhew, who's got about 10kg on To'o, the issue was much simpler — there's never been any fear because he has always felt made for this

"Nah, that's the job description [running into people]," said Marzhew.

"That's what I signed up for."

The duo have plenty in common aside from their belief that the best way to solve a rugby league problem is to run right through it.

Both can really put on the dancing shoes — To'o's been hitting a little samba-type number after scoring recently, most notable after wrapping up Penrith's qualifying final over the Roosters with a late intercept try following one of his best games of the season.

"It's a Brazilian dance on TikTok, all the kids in my family, my nieces and nephews are always doing it," said To'o.

"My son does the dance and a Spider-man celebration as well, so I just wanted to honour all the kids.

"Now it's become a thing, I'll see kids down at the shops and they'll ask me to do it.

"But Greg's got me. He's built different. I've seen his moves, he's got the hips for it."

To'o's not kidding — Marzhew was a champion breakdancer in his youth, twice travelling to the United States to represent Australia in the world championships.

He says he's too big to move like he used to but the popping and locking and clean backflip he landed at the NRL's fan fest before the season opener in Las Vegas says otherwise.

But Marzhew needs just one try to equal Dom Young's record for most four-pointers in a season for the Knights and he'll likely have to go over To'o to do it, so the dancing will have to wait.

Marzhew and the Knights will be out to defy the odds yet again. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

"I'll let him take it, my mind is on something else — maybe after the game," said Marzhew.

"No dance, but I'd love to equal the record and share it with my brother, Dom Young, on the other wing."

If Penrith win, it will mark To'o's sixth grand final appearance while Marzhew is after his first.

A crowd of over 50,000 is expected, with a horde of Knights fans expected on hand for the club's first preliminary final since 2013.

The support comes as no shock to Marzhew, who has loved the city ever since arriving from Gold Coast in 2023, and he's ready to run into, over or through anything that gets in the way of Newcastle premiership dream.

"It's not a surprise, I wouldn't expect it but I love it and to play for them in this situation is an honour," said Marzhew.

"It's always a privilege to play in any game for Newcastle. I love playing for this town. It was home right from that first year."

World.title: Umpire felt 'threatened' by player, fan abuse after unruly AFL finale
World.content:
A 34-year-old Seaford man is expected to be charged for allegedly throwing a plate of food at a woman and child during last week's AFL preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane.

He is expected to be charged on summons with aggravated unlawful assault and discharge a missile.

AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

Police have interviewed the man and another 56-year-old Tullamarine man, who was identified after allegedly throwing a bottle onto the MCG's field of play at the conclusion of the match.

The Tullamarine man has been fined $418 under the Major Events Act.

He is the second man to be fined after security detained a 40-year-old Croydon man for throwing a bottle onto the field of play, before he was spoken to by police.

Bottles and cans were thrown onto the field after the game, including some aimed at the umpires as they walked off the MCG after a holding-the-ball decision by field umpire Hayden Meyer against Jarman Impey that gave Brisbane a go-ahead goal with 18 seconds remaining.

Umpire says he felt 'threatened' by Hawks duo

Sicily and Barrass (number 37) were seen having words with Meyer (left) immediately following the final siren. (AFL)

Meyer, who will officiate in this weekend's AFL grand final, was confronted by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass in the aftermath of his decision.

He said he had received an apology from Barrass but was still waiting to hear from Sicily.

"The abuse that came my way, I felt threatened," Meyer told reporters on Wednesday.

"I expressed exactly that [to the AFL] — the language, and the way that those two players, James [Sicily] and Tom [Barrass], came at me, I felt threatened and intimidated in that situation.

"So I spoke to [umpires boss] Steve McBurney the day after and gave my view of the situation, and how I felt and what occurred, and he then transferred that to Swanny [AFL football boss Greg Swann] and the MRO to eventually come up with a decision around the fines.

"[Barrass] was very apologetic and very sincere in his apology. I accepted his apology and thanked him for taking the time out of his day to give me a call."

Meyer says Sicily (pictured) is yet to apologise for abusing him on the final siren. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Meyer refused to make a call on whether the Hawks pair, who were fined over their actions, should be suspended instead.

"That's out of my control, that's not my decision … I suppose what I take from it is that it's not a great look for junior umpires and kids that are sitting on the couch that we want to recruit into umpiring," he said.

"They see that after the game on the weekend and, if I'm sitting on the couch, I'd be like, 'Do I really want to go to my local umpiring community group and sign up to be an umpire?'

" That was the big disappointing thing for me, that we struggle with umpiring recruitment in local communities, and that doesn't help. "

Despite the protestations from Hawthorn fans, Impey admitted the umpires made the right call.

"It was the right decision," he told the Kick It Forward podcast at the Brownlow Medal on Monday night.

"Naturally, when you think there are 30-40 seconds to go, you try and hold it in go from there, but credit to Hayden.

"I hope there was no hate message towards him, so sending love to him."

Jarman Impey (left) admitted the umpires had made the right call in penalising him for holding the ball in the final seconds. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

Ahead of this weekend's grand final, Meyer pleaded for fans to not "cross the line" again.

"I've never experienced bottles being thrown at me post-game. It was pretty scary, to be honest, and I hope it never happens again in any game, any sport," he said.

"[To fans attending the grand final], I would say be passionate, cheer for your team, but respect others, respect the people you're sitting next to, respect the umpires — have fun, but don't cross the line."

Police are continuing to make enquiries regarding the fan behaviour during and after the match.

World.title: Neale breaks silence on grand final ban as Lions downplay appeal impact
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Lachie Neale says he will remain in Melbourne to support Brisbane in Saturday's AFL grand final even if he is not successful with his appeals board hearing.

An appeals board hearing is the final avenue available for Neale, who unsuccessfully challenged the ban at a tribunal hearing last night.

The Lions announced this afternoon they would appeal the tribunal's decision.

Neale's dad 'worried for him' if ban keeps him from playing grand final Lachie Neale's father says the family is "worried" about the star Lion missing the AFL grand final at the end of a tumultuous year.

Neale has travelled to Melbourne with the Lions squad. The appeals board hearing will be held tomorrow, beginning at 4pm, AEST.

"Obviously, as you guys will be aware, the club and myself have decided to appeal the decision," Neale told reporters at Melbourne Airport.

"Obviously very hopeful that that's successful, but regardless of the result, I will be here to support the boys and the club this week. It's a big week for the club."

Neale did not take any questions from reporters and departed after giving a brief statement.

Brisbane veteran Dayne Zorko said the lead-up to this year's grand final was "not too dissimilar" to last year', when Neale was under an injury cloud.

There were doubts over Neale's availability in the lead-up to last year's grand final against Geelong due to a calf injury. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"There was a lot of scrutiny last year about whether he'd play or he wouldn't [and] in '24 he had a broken foot, so we're used to it," he said.

"He [Neale] seems to be fine. He wants to play and he's just taking it in his stride.

"You work so hard to get to this position, so he is disappointed, but we'll appeal it and go from there.

"We've had this stuff in the past. It's water under a bridge for us. We just keep going forward with our process and worry about what we can control.

"[Neale has an] impeccable record, you'd like to think that would carry a bit of weight [at the tribunal]. Maybe it doesn't.

"We can't get too carried away about it just being a Lachie Neale team. We're the Brisbane Lions, we've got a lot of players on our list.

"We played a few finals last year without him, as well. We'll just let that run its course. We're not going to get distracted by that, it's not our business to get distracted by it.

"We'd love for him to be out there, we hope he's out there, but if he's not, the next man up mentality is going to come into play."

Brisbane has brought an extended squad down to Melbourne ahead of the grand final.

No decision has been made yet on who will replace Neale if his suspension is upheld.

To succeed at the appeals board hearing, the Lions will have to prove the tribunal finding was either an error of law, an unreasonable decision, a manifestly excessive classification, or a manifestly excessive sanction.

They face Fremantle in Saturday's grand final at the MCG, chasing a third successive premiership.

Neale was suspended after the tribunal rejected his "inconsistent" evidence in a landmark case.

Why Neale's grand final ban was upheld The tribunal says it had reason not to overturn Lachie Neale's appeal. Now the AFL world waits to hear whether the Lions will launch an appeal.

He was found guilty of striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The two-time premiership captain argued his action was not a strike, but a body-check.

After a dramatic four-and-a-half-hour hearing, the tribunal upheld the charge and dismissed pleas for a downgrade due to exceptional and compelling circumstances.

The off-the-ball blow on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

Neale argued contact was made with his shoulder and chest and was not a strike.

He said Ginnivan "might have taken a bit of a dive to get a free kick".

"My shoulder made contact with his body and shoulder first and my arm wrapped around Jack," he said.

"But I didn't feel like I was striking him at all. It was more a bump or body-check."

The Lions will roll the dice on Lachie Neale's ban at an appeals board hearing. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

But tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC dismissed Neale's version of events.

"We find that this was a forceful blow delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand," Gleeson said.

"When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts.

"We are comfortably satisfied that this is what occurred. We find that this is what Neale intended.

"We have listened carefully to Mr Neale's evidence but we find it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video and, to that extent, we do not accept it."

ABC/AAP

World.title: Neale's dad 'worried for him' if ban keeps him from playing grand final
World.content:
Lachie Neale's father says the family is "worried" about the star Lion missing the AFL grand final at the end of a tumultuous year.

Neale copped a one-game suspension for striking Jack Ginnivan during the Lions' stunning preliminary final victory at the MCG on Saturday night, but the club has confirmed it will appeal against the decision.

Before the appeal was revealed, Robbie Neale told ABC Radio Adelaide in the lead-up to Saturday's decider against Fremantle that he felt the suspension was "just plain wrong".

"[He's played] 320 games, never been suspended," he said.

Why Neale's grand final ban was upheld The tribunal says it had reason not to overturn Lachie Neale's appeal. Now the AFL world waits to hear whether the Lions will launch an appeal.

"I just think to miss the grand final for this, it just … I've followed footy for a long time [and] it just doesn't add up to me."

Before the appeal was confirmed, Robbie said Lachie would have been torn on whether to appeal and prolong the process in grand final week.

"Lachie won't want the distraction for the team," he said.

Neale was also the centre of attention leading up to last year's grand final win over Geelong as he raced the clock to recover from a calf injury.

Neale was under an injury cloud heading into last year's decider. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

He ultimately played only the second half, kicking a crucial long-range goal in the third quarter.

"This one [the suspension], we're worried for him, because I know this means everything to him to play in this grand final," Robbie said.

"Easy to say that he's already played in a few, but they've got a chance to create history here."

The two-time Brownlow medallist has been in the headlines a lot this year, including giving up the captaincy before the season following a widely publicised marriage breakdown.

He was permitted to leave the team at the end of the season and went into Collingwood for a medical ahead of a reported move to the Magpies next year.

"The last thing Lachie wanted this week was another headline. It's just so disappointing," Robbie Neale said.

Robbie Neale said there had been "fabricated garbage" around his son, particularly regarding the Collingwood visit during the season.

"He does even amaze me in terms of how he's been able to compartmentalise and just focus on his job and play footy," he said.

"And he's had a pretty good year."

World.title: 'Flying mullet' Browning announces athletics retirement
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Two-time Olympian Rohan Browning has reflected on the moment that changed his life, as he announced his retirement from athletics.

Browning finishes his career as the fourth-fastest Australian over 100 metres, having run a personal best of 10.01 seconds at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

Sporting a distinctive hairstyle which earned the nickname 'Flying mullet', Browning recorded the time in the heats to qualify for the semifinals in his Olympic debut.

"That was a moment that changed my life," Browning said in an Australian Athletics statement.

"It gave me a really healthy dose of self-belief because it had been a quiet period for Australian men's sprinting.

Bizarre end to Australia's athletics campaign A hilariously understated celebration marked the end of an enthralling athletics campaign in Glasgow, and the beginning of Australian track and field being taken seriously around the world.

"There weren't many role models on the scene, and I feel like I had to forge that path myself."

A four-time national champion, Browning was content to call time on his career following Australia's shock victory in the men's 4x100m relay at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

The 28-year-old joined Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi and Calab Law in winning Australia's first gold medal in the event since 1974.

"I really wanted to go out on a high note, and after winning the gold medal at the Commonwealth Games in the relay, it was only going to go downhill from there," Browning said.

"The athlete in me still thinks that I could get back, run personal bests and compete at the highest level, but no athlete is ever going to be truly satisfied.

Rohan Browning (left) helped Australia win a drought-breaking relay gold at the Commonwealth Games. (Getty images: Ian MacNicol)

"The thing that I'm actually proudest of is that I made every team from my debut in 2017 to my retirement in 2026."

Australian Athletics chief executive Simon Hollingsworth said Browning did himself proud during his career.

"Rohan has been a fantastic athlete and ambassador for our sport," Hollingsworth said.

"His 2021 Tokyo performance inspired Australians and the generation of sprinters who followed.

"To go out with a superb relay run for gold in Glasgow is a fitting finale."

Although Browning was unable to dip under 10 seconds legally, he did run a wind-assisted PB of 9.89 in Austria earlier this year.

Browning also competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

He ran at five World Athletics Championships, with his best finish in the 100m being a semifinal appearance at the 2023 edition in Budapest.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026: The biggest news and announcements
Tech.content: It’s about time for Meta Connect, the company’s annual product launch event. This year, given the company’s major focus on AI and wearables like smart glasses, it seems likely that we’ll see updates from CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team on those categories. The company has been facing significant scrutiny because of how some users have been covertly recording other people using the glasses, meaning that one of the biggest announcements of the show could be its rumored camera-free pair.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026 live blog: On the ground at Mark Zuckerberg’s next big product launch
Tech.content:
It’s time once again for Meta’s annual September product launch event, and The Verge is on the ground in Menlo Park to cover the show live. Meta says that today’s keynote by Mark Zuckerberg will be about how “Meta is building a future for everyone” — something he wrote at length about in a recent essay about AI, smart glasses, and more. That means we can expect more news from Zuckerberg and his team on those topics; perhaps we’ll hear more about Meta’s recently launched Muse AI agent and new glasses hardware.

Whatever Zuckerberg and Meta have to say about smart glasses will be particularly notable. The company is dealing with an outpouring of privacy and harassment concerns stemming from the product line’s built-in camera, which has led to them being derided as “pervert glasses.” Meta has already tried to tackle that reputation with recent privacy fixes and a new marketing campaign, but it could introduce more updates on the Connect stage.

The show is scheduled to begin at 7PM ET / 4PM PT, and you can follow our live updates here.

Tech.title: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).

While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.

Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.

Image: Microsoft

That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).

Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.

Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.

I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.

Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is launching a second generation of its Surface Mouse next month that includes haptic feedback support. The Surface Mouse also has a customizable action button for the first time, which is primarily designed for quick access to Copilot (of course), but can be configured to work with other shortcuts from the Surface app.

“Its haptic feedback adds a small, purposeful physical response to the moment you usually only see on a screen: a click registering, a window snapping into place or an object aligning just right,” says Brett Ostrum, corporate vice president of Surface Devices. “It is subtle by design, but noticeable within seconds — and hard to give up once you have it.”

The haptic feedback works with things like clicks, drags, and alignment throughout Windows 11, but the tactile feedback also triggers in apps like PowerPoint, Affinity, Concepts, and Filmora. Microsoft added support for haptic feedback in Windows 11 earlier this year, and so far it’s mainly Microsoft and Logitech that are supporting it with dedicated hardware. Logitech’s MX Master 4 has haptic feedback, and its Pro X2 Superstrike (and today’s new X3) includes a haptic-based clicks system that doesn’t support the Windows 11 haptic feedback. The upcoming Surface Laptop Ultra also has a haptic trackpad.

After originally launching the Surface Mouse in 2016 and not updating it since, Microsoft has now redesigned it to be more comfortable for all-day use, with a soft-touch material at the top. Thanks to Bluetooth 6.0 support, you can now also pair it with up to three devices.

The new Surface Mouse will be available on October 13th, the same day Microsoft launches its refreshed Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices. It will be priced at $79.99, and available in black and platinum color options.

Tech.title: Meta’s AI agent is a cute little guy who’s great at spending my money
Tech.content:
Modern life comes with an unending, auto-populating to-do list.

It never ceases to amaze me how I can be doing nothing at all, minding my own business, and suddenly something needs to be taken care of. You’re telling me a tree branch fell in the backyard and now I have to figure out what to do with it? The tree just assigned me homework? Oh, our trash collection company canceled our account out of nowhere and now I have to send email about it? Repeatedly? Totally unfair.

These are the things that we’ve been told for years that AI will help us with. We’ll all have a smart virtual assistant to triage and handle the tedious tasks we’d rather not face. If you believe Meta, that future is available right now in the form of Muse, its AI agent for the masses. I put it to the test doing exactly what it’s advertised to do: taking care of tedious crap I’ve been putting off for ages. And it worked better than I expected — especially when there was a credit card transaction to be made.

It was dizzying watching Marley spin up virtual browser windows chasing down my requests

Marley — one of the suggested names you can give Muse’s avatar — had been pinging me all of last week. It wanted me to know all the ways it could be useful; I was too busy to engage with it. But I sat down with it this week and set it to work on a task. And while it worked on that task, I gave it another. Then another. The thing about AI agents is that they’re most useful when you use them in parallel with each other. Or that’s the theory I was working on. In reality, it was dizzying watching Marley spin up virtual browser windows chasing down my requests. I went with a generically cute snowman-meets-puppy avatar that Meta suggested at setup, and Marley tapped cheerfully on a keyboard as it worked its way through my commands.

In the span of a morning, I gave it the following tasks to help me out with. None of them were critical; mostly they were the kinds of pebble-in-your-shoe annoyances I’d put off for weeks, months, or maybe years. Here’s how it went.

Task: Follow up with the landscaper working on a bid for our backyard renovation

Effort rating: Extremely low

Time I have been putting it off: Two weeks

Was Marley able to complete it? Yes

I asked Marley to help me nudge the person I’ve been emailing at a local landscaping company. I’m expecting them to price out some yard renovations for us, so Marley requested access to my Gmail to check on the status of that project. It confirmed that more time had passed than the landscaper initially estimated the bid would take, and drafted a rather snippy but wordy email. “Make it shorter,” I said. To be clear: As a rule, I do not use AI writing tools. Definitely not in my work, and not even for email. What’s the point? Just don’t send email if you’re going to have a robot write it. In fact, I think we should abolish email. Anyway, I broke my own rule for testing purposes; hitting send on that message made me cringe.

Task: Buy a replacement steam wand assembly for my espresso machine

Effort rating: Low

Time I have been putting it off: [redacted] years

Was Marley able to complete it? Mostly

My Breville Barista Express has held up spectacularly for six years and counting, but it isn’t immune from user error. I took the steam wand apart to clean it a few years back and tore the little silicone washer that goes inside of it. Instead of ordering a new one, I just shoved it back into place and screwed the thing back together. It works okay, but every few months when I’m cleaning the machine it nags at my conscience. It’s probably why the hot water dispenser drips sometimes when I run the steam, too. Ordering a new steam wand assembly costs like 7 bucks and is as difficult as entering my credit card number on Breville’s website. Naturally, I put it off for an unreasonable amount of time.

I opened up my chat with Marley and told it what I needed; it found the part and added it to a shopping cart. I had to finish up the order myself, but it’s done and the part will be here in five to seven business days.

Task: Downgrade my security system account to the cheaper one

Effort rating: Medium (requires a phone call)

Time I have been putting it off: A year? Two years???

Was Marley able to complete it? Not fully

I approved Marley to log into my account, which also required me to verify my email. While I was making the trip to my inbox I saw I had a follow-up to my follow-up with the landscaper. He was apologetic for the delay and I felt a little bad about the slightly abrupt tone of the email Marley sent. I wrote a friendlier reply the old-fashioned way.

With access to my account, Marley reported back what I already knew: You have to call the company to change your plan. Muse wasn’t able to make a phone call for me, though apparently that ability is in the works. This seems like the logical next frontier for these AI agents, and also a weird future to consider. I call the company and answer a few questions from their robot before I’m routed to a human. No doubt there’s a future soon where Marley talks to the security company’s robot before any human being enters the chat. Or more likely in the short term, a human in a call center talks to the other company’s robot before eventually getting to another human in a call center, which feels even weirder. But surely the end state is that my robot will just talk to their robot and they’ll do business without any intervention at all. Anyway, a nice guy answered and made the change to my account. I think he was real.

Task: Contact a junk removal company to get rid of a fallen tree branch in the backyard

Effort rating: Medium

Time I have been putting it off: A week

Was Marley able to complete it? Mostly

The tree branch is a real problem I need to deal with. It didn’t do any damage, but it’s big enough that it’ll either take an afternoon to hack apart and haul to the dump or requires a visit from a junk removal service. Marley was most useful here — it set off looking through listings for hauling services and highlighted a few in the area. It asked for my address, phone number, and a photo of the tree limb, and used that information to put together requests for quotes from a couple of companies using online form submissions. I got a text back from one company not long after, and confirmed a time the following day for tree limb removal. Very little was required on my part, and assuming the tree branch is gone by this time tomorrow, I’ll consider this mission accomplished for Muse.

Task: Shop for camping kitchen gear, either as a set or assembled piece by piece

Effort rating: Medium

Time I have been putting it off: A few days

Was Marley able to complete it? Yes

If our wallets were already defenseless in the era of one-click checkout, we’re so cooked when AI agent shopping truly arrives. I gave Marley some requirements for my outdoor cooking setup and it set out finding the necessary items. It made an attempt to access Amazon and was roundly blocked, complete with a spicy message about AI agents violating terms of service. Anyway, it found what I was looking for between OXO’s own website and Walmart.

You really can’t go wrong with OXO stuff. Kudos to Marley for shopping local.

While I was at it, I wanted to add a propane fire pit to the mix. Not for cooking — for ambience and marshmallows. I’d borrowed a couple of different kinds from friends, and after weighing the pros and cons of each with Muse I landed on a LavaBox and a handy carrying case. The grand total for my camp kitchen and burn-ban-safe fire pit: $500! I told Muse we’d have to pump the brakes and spread these purchases out over the winter. It obliged and helped me prioritize what would make sense to buy first and what was likely to go on sale toward the holidays.

In the meantime, I had Marley find and purchase some other espresso machine supplies. I had to connect my credit card via Stripe, but after I’d done that once it became dangerously easy to tell Marley “Go for it” and approve whatever it had just put in my shopping cart. I watched it fill in my address details in the virtual browser window and confirmation emails started filing into my inbox. Marley did a little shopping around to find slightly better prices, and I didn’t buy anything egregious — just some descaling powder and water filters. It also did the math to calculate whether powdered Dezcal would be a better value than the liquid stuff (way better, not surprisingly). But it is shockingly easy to spend money when a cute little guy is running around the internet with your credit card.

It is shockingly easy to spend money when a cute little guy is running around the internet with your credit card

There’s a danger in overcommitting yourself when you feel like these AI tools are speeding you up. In a few cases, Muse helped me get started by putting the details I needed in front of my face. I had the phone number for the home security company at hand, as well as the name of my current plan and the one I wanted to downgrade to. Getting that little speed bump out of the way was what I needed, I guess. But the dirty secret of productivity hacks is that doing more stuff often doesn’t feel like things are being removed from your plate; somehow it just invites more tasks.

If you’re willing to give a lot of information and trust to Meta — a massive caveat! — Muse can genuinely help you get things done. I’d been using it for all of 40 minutes and already given it my full name, address, credit card number, a photo of my backyard, and the credentials for my home security account login. Going great, I’d say! If AI decides to kill us all I just secured my spot at the front of the line. Meta of course says that all of these details are stored securely, Marley allegedly can’t even see them, etc., but still. Unsettling.

But I think the underlying question we need to ask ourselves as we enter the era of AI agents is what we do with the time we’re supposedly freeing up. Will we use it to take on more commitments? And then ultimately feel overwhelmed again when the to-do list keeps piling up? After a morning crossing items off my list with Marley, I didn’t spend the hours that followed doing anything consequential. In fact, I spent that time chatting with Marley, seeking reassurance about the direction of the yard project and brainstorming fall camping trips I probably won’t take. It’s a gorgeous day outside, the kind we really can’t take for granted in late September, and I wish I’d spent that time outdoors rather than inside talking to a robot, cute little guy or otherwise.

Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

Tech.title: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of bills on Monday that could finally give communities better data — and more say — on how data centers impact their electricity bills and water supply.

As data centers invade a growing number of communities across the US, they’ve triggered protests over how the infrastructure underpinning AI might stress power grids and local water systems. That’s fueled partly by concerns about how difficult it is to see just how much electricity or water they’re actually gobbling up. California’s new disclosure rules won’t offer a full picture, but starting next year, data center operators will have to start sharing some of these details. The transparency will help scientists and the public see whether data centers are raising bills, draining dwindling resources, and making good on sustainability commitments.

“It’s extremely frustrating to try to understand basic information,” says Mark Specht, senior manager for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS). “There’s a lot of hype about data centers right now … It doesn’t help that we just don’t have basic facts about what’s happening with them to try to understand how much of a problem they are.”

“It’s extremely frustrating”

The seven bills Newsom signed go beyond requiring disclosures. Senate Bill 886, Assembly Bill 2383, and Senate Bill 1168 direct the California Public Utilities Commission to create separate power rates for data centers to recoup the costs of connecting such power-hungry facilities to the grid. That’s supposed to prevent data centers from passing on the costs to other consumers of new infrastructure built to satisfy their energy demand. On top of that, AB 2383 also pushes data centers to use more renewable energy.

The rest of the legislation grapples with the enormous gaps the public has when it comes to how data centers impact surrounding communities and the environment. AB 1577 requires monthly reporting on data centers’ energy consumption. AB 2619 and AB 2469 require water disclosures, and the latter also makes data center operators responsible for covering the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve them. And SB 887 eliminates categorical exemptions from the California Environmental Quality Act for data centers, ensuring that they’re subject to environmental review.
