Tech.title: A Startup Wants to Power Data Centers With ‘Supercritical’ Carbon Dioxide
Tech.content:
A new company has a plan to make the dirty gas turbines powering data centers more efficient: liquid carbon dioxide.

American Supercritical came out of stealth Wednesday, announcing $8 million in funding. It wants to retrofit inefficient gas turbines that many data centers rely on for power with units that can generate more power, without adding more emissions (though the gas-fired turbines will continue to emit carbon pollution). The technology can also theoretically be used on a wide variety of energy sources at a time when power demand is skyrocketing.

“We want to start with gas turbines but eventually expand beyond that,” says cofounder Simon Shuham.

Most large gas-fired power plants in the United States use an array of heat engines in what’s known as a combined-cycle process: First, turbines generate electricity from burning compressed air and natural gas, then a separate engine uses the hot exhaust to make steam and create additional energy. But for a variety of reasons, data centers across the US have opted to power their operations with what are known as simple-cycle turbines, and exclude the steam component.

These turbines are much less efficient than combined-cycle plants. Usually, only about 35 percent of the energy from simple-cycle turbines is converted to electricity, while the rest escapes as exhaust. (In combined-cycle plants, that figure hovers closer to 60 to 65 percent.) That exhaust includes greenhouse gases, making plants that run on simple-cycle turbines a much worse choice for the environment than combined-cycle plants.

The size of some of these plants combined with their inefficiency is a recipe for climate disaster. A massive data-center power plant in Texas that Amazon is building with just simple-cycle turbines, for instance, is permitted to emit more than 33 million tons of greenhouse gases per year—more than the annual total of some small countries.

But all these small, inefficient turbines could be a great match for supercritical CO 2 technology, American Supercritical’s founders say. Carbon dioxide becomes supercritical when it’s pressurized and held at a certain temperature. In this state, it gets the density of liquid but still behaves like a gas, meaning it can move energy more efficiently through much smaller amounts of equipment.

American Supercritical wants to attach its units to small gas turbines and help generate more energy. While the turbines themselves would still use gas, the supercritical CO 2 unit can use the hot exhaust generated from those turbines to create additional electricity. Instead of using that heat to boil water and create steam, the heat is transferred directly by the pressurized CO 2 to generate additional energy with no additional emissions.

“We’re essentially building miniature combined-cycle plants,” says Shuham.

Using supercritical CO 2 also can eliminate or greatly reduce water use in the power generation process—something that’s drawn intense scrutiny when it comes to data centers. Importantly, the CO 2 involved operates in a closed-loop system, meaning that it doesn’t have to be refilled. Cofounder Matthew Carlson, who researched supercritical CO 2 for more than a decade, likens it to refrigeration systems that circulate CO 2 to facilitate cooling.

The company plans to initially sell a 10-megawatt unit—relatively small by gas plant standards. By American Supercritical’s math, adding supercritical CO 2 units could increase turbines’ efficiency by up to 50 percent without adding any more greenhouse gas emissions or water use.

Tech.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo: Comparing Apple’s New Pro Phone Against Its First Foldable
Tech.content:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro is now on sale, but the foldable iPhone Duo is still awaiting its big debut on Oct. 23. While both phones are premium showstoppers, they’re also very different.

The 18 Pro features the company’s best camera yet on an iPhone, including a variable aperture for the first time. That feature helps you control light exposure, which can improve low-light photography, and you can use the new Pro Controls for additional features, like adjusting shutter speed. And while the outside is similar to the iPhone 17 Pro, the inside has been redesigned to accommodate a larger vapor chamber that helps keep the phone cool during intensive use.

But it’s the iPhone Duo that really captured people’s attention. It’s Apple’s first foldable phone, with a passport-style design that’s made to fit in your hand when closed. Then you can unfold it like a book to reveal a wide screen that’s almost the size of an iPad Mini (an open iPhone Duo has a 7.6-inch screen while an iPad Mini measures 8.3 inches). Yet, it only has two rear cameras rather than the three that the 18 Pro has, so it won’t have a telephoto lens for zooming into a subject as far as the Pro and Pro Max can. It also doesn’t have the aforementioned variable aperture.

On top of that, the iPhone Duo is extremely expensive: It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB version. The iPhone 18 Pro isn’t cheap either, but it is less of a stretch, with a starting price of $1,199 for the 256GB version.

Here are the top highlights for each phone, and you can use our specs chart to compare them further.

The Duo’s inner selfie camera is geared toward FaceTime videos. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Design and display

The primary difference between the two phones lies in their designs. The iPhone 18 Pro has the usual slab iPhone design that we’ve come to know over the years. It even has the same dimensions as its predecessor, measuring 5.9 by 2.3 by 0.3 inches. This means you can use the same phone cases whether they were designed for the iPhone 17 Pro or the 18 Pro. The 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design with a triple camera array on the back. On the front is a 6.3-inch OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. The display also includes a slimmer Dynamic Island cutout for the front-facing camera and Face ID, which can now display three Live Activities at once.

The iPhone Duo, on the other hand, is quite the departure from Apple as the company’s first foldable. Closed, it has rounded corners on the upper and lower right along with flat titanium sides. Due to its passport size, it has a rather squat 5.4-inch cover display on the front. When it’s closed, it measures 4.6 by 3.3 by 0.4 inches.

The iPhone Duo when closed. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Open the Duo up, and you will see a 7.6-inch OLED display. While the cover screen has the usual glossy glass display of other iPhones, the main internal display of the iPhone Duo has a matte nano-textured finish designed to reduce reflections and minimize the appearance of the crease. Also, when the Duo is open, it’s just 0.2 inches thick, which is even thinner than last year’s iPhone Air (0.22 inches). Both displays support a 120Hz refresh rate, and the phone can use StandBy mode widgets when folded into a tent-like position. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have Face ID and instead uses a side fingerprint sensor for Touch ID unlocking.

Both phones are IP68-rated for dust and water resistance. That’s particularly notable for the Duo, as it’s one of the few book-style foldable phones to carry that rating. (Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold and 11 Pro Fold are also rated IP68.)

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max on display at Apple’s store on Fifth Avenue in New York for the phones’ launch. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Cameras

The iPhone 18 Pro has the best camera features that Apple has to offer. It has a triple rear camera array: a 48-megapixel wide, ultrawide and telephoto. Its new variable aperture, lets you control how much light hits the sensor, allowing for improved low-light photography, greater depth-of-field for close-up shots and overall a lot more flexibility for creative photography.

While the iPhone Duo has a compact foldable design as its spotlight feature, its camera system harkens more to what’s included on the iPhone 17. Despite being substantially more expensive than the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo has a 48-megapixel wide camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. It does not have a telephoto camera, but its camera system does allow for a 2x optical quality zoom along with a digital zoom to 10x. It also does not have the variable aperture that’s included on the 18 Pro.

Both phones have selfie cameras; the 18 Pro has a 18-megapixel front-facing camera, while the Duo has a 12-megapixel Center Stage selfie camera on the cover display as well as a hidden under-display FaceTime camera on the main display. The benefit of the Duo, however, is that you can actually use the 48-megapixel rear camera as your “selfie” camera when the phone is open as the cover display becomes a viewfinder.

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Performance and battery

Both phones ship with Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, which is the company’s first to be made with a 2-nanometer process. The processor is therefore denser and should result in a 20% faster CPU and a 40% faster GPU than last year’s A19 Pro. It should also help keep the phone cool even during intensive use.

As for battery life, Apple doesn’t give the specific capacity for both phones, but it does say that the 18 Pro should last up to 24 hours, while the iPhone Duo will last up to 44 hours while watching videos when closed, and up to 31 hours when open.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is able to show three Live Activities at once. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

In our preliminary test with the 18 Pro, we found that it lasted almost a full day before needing to be charged. It’s also one of the fastest-charging phones CNET has tested, charging from 0% to 82% in just 30 minutes. According to Apple, the iPhone Duo will charge to 50% in about 15 minutes with a 60-watt charger, or to 50% in 30 minutes with a 35-watt wireless MagSafe charger. We’ll have to perform further tests to be sure.

Check out the specs chart to further compare the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo specs

Tech.title: Microsoft Brings Snapdragon X2 to Smallest Surface Pro and Laptop Lines
Tech.content:
I’m the first born in my family, so I haven’t experienced this feeling directly, but my younger brother tells me it wasn’t all that fun when I would get a gift that he was too little to receive along with his big brother (like the time I got my first bike for my 6th birthday while he was still circling our cul-de-sac on a Big Wheel). On Wednesday, Microsoft granted upgrades to its littlest Surface models, which lets them two-wheel around the neighborhood with the bigger models.

The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop have each been upgraded to Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 series processors, bringing them in line with the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and 13.8- and 15-inch Surface Laptops that received the Snapdragon X2 jolt a few months ago.

The second-generation Qualcomm processors offer a tick up in application performance and battery life, a larger leap in graphics performance and a giant jump in local AI capabilities, according to Microsoft. My tests with other laptops based on Snapdragon X2 series processors support Microsoft’s estimates.

Along with the two new Surface models, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Mouse that offers haptic feedback. Let’s have a look at the two Surface updates and new mouse.

12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition)

The new 12-inch Surface Pro is based on a Snapdragon X2 Plus processor and available in business black. Katie Collins/CNET

The second-gen 12-inch Surface Pro trots out the same design as the inaugural model, but inside it has moved to a six-core Snapdragon X Plus X2P-42-100. You are actually giving up two cores from the previous Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 but getting a more advanced X2-45 integrated GPU and neural processing unit. The NPU is designed for the integer math required for AI tasks, and the Snapdragon X2’s NPU is capable of 80 trillion operations per second. That’s nearly double the 45 TOPS of the NPU of the first-gen Snapdragon X Plus.

The 12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition) also ups the memory, giving you the choice of 16GB or 24GB of RAM. That’s an increase from the previous 8GB and 16GB options. Storage remains the same and rather uninspired: 256GB or 512GB.

The display also stays the same: a 12-inch PixelSense touch LCD with a 3:2 aspect ratio, a resolution of 2,196×1,464 pixels and 90Hz refresh rate. The only difference is it’s 25% brighter, pushing the max brightness from 400 to 500 nits.

And there’s a new color option, but it might not excite you. In addition to platinum and violet, the new 12-inch Surface Pro comes in black. The bluish-gray ocean color has been discontinued.

The new 12-inch Surface Pro comes preinstalled with Microsoft Ink Canvas, a new AI-powered app for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the screen with the Slim Pen.

The 12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition) will be available on Oct. 13, starting at $1,150. As with all Surface Pro pricing, the starting price is misleading because Microsoft charges extra for accessories, including the keyboard. Microsoft hasn’t divulged accessory pricing, but the keyboard for the first-gen 12-inch Surface Pro, which is very much needed, adds $150 to the bill. Still, it’s nice that the entry-level model starts at 16GB of RAM, saving you from having to spend extra to move up from the meager 8GB.

13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition)

The 13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition) looks no different than the first edition, but it offers newer Qualcomm processors, more RAM and a brighter display. Katie Collins/CNET

The 13-inch Surface Laptop has two big brothers in the 13.8-inch Surface Laptop and 15-inch model. They have each offered Snapdragon X2 series processors since May or June, and now the smallest Surface Laptop gets its Snapdragon X2 upgrade. It offers the same configuration options as the new 12-inch Surface Pro:

Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 CPU

16GB or 24GB RAM

256GB or 512GB SSD

There’s no change to the display other than the same bump in brightness as the second-gen 12-inch Surface Pro got. It’s a 13-inch PixelSense touch LCD with a 3:2 aspect ratio, a pixel resolution of 1,920×1,280 and a 60Hz refresh rate, but it is now rated for 500 nits of brightness. It also comes in the same three colors as the new 12-inch Surface Pro: platinum, violet and black.

Microsoft says you can expect up to 22.5 hours of battery life from the second-gen 13-inch Surface Laptop. That would actually be slightly shorter if our tests bear that out. The previous 13-inch Surface Laptop lasted more than 24 hours in testing.

The 13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition) will be available on Oct. 13 starting at $1,199.

Surface Mouse (2nd Edition)

The new Surface Mouse has haptics to provide physical, tactile feedback. Katie Collins/CNET

If you’re more of a mouser than a touchpad user, Microsoft has a new mouse it’s hoping you’ll pick up with your next Surface purchase. The most interesting part about the second-generation Surface Mouse is the inclusion of haptics that offer tactile feedback across its entire surface. These pulses can confirm clicks, drags, alignment and other actions in apps including PowerPoint, Concepts, Affinity by Canva and Filmora.

The Surface Mouse also adds a customizable action button that sits in front of the scroll wheel. The Bluetooth 6.0 mouse will be available in black and platinum for $80. Like the new Surface computers, the Surface Mouse (2nd Edition) will start shipping on Oct. 13.

Tech.title: People’s Picks: Shopping for a TV for the Holidays? This Is the Brand Readers Say You Should Stick To
Tech.content:
Early holiday sales will kick off in the next few weeks, like Amazon’s October Prime Day sale that’s Oct. 6 and 7. And between the NFL season in full swing and new shows launching for the fall, now’s a good time to start taking your TV upgrade seriously if you’re considering a new one.

Choosing a new TV comes down to a few specifications, like price, picture quality and your specific use cases — whether it’s gaming or movies. With so many features and factors to consider, choosing the right one can be overwhelming. But our readers may help narrow down your choices.

CNET’s People’s Picks gives readers a chance to share their opinions on their TV brand. Many of you love LG, but some readers have opinions on other brands that you may not have considered before. Here’s which brands won over readers and what our experts think.

LG/J. Hazelwood/CNET Overall People's Picks winner LG Expert Take LG is well-known among TV brands for its OLED screens, and it’s a favorite among CNET editors and readers. LG earns high marks in many of CNET’s People’s Picks categories and wins three awards from readers: picture quality, fast-moving content and OLED/QD-OLED.



CNET editors give LG several nods for recent OLED TVs, lauding the contrast in the new C6H, the color accuracy of the G5 — recipient of a CNET Lab Award — and the contrast and brightness of G6 for movie buffs. The LG OLED G4 is one of the best gaming TVs for its top-notch gaming features, especially as a more cost-effective option compared to the LG G6.



Picture quality

Runner-up: Sony

CNET readers crown LG as a winner for picture quality. More than 3 out of 5 (61.7%) of CNET readers who own an LG TV reported an “Excellent” experience with their LG TVs in bright rooms and during the day. Readers say there’s no glare and it’s beautifully bright, and 65.1% of readers with LG TVs report perfect dark scenes with inky blacks and zero light bleed — performance that’s common on OLED models and can really improve the look of movies and TV shows. That brings LG’s picture quality to 63.4%.

Sony is a runner-up for picture quality, based on nearly half (49.8%) of readers with a Sony TV saying the brand has inky blacks with no bleed and great daylight performance.

Fast-moving content

Runner-up: Sony

LG wins for flawless, fast-moving content. Of readers, 71% say LG TVs are perfectly smooth, are without blur and are without weird, artificial artifacts with fast-moving content, whereas 28% say LG’s fast-moving content quality is natural but occasionally slightly blurry. When it comes to gaming, CNET readers (59.8%) who have an LG TV say fast-moving content is flawless and incredibly responsive and that the TV has great gaming menus.

Sony is the next top pick, with 60% of readers saying its fast-moving content is flawless on Sony TV screens.

OLED/QD-OLED

Runner-up: Samsung

Lastly, LG sweeps the OLED/QD-OLED category with 82.4% of readers with an LG TV preferring the brand for its OLED displays. If you’re considering an LG OLED TV, the latest LG OLED G6 has excellent contrast, an improved antireflective coating and good brightness for gaming. One of CNET’s lab-tested favorites is the previous LG OLED G5. CNET editors say it has the best color accuracy. The C4 is still a favorite, but if you want the latest and greatest, LG’s C6 and C6H are standout OLED picks. The C6 is the ultra version of the C6 TV, and it comes in larger sizes with higher brightness and better colors.

Samsung trails behind LG with 45% of readers who own a Samsung TV have an OLED or QD-OLED model. That’s not surprising because Samsung has only been selling OLED TVs since 2022, after a single model in 2013, whereas LG’s OLED models have been on sale for more than a decade. Both the S90F and S95F are Samsung OLED TVs that get praise from CNET for image quality and glare reduction.

Roku

Roku/J. Hazelwood/CNET

Budget TV

Runner-up: Vizio

Roku wins three categories in CNET’s People’s Picks — budget, smart TV ecosystem and standard LED/LCD. Roku has several affordable TVs. Most CNET readers (72%) have purchased a Roku TV that’s under $500. And nearly half of readers with Roku TVs have purchased their TV within the past year.

Roku has a few popular TV picks under $500, including the TCL 4-Series, the Pioneer 50-inch 4K smart Roku TV and the Roku – 40″ Class Select Series Full HD (1080p) LED Smart RokuTV. Roku’s cost-effective options don’t skimp on quality. For instance, the Pioneer 4K Roku TV is an LED TV with 4K resolution and a smart TV interface, and it supports High Dynamic Range to improve your picture quality.

Vizio is next up to Roku, with 45% of readers having Vizio TVs costing less than $500. If you’re in the market for a mini-LED TV, Vizio has its Mini LED Quantum Series 4K TV for under $500 in two sizes (65 and 75 inches). Interestingly, 40.8% of CNET readers with Vizio TVs have had them the longest (over five years) — speaking to its quality and longevity for the price.

Smart TV ecosystem

Runner-up: TCL

Trust me, a smart TV’s interface can make or break your day-to-day experience. Roku understands that and wins over 59.1% of CNET readers.

Most readers with a Roku TV say its interface is fast, clean and very easy to navigate. No readers reported the interface being cluttered, slow or frustrating to use — the only TV brand to do so. Roku recently released a new interface that includes a “For You” section, which combines AI suggestions, saved entertainment and what you’re already watching. And the new interface has a “Quick Access” section to get to your most used apps faster, but we have a guide if you’re not a fan and want to turn it off.

TCL is a runner-up for the Smart TV ecosystem category. Over half (56.5%) of readers who own a TCL TV say the interface is fast, clean and easy to navigate, while 22.5% say the interface is good but has too many ads or sponsored recommendations.

Standard LED/LCD

Runner-up: Vizio

Standard LED and LCD TVs use LED backlights and are usually the most cost-effective compared to other TVs. Roku wins 34.8% of its owners over for this category. There are a few budget-friendly Roku LED TVs worth considering, including the Onn 43-inch Class 4K Roku smart TV and the Hisense 50-inch Class 4K LED Roku smart TV. The Roku Select Series LED TV is a CNET favorite for its usability features, like Roku’s interface and remote finder.

Readers say Vizio is the next top pick for LED/LCD TVs, with 32.7% owning an LED or LCD Vizio TV.

Hisense

Hisense/J. Hazelwood/CNET

Sound quality

Runner-up: Sony



Hisense wins CNET’s People’s Picks for its sound quality. Nearly half of readers (45.7%) with Hisense TVs rate the internal audio as “great.” And that’s nearly double CNET readers’ satisfaction with popular brands like Sony (25.2%), Samsung (23.8%) and Vizio (22.2%). One of the perks of Hisense’s latest U7 and UR8 models is Dolby Atmos, which uses surround sound to deliver 3D audio. The U7 models also have a built-in 2.1.2-channel speaker system for more immersive sound. CNET’s favorite budget TV, the Hisense QD7 TV, also supports Dolby Atmos.

Sony is next up for the sound quality category, with 25.2% of owners saying Sony TVs have great sound quality with clear dialogue and decent bass. Some (41.7%) say it’s adequate for casual watching.

TCL

TCL/J. Hazelwood/CNET

Mini-LED/QLED

Runner-up: Hisense

Mini LED TVs use tiny LEDs to give you better brightness, blacks and contrast compared to most standard LED TVs. When it comes to mini-LED and QLED TV panels, TCL wins, with 57.5% of readers owning mini-LED/QLED TCL TVs and naming it their primary TV brand. TCL has been producing mini-LED TVs longer than most TV makers, and many of them have earned CNET’s praise.

According to CNET editors, the TCL QM8K is nearly comparable to an OLED TV in terms of picture quality for less money. TCL’s QM8L is another mini-LED QLED TV that CNET loves for its brightness, color and contrast, too.

Over half (52.1%) of readers with a Hisense TV have a mini-LED/QLED TV, with its model ranking second to TCL. Hisense has a few mini-LED models, including the U6, U7 and the new RGB mini-LED UR8, which we got a glimpse of at CES 2026. It’s around $1,300 and comes with better-than-before color reproduction.

Don’t buy a new TV without reading this first

Many TVs have similar features that may make it seem like the best deal is the biggest screen for your buck. Of everything to consider, CNET’s TV expert Ty Pendlebury advises looking at price, size and picture quality to help narrow down your options.

“It’s always what fits their budget, so not necessarily a ‘budget’ model. If an OLED is within your budget, get it, that’s the quickest shortcut,” said Pendlebury.

And don’t worry about perfecting your TV’s sound quality during your upgrade. Pendlebury says that most TVs sound tinny, so you should consider a soundbar as a separate purchase for better audio.

CNET’s editor-in-chief, David Katzmaier, has 26 years of experience reviewing TVs and has some practical advice to help you feel more satisfied with your purchase years later. For instance, bigger doesn’t always mean better.

“A bigger TV is great, but it can expose lower-quality sources,” said Katzmaier. The reason is that a bigger screen can show imperfections more than a smaller one. If you still want a bigger screen, consider subscribing to 4K plans to streaming services like Netflix and YouTube TV for better picture quality. You can also try adjusting your picture settings, such as putting the TV in Filmmaker Mode, but Katzmaier says that’s not a cure-all.

Instead of screen size, focus on getting a picture quality you’re satisfied with. “The biggest improvement would be getting a new display technology, especially QD-OLED/OLED,” said Katzmaier. “TVs with those kinds of screens deliver clear improvements in contrast and viewing angle that the others can’t match.”

CNET editors and readers highly recommend LG. But other brands were close runners-up. If you’re looking for deep black levels and strong color reproduction, readers recommend Sony as a second contender. Or if you’re struggling to watch TV in a room with a big window, consider TCL or Samsung — all CNET favorites.

“I’ve always liked Roku and Google TV better than proprietary systems from Samsung and LG, and I’m happy to see that CNET readers took our advice and bought LG and Samsung OLED TVs — because they’re the picture-quality champs,” said Katzmaier.

CNET has plenty of reviews of some of the latest TVs, like the TCL QM8L, if you’re looking for a brighter TV, or the Samsung S90F, if you’re looking for the best value for overall picture quality. Regardless, there are also guides to help narrow down your TV choice, like choosing between LCD and OLED TVs, what to know about micro-LED and a list of everything to look for when buying a new TV.

Did you like these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing mobile carriers survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Tech.title: From Audio Glasses to Earbuds With Cameras, Headphones Are Getting a Major AI Rebrand
Tech.content:
You’ve likely noticed AI has increasingly been sneaking into more of your new devices over the past few years, whether you asked for it or not. The next frontier? It’s time to ready yourself for an influx of AI-powered headphones.

On Wednesday at its Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, Qualcomm announced the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 chip, which will bring new features to audio wearables, or “hearables,” as they’re sometimes referred to in the tech industry. These might look and feel like the audio products you’ve been strapping to your head for many years, but they’ll have a whole different set of features and capabilities.

Plaud One brings AI note-taking to headphones. Plaud/CNET

Some might use AI to provide you with a better sound experience, improving music quality and making your headphones able to more intelligently adapt to your world – identifying an approaching siren and lowering the volume of your music so you know not to step onto the road, for example. Others might use AI to enable real-time translation as a conduit for interacting with agents or for note-taking, like the recently revealed Plaud One. Hidden use case C could enable so-called multimodal interactions – for example, combining audio with vision and AI in audio-forward glasses or headphones with cameras.

Qualcomm envisages the Sound Elite Gen 2 chip being used in a range of different audio devices. These include the usual suspects – earbuds, headphones, open-ear and hybrid audio devices. But it also says they can be used in audio glasses and “future multimodal wearables” – a vague term that can be broadly interpreted as new types of product that haven’t been invented yet.

Qualcomm’s chips are designed both with specific devices in mind and for companies to run with and build something new. Just take last year’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5: It was designed for top Android phones, such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, but it was also used by Honor to build its Robot Phone – a novel handset with a built-in robotic gimbal.

While there’s some level of predictability to the types of devices the Sound Elite Gen 2 will feature in, the platform is also open-ended enough for companies to use it in ways even Qualcomm hasn’t foreseen. Ziad Asghar, a senior vice president at the company, said that he’s surprised “all the time” at what the chipmaker’s partners dream up.

“The innovation [in] form factor right now is still morphing, it’s still changing,” he said. “We don’t know what end product [the chip] might even go into.”

What’s new in the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 Chip?

The footprint of this latest Sound Elite chip is 30% smaller than that of its predecessor, as well as having double the AI capability and offering up to 40% lower power consumption. This combination of being smaller, more powerful and more power efficient is the chip upgrade trifecta, but what difference will that actually make?

Qualcomm thinks it will move you closer to your personal AI future. This is the idea that thanks to your always-sensing, always-on galaxy of devices – which could include your watch, phone, glasses, earbuds, car and home tech – the combination of constant context capture and AI agents will enable better understanding of your wants and needs.

The new chip will enable next-generation AI wearables.

Hearables play an important role in bringing the vision for personal AI to life because they sit close to your ears and mouth, allowing for both input and output of audio.

“As AI becomes a core capability, users will increasingly expect more natural ways to interact with it,” said Asghar, speaking at the Snapdragon Summit. “Those interactions won’t always happen through a screen. They will happen through natural conversations, where users can simply speak to an AI assistant and receive help in real time.”

Another technical aspect of making this happen is the Sound Elite Gen 2 chip’s direct-to-cloud connectivity, enabled by micro-power Wi-Fi 6E. This technology was designed to give Wi-Fi connectivity with the power of Bluetooth inside tiny products. For the generation included in this chip, Qualcomm has reduced the power requirements even further and increased the speed to provide always-on availability.

Additionally, the chip will include Qualcomm aptX Lossless – an audio quality boost to appease the audiophiles among us – and Qualcomm XPAN, which extends connectivity beyond the range you’d typically expect from Bluetooth. Qualcomm is also deploying AI to improve active noise cancellation, speech capture and voice clarity by providing more advanced support for multiple mics.

Keep your ear to the ground for devices making use of this chip for more personalized and intelligent audio experiences – and remember, they might not look exactly how you expect them to.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs were covered by Qualcomm. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Disney Plus and Hulu Prices Go Up, With Ad-Free Plans Hit the Hardest
Tech.content:
Mickey Mouse is taking a bigger bite out of your wallet. Disney Plus and Hulu subscription prices are going up by about $2 per month, with the biggest increases on premium ad-free plans.

As detailed on this help page, the Disney Plus-Hulu Premium bundle will cost $22 per month (up from $20), Hulu Premium will cost $21.49 (up from $19), and Disney Plus Premium will cost $21.49, too (also up from $19). The price hike takes effect on Wednesday for new subscribers, and current subscribers will see the increase on their next bill.

The most expensive plan — Disney Plus, Hulu, ESPN Unlimited Bundle Premium — remains at $45 per month.

Nonpremium subscriptions went up less than a dollar, with Disney Plus and Hulu each costing $12.49. Those plans cost $12 previously.

The price hikes come exactly one year after Disney’s last price increases. This is the fourth time in four years that subscription prices have gone up for both Disney Plus and Hulu.

Streaming channels will continue to raise prices while trying to lure subscribers with lower-cost plans that include ads, but Disney “needs to tread carefully,” says tech analyst Paolo Pescatore.

“Like Netflix, Disney has some leeway to raise prices given the breadth of its offering and the strength of its brands,” Pescatore told CNET. “But consumers are becoming more selective, further increasing risk and encouraging more people to dip in and out rather than remain permanently subscribed.”

Disney has run Hulu since 2019 and took full control of the streaming service in 2025.

Disney plans to launch a single app combining both services by the end of the year, outgoing CEO Bob Iger said at the company’s Q1 earnings call in February. Currently, Disney Plus and Hulu each have their own apps, but Hulu subscribers can watch most of their content in the Disney Plus app by linking to their account.

Disney Plus ranks third among the top streaming channels in the US, behind Netflix and Amazon Prime. Combined with Hulu, which is sixth, they make up nearly one-quarter of all streams among subscription services.

Tech.title: The FAA Is Testing an AI-Powered Air Traffic Management Tool
Tech.content:
For years, there have been shortages of air traffic control personnel, leading to delays and congestion. To remedy these troubles, the Federal Aviation Administration and the US Department of Transportation are turning to a new tool: AI.

On Monday, these agencies announced that they’re beginning a trial of the new system, called Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories, at three airports around the nation’s capital – Reagan National Airport, Dulles International Airport and BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport.

This $875 million software overhaul is not a replacement for human air traffic control operators, the DOT said, but is intended to reduce pressure on personnel by predicting delays and cancellations, and providing recommendations to the humans who retain control over flight operations.

Margaret Wallace, an assistant professor of aviation management at the Florida Institute of Technology, said meaningful action is necessary to address the aging air traffic control infrastructure, and calls to modernize the system have been ongoing – yet unanswered – for years.

While SMART is an important first step, she says, it “does not eliminate the human element,” and controllers need to remain at the forefront of every stage of implementation.

“If implemented carefully, however, the technology behind this initiative has the potential to begin a significant transformation in the efficiency and modernization of the US air traffic system,” Wallace said in an email.

How the SMART system works

It may be alarming to read “artificial intelligence” and “air traffic management” in the same sentence. So let’s unpack what this system actually is before deciding to never get on another flight again.

Each day, the FAA manages close to 45,000 flights in the US. Even slight delays, changes in weather conditions, and reroutes can lead to airspace congestion and overcapacity. SMART was designed to centralize 200 data streams of flight paths, wind, weather, staffing metrics and more into one platform for a comprehensive overview of what’s happening in the sky and on the ground at airports for better management of these flights.

From this consolidated data, human controllers can “anticipate demand, weather and airspace constraints and plan hours, days and even weeks ahead,” according to the press release.

The US DOT says these measures are to upgrade “the FAA from a reactive approach to a predictive one.”

“By fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace and preventing problems before they happen, SMART will slash those frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers and lower travel prices,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement.

Will it actually help? It’s too early to tell, and the union representing air traffic controllers said it was not involved in the program’s development.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association said in a statement it “believes any new technology should complement and not replace the experience, training and professional judgment of air traffic controllers who are responsible for the safety of the National Airspace System.”

The system was built by a company called Air Space Intelligence, an aerospace and defense AI company based in the US that has already partnered with the US Air Force, major US airlines (Alaska Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines) and the Department of Defense.

In the press release announcing the rollout of the air traffic management system, CEOs from top airlines, including United, Delta, American and Southwest, expressed encouragement over the initiative.

Still, air traffic experts emphasize the importance of remaining cautious as this new system rolls out.

“My biggest initial concern is controller training and human-factors integration,” Wallace said. “That is not necessarily a criticism of this particular system; it is a challenge that comes with introducing any significant new technology into a complex, safety-critical environment.

“FAA leadership will need to ensure that implementation and testing are deliberate, that controllers receive adequate training and that appropriate safeguards remain in place throughout the transition,” she said.

The FAA plans to gradually expand SMART to other airports across the country.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI Agent Has Been Downloaded Half a Million Times — With a Serious Bug
Tech.content:
If you’ve seen a cartoonish character at the top of your Instagram feed lately, that’s Muse. Meta’s newest AI agent, or bot, wants to be your digital assistant. But Meta had to rush to patch a serious zero-day bug in Muse’s code this week, highlighting just how treacherous it can be to hand over the keys to your digital life to agentic AI.

Patrick Wardle, founder of the cybersecurity firm Objective-See, was the first to spot the zero-day bug. He outlined the vulnerability in X posts, showing how a bad actor could trick the AI agent into sending a person’s Muse dictations, or audio captures, and access tokens to their own malicious server, not Meta’s servers. Wardle has a long history of finding bugs in Meta’s software.

The head of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, David Singleton, replied to Wardle’s X post on Tuesday to confirm the company has patched the vulnerability. He added that the bug required malware to already be on a user’s computer for the exploit to work; Wardle disagrees, saying it is possible for a hacker to exploit this flaw remotely.

To prevent your Muse AI agent from being hacked, update your MacOS Muse app right now. This will ensure you’re running the latest version of the program, including the new security fix. No additional action is needed from you.

A one-off bug or persistent pattern?

Singleton wrote of the incident: “We strive to be extremely transparent about privacy and security in Muse as we know this is important to maintain your trust.” We absolutely need tech companies to be transparent, but there is still a lot unknown about AI agents like Muse.

At first glance, Muse has had a successful entrance into an already crowded field of AI agents, including those from OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Anthropic. The MacOS app was downloaded more than half a million times during its first week, according to internal data seen by The Information, making it one of the more popular AI agent choices. But to get the most value out of your AI agent, you need to grant it permission to access a lot of different things. To have Muse make you a dinner reservation, for example, it needs to be able to use your computer, access the web and potentially use your credit card info to hold the table.

Privacy and security concerns are two of the most serious concerns with generative AI. No tech company has fully addressed all the various harms that will come from AI, be it cybersecurity hacks or losing control over our personal information used by the AI. But Meta has a longer track record than most AI startups, and its history isn’t the most reassuring. Just consider the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal that revealed millions of Facebook users’ data had been used improperly, or its more recent court battle and settlement over failing to protect children online.

These security reports come ahead of Wednesday’s Meta Connect, where CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to show us more about how the company is thinking about AI and AI hardware. Meta Connect has traditionally focused on Meta’s smart glasses, but rising public backlash has cast a lot of doubt on the long-term viability of the devices, sometimes dubbed “pervert glasses” due to their recording capabilities.

If Meta is going to continue down the agentic AI path, tech users need to be able to trust the company to build it responsibly. But the public’s faith in AI companies has dwindled in recent days, thanks to AI researchers airing concerns that the technology could lead to the extinction of humanity.

Tech.title: Apple’s Clever New iPhone Feature Will Cost $5 on T-Mobile, Is Coming to Verizon – and AT&T Isn’t Interested
Tech.content:
You might not need to use it much, but Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature in iOS 27 is certainly convenient: Easily switch between two iPhones using a single phone number, activating it on whichever phone is unlocked. Your texts, calls, voicemails and Find My location automatically follow you to the phone in use.

At launch, however, the feature is supported only by T-Mobile in the US, and the carrier is charging $5 a month to use it. And while Verizon support is expected by the end of the year, AT&T appears to be sitting this feature out for now.

iPhone Handoff is similar to what the Apple Watch has done with data for a few generations, where taking off one watch and putting on another automatically switches all of your information, such as activity tracking, to it. For example, some people use one watch during the day — perhaps the rugged Apple Watch Ultra — and switch to a slimmer, older Apple Watch at night, allowing the first to charge for the morning.

But replicating that behavior to the iPhone requires coordination with cellular providers. Each phone’s eSIM needs to be configured for iPhone Handoff by a carrier, and service needs to switch cleanly on the network side.

Ironically, the Apple Watch gets left out of the iPhone Handoff transaction: Your watch remains paired with just one watch, communicating with it via Wi-Fi or cellular (if that’s an option). “If neither is available,” Apple writes, “calls, messages, notifications, certain health and fitness features, Siri AI or other app experiences relayed from your paired iPhone may not be available.”

In its press release about offering the iPhone 18 Pro, T-Mobile writes, “iPhone Handoff is available on any iPhone with iOS 27 via iPhone settings and ready to use from day one on the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iPhone Duo. T-Mobile is introducing the feature at $5/month.”

When I reached out to T-Mobile asking about the charge, a spokesperson wrote via email, “The $5/month charge reflects the added service that powers the experience on both devices.”

While iPhone Handoff appears to seamlessly switch your eSIM just by picking up the phone you want to use, it’s not yet clear what else is different with this process versus just transferring your eSIM manually using your iPhone’s settings menu.

Notably absent from Apple’s news was the other major US carrier, AT&T. I contacted a spokesperson there to learn more about the company’s plans for the feature, but it sounds like it’s not a priority.

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

In addition to T-Mobile, iPhone Handoff is currently supported by Telekom in Germany. The UK carrier EE will also support the feature later this year, according to Apple.

A Verizon representative confirmed the projected timeline for support but did not have further details to share.
